lectures.name: Neuroanatomy of the Brainstem, Basal Ganglia, and Diencephalon
lectures.title: Neuroanatomy of the brainstem, basal ganglia and diencephalon
lectures.framing: Four deep structures, each with one job to learn: the basal ganglia choose which movement goes ahead, the diencephalon relays and regulates, the brainstem carries the tracts and the cranial nerve nuclei (III to XII), and the cerebellum coordinates the same side of the body. For the brainstem, the question is always which level, and which part of that level, because that decides what a lesion takes out.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Direct pathway (D1) releases the thalamus = GO; indirect pathway (D2, through the GPe and subthalamic nucleus) inhibits it = STOP. Lose nigral dopamine → Parkinson bradykinesia; lose the striatum → Huntington chorea. The subthalamic nucleus is the only excitatory basal ganglia nucleus. Ventral medulla lesion → contralateral hemiparesis; lateral medulla → ipsilateral face pain and temperature loss. Motor nuclei medial, sensory lateral to the sulcus limitans. CN IV leaves the back of the midbrain. A midline (vermis) cerebellar lesion gives truncal ataxia; the cerebellum works on the same side.

blocks.html: 1. Basal ganglia: the parts
Deep forebrain nuclei inside the cerebral white matter that integrate cortical activity into one motor output (also roles in cognition, learning and emotion).

• Formed from: caudate nucleus (arches over the thalamus) · putamen · globus pallidus · amygdala · the substantia nigra of the midbrain also influences them
  • Striatum = caudate + putamen = the input (receives excitatory glutamate from the cortex)
    • putamen = mostly movement (from sensory and motor cortex) · caudate = more cognitive (from association cortex)
    • nucleus accumbens = the ventral striatum
  • Lentiform nucleus = putamen + globus pallidus · the internal capsule separates them from the caudate and thalamus
  • Globus pallidus external (GPe) = relay of the indirect pathway · globus pallidus internal (GPi) = the output to the thalamus
  • Subthalamic nucleus (STN) = the only excitatory (glutamate) nucleus · every other basal ganglia projection is GABA (inhibitory)
  • Substantia nigra pars compacta (midbrain) sends dopamine to the striatum (mostly the putamen) and tunes both pathways
2. Direct vs indirect pathway

blocks.lead: The thalamus is under constant inhibition from the GPi. Release-inhibition model: the direct pathway releases the thalamus (inhibits the inhibitor) → more cortical output; the indirect pathway adds inhibition → less cortical output.
rows: Cortex → striatum ⊣ GPi ⊣ thalamus → cortex (bypasses the STN)
Released (ventral anterior and ventral lateral nuclei → supplementary motor and premotor cortex)
Parkinson disease: substantia nigra dopamine lost → direct pathway hypoactive (and the indirect one released) → GPi overactive → thalamus over-inhibited → bradykinesia, akinesia
Huntington disease: caudate and putamen degenerate → indirect pathway lost → STN and GPi under-active → involuntary movements (chorea)

blocks.html: (→ excites · ⊣ inhibits) · The opposite imbalance (STN and GPi too inhibited, thalamus too free) causes the hyperkinetic disorders and drug-induced dyskinesias in Parkinson disease.

blocks.cap: Direct pathway: the striatum inhibits the internal globus pallidus, releasing the thalamus to drive the motor cortex
Indirect pathway: through the external globus pallidus and subthalamic nucleus, ending in more inhibition of the thalamus

blocks.html: 3. Diencephalon

blocks.lead: The centre core of the forebrain, surrounded by the cerebral hemispheres · paired, mostly grey matter · borders the third ventricle.
rows: Middle of the brain · 80% of the diencephalon · ~a dozen nuclei

The relay ("gateway") to the cortex: every part of the brain that talks to the cerebral cortex relays through a thalamic nucleus · sensory nuclei for every conscious sense except smell · organizes, amplifies or tones down signals
Between the optic chiasm and the mammillary bodies · pituitary hangs below · ~a dozen nuclei
Main visceral control centre ("the master gland's master"): autonomic system · emotion · temperature · hunger, thirst · behaviour · sleep-wake · endocrine control · memory
Secretes melatonin (under the hypothalamus) → circadian rhythm, sleep at night

blocks.html:
• Thalamic nuclei on the slide: anterior · medial · pulvinar · lateral geniculate (vision) · medial geniculate (hearing) · ventral posterolateral (body sensation) · ventral posteromedial (face sensation) · ventral lateral · ventral anterior (motor loops)
  • Hypothalamus, by function (homeostasis): hunger · satiety · cooling + parasympathetic · heating + sympathetic · circadian rhythm · makes ADH and oxytocin · thermoregulation, sexual behaviour, releases GnRH
4. Brainstem: surfaces and levels

blocks.lead: Rostral → caudal: midbrain → pons → medulla, in the posterior cranial fossa. Three jobs: a passageway for the tracts between cerebrum and cord · 10 of the 12 cranial nerves attach (face and neck) · automatic survival behaviours. The fourth ventricle lies between the pons and cerebellum; the cord's central canal opens into it at the obex.
rows: Tectum (roof, behind the cerebral aqueduct) · tegmentum · substantia nigra · cerebral peduncles
Superior colliculi = visual reflexes (saccades, eye and head turning) · inferior colliculi = auditory relay
Tegmentum: tracts, cranial nerve nuclei, reticular formation, red nucleus, mesencephalic nucleus of V · substantia nigra (melanin, a by-product of dopamine)
Basal pons: pontine nuclei relay the cortex to the opposite cerebellum (crossing into the middle cerebellar peduncle) · corticospinal, corticobulbar, corticopontine fibres
Tegmentum: tracts, cranial nerve nuclei, reticular formation
Fasciculus gracilis + cuneatus (posterior columns) · obex · inferior cerebellar peduncle

blocks.lead: The medulla's three areas, and what a lesion of each does:
rows: Corticospinal tract · ~85% cross at the pyramidal decussation (caudal medulla) → lateral corticospinal tract; the uncrossed rest → ventral corticospinal tract
Contralateral hemiparesis of the body (medial medullary syndrome)
Olive (inferior olivary nucleus → opposite cerebellum, motor learning) · spinal tract + nucleus of V
Ipsilateral loss of pain and temperature from the face (lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome)
Gracile + cuneate fasciculi and nuclei (proprioception, fine touch, vibration) → cross as the medial lemniscus

blocks.html:
• Reticular formation: lateral (small cells) runs cranial-nerve reflexes (eating, eye movements) · medial (large cells) projects long tracts for pain, posture, autonomic function, arousal and consciousness · also central pattern generators
  • Tracts passing through: up - spinothalamic, posterior column-medial lemniscus, spinocerebellar · down - corticospinal, corticobulbar (synapses bilaterally on cranial motor nuclei)
5. Cranial nerves: where they leave, and their nuclei

blocks.lead: Rule of 4s: above the pons I, II (forebrain), III, IV (midbrain) · pons V, VI, VII, VIII · medulla IX, X, XI, XII
rows: Back (dorsal surface) of the midbrain, just below the inferior colliculus, then curves around it
Side of the pons, at the middle cerebellar peduncle
Pontomedullary junction, between pyramid and pons
Side of the pontomedullary junction (VII medial) = the cerebellopontine angle, common site of an acoustic neuroma (vestibular schwannoma)
From the cervical cord (C1-5), up through the foramen magnum
Medulla, between pyramid and olive (pre-olivary groove)

blocks.html:
• Functional groups: sensory I, II, VIII · motor III, IV, VI, XI, XII · mixed V, VII, IX, X (more than one nucleus each)
  • Nuclei form discontinuous columns: motor nuclei MEDIAL to the sulcus limitans, sensory nuclei LATERAL

rows: Oculomotor (III, superior colliculus level) · trochlear (IV, inferior colliculus level) · abducens (VI, mid-pons) · hypoglossal (XII, medulla)
Edinger-Westphal (III) · superior salivatory (VII) · inferior salivatory (IX) · dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus (X)
Trigeminal motor (V, rostral pons) · facial motor (VII, caudal pons) · nucleus ambiguus (IX, X) - most parasympathetic fibres to the heart · accessory (XI, C1-5)
Solitary nucleus: rostral = taste (VII, IX, X) · caudal = visceral (IX, X)
Vestibular + cochlear (VIII), caudal pons and rostral medulla
Mesencephalic (midbrain) · principal sensory (rostral pons) · spinal nucleus + tract (caudal pons to medulla; also takes VII, IX, X)

blocks.html: • Trigeminal sensation, face → cortex: pain and temperature → spinal tract of V → spinal nucleus of V → cross (trigeminothalamic fibres) → ventral posteromedial (VPM) thalamus → postcentral gyrus (areas 3, 1, 2) · proprioception from the chewing muscles, jaw joint and teeth → cell bodies in the mesencephalic nucleus

blocks.cap: The brainstem cranial nerve nuclei: motor columns medial to the sulcus limitans, sensory columns lateral

blocks.html: • Facial nerve (VII) leaves at the pontomedullary junction: facial motor nucleus → facial expression · superior salivatory → lacrimal, submandibular, sublingual glands · solitary → taste, front 2/3 of the tongue · spinal trigeminal → skin of the outer ear
6. Cerebellum

• In the posterior cranial fossa, under the tentorium cerebelli · the fourth ventricle separates it from the pons · develops from the pons · joined to the brainstem by three peduncles
  • Surface = folia (not gyri) · cortex outside, white matter (arbor vitae), deep cerebellar nuclei inside: fastigial, interposed, dentate (medial → lateral, smallest → largest)
  • Peduncles: superior → midbrain and diencephalon · middle (largest) → pons · inferior → medulla and spinal cord
  • Vermis (midline) · hemispheres · tonsils · flocculus
  • Controls muscles on the SAME side (input from the same side of the cord) - unlike the motor cortex · compares the planned movement with body position and ongoing movement, then corrects the cortex · motor memory

rows: Coordinates and corrects trunk and limb movement · vermis = trunk and proximal limbs · intermediate zone = distal limbs
Streamlines cortical output · motor planning for the limbs
Balance, vestibulo-ocular reflex, trunk and limb stability

lectures.name: Neuroanatomy of the Spinal Tracts and Cerebellum
lectures.title: Neuroanatomy of the spinal tracts and cerebellum
lectures.framing: Every tract question comes down to two facts: what it carries, and where it crosses. Put those together and a lesion's level and side tell you which modalities go, and on which side, which is how the tracts localize lesions in the cord, brainstem and cortex.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Dorsal columns cross in the medulla, spinothalamic fibres cross in the cord where they enter, and the lateral corticospinal tract crosses at the pyramids, so a one-sided cord lesion takes vibration, position sense and power on its own side but pain and temperature on the other. Gracilis = medial = below T6; cuneatus = lateral = above T6. Spinocerebellar tracts end on the same side. Lateral system = contralateral, distal limbs, skilled; medial system = bilateral, axial, posture. Sensory = 3 neurons through the thalamus; motor = 2 neurons, UMN and LMN.

blocks.html: 1. How the pathways are built

• Afferent = toward the central nervous system (CNS) (ascending, sensory) · efferent = away from it (descending, motor) · in the CNS cell bodies sit in nuclei and axons run in tracts; in the peripheral nervous system (PNS) they sit in ganglia (e.g. the dorsal root ganglion) and run in nerves
  • A pathway is a chain of neurons · bilateral (one each side) · named origin → destination (spinothalamic = spinal cord → thalamus) · most decussate (cross the midline): ipsilateral = same side, contralateral = opposite side
  • Spinal cord: 31 pairs of spinal nerves (8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, 1 coccygeal) · the cord ends at the L1/L2 vertebra · ascending tracts mostly in the dorsal (back) compartment and the edge of the cord, descending tracts in the lateral and ventral white matter
  • Sensory chain = 3 neurons
    • 1st order: pseudounipolar, cell body in the dorsal root ganglion (PNS), axon into the CNS
    • 2nd order: cell body in the dorsal horn or a brainstem nucleus; its axon crosses and synapses in the opposite thalamus
    • 3rd order: cell body in the ventral posterior nucleus of the thalamus → internal capsule (posterior limb) → primary somatosensory cortex (postcentral gyrus)
  • Motor chain = 2 neurons: upper motor neuron (UMN), cell body in the cerebral hemispheres or brainstem, axon usually crosses → lower motor neuron (LMN), cell body in a cranial nerve motor nucleus (face) or the ventral horn (body) → cranial or spinal nerve → skeletal muscle

blocks.alt: spinal cord cross-section ascending and descending tracts - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: Spinal cord cross-section: ascending tracts (blue) and descending tracts (red)

blocks.html: 2. The three ascending pathways

rows: Fine touch, vibration, pressure, conscious proprioception
Brainstem (caudal medulla): internal arcuate fibres → medial lemniscus
Lost on the same side, below the lesion
Spinal cord, at the level of entry (anterior white commissure)
Primary somatosensory cortex + cingulate and insular cortex
Lost on the opposite side, below the lesion
Posterior: never → inferior cerebellar peduncle · anterior: not at all, or twice (cord + superior cerebellar peduncle)

blocks.html:
• Dorsal columns: fasciculus gracilis is medial = below T6 (lower limb and trunk) · fasciculus cuneatus is lateral = above T6 (upper limb and neck) · first-order axons climb the same side to the caudal medulla, the second-order axons cross as the internal arcuate fibres and climb as the medial lemniscus to the ventral posterior lateral (VPL) thalamus
  • Spinothalamic: the first-order neuron synapses straight away in the dorsal horn; the second-order axon crosses immediately in the anterior white commissure and climbs the opposite side to the thalamus
  • Somatosensory cortex = postcentral gyrus of the parietal lobe, mapped as a homunculus (lips, tongue, hand large)

blocks.alt: medulla oblongata cross-section (nucleus gracilis, nucleus cuneatus, and medial lamniscus).png
blocks.cap: The medulla: nucleus gracilis and cuneatus send fibres across the midline to form the medial lemniscus

blocks.html: 3. Lower motor neurons: where they sit

• Face: cell bodies in cranial nerve nuclei of the brainstem → axons in cranial nerves
  • Body: cell bodies in the ventral horn → ventral root → spinal nerve → peripheral nerve
  • Medial motor column: every spinal level · axial muscles (posture, balance) · lateral motor column: cervical and lumbosacral cord only · limb muscles (skilled movement) · both act on the same side
  • The LMN is the final common pathway: it integrates every descending tract (cortex, red nucleus, reticular formation, vestibular nuclei) and sensory input into one signal to the muscle
4. Descending (UMN) pathways: lateral vs medial

rows: Medial motor column → axial and proximal limb muscles

blocks.html:
• Lateral corticospinal tract (the largest and clinically most important motor pathway): primary motor cortex (precentral gyrus, Brodmann area 4, plus premotor and sensory areas) → posterior limb of the internal capsule → crus cerebri → pons → pyramids → crosses at the pyramidal decussation (medulla-cord junction) → lateral funiculus → LMNs of the lateral motor column (cervical and lumbosacral enlargements) → opposite-side limb muscles · needed for individual finger movements
  • Corticobulbar tract: primary motor cortex → cranial nerve motor nuclei, with a bilateral distribution of UMN fibres → face and head muscles
  • Motor map (primary motor cortex): face lateral → fingers, hand, arm, trunk → legs on the medial surface

blocks.cap: Corticobulbar pathway: motor cortex to the cranial nerve motor nuclei in the pons and medulla

blocks.html: 5. Cerebellum: the connections

• Peduncles: superior → midbrain · middle → pons · inferior → medulla
  • In: spinocerebellar tracts (inferior and superior peduncles)
  • Out: the major output is relayed through the ventral thalamus

lectures.name: Neurophysiology of Sensation
lectures.title: Neurophysiology of sensation
lectures.framing: Each skin receptor reports one kind of touch down its own "labelled line", and two pathways carry sensation to the cortex: one crossing in the medulla, one in the cord. That split is what lets you predict the side of a deficit after a one-sided cord lesion.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Touch and proprioception cross in the medulla; pain and temperature cross in the cord where they enter, so a cord hemisection loses touch and position sense on the lesion's side and pain and temperature on the other. Pacinian = vibration (rapid, large), Meissner = fine texture (rapid, small), Merkel = edges (slow, small), Ruffini = stretch and finger position (slow, large). Test pain or temperature, not touch, to map a dermatome. Burning and freezing are felt by nociceptors. Cuneate = arm, gracile = leg.

blocks.html: 1. Receptors in the skin

• Skin mechanoreceptors respond to physical distortion (bending, stretching) and differ by depth in the skin, structure and rate of adaptation
  • Touch is needed for fine motor control: a nerve block of the fingertips (which spares the muscle receptors) makes delicate tasks clumsy

rows: Meissner corpuscle (stacked flat cells, mainly hairless skin)

blocks.html:
• Deep receptors have larger receptive fields because skin compression over a wide area reaches them
  • Hair follicle receptors (free nerve endings wrapped around follicles, very sensitive): localized flutter, a bug landing on the skin
  • Nociceptors (pain), two kinds of free nerve ending
    • on a myelinated axon: fast → early, localized, intense pain that can start a withdrawal reflex
    • on an unmyelinated axon: slow → later, diffuse, long-lasting pain (dull, throbbing)
  • Thermoreceptors: heat-sensitive (hot, not burning) · cold-sensitive (cold, not freezing) · burning or freezing stimuli activate nociceptors

blocks.cap: Skin receptors by depth: Merkel disc and Meissner corpuscle near the surface, Pacinian corpuscle and Ruffini ending deep in the dermis

blocks.html: 2. How a stimulus is coded

• Mechanotransduction (Pacinian corpuscle): pressure deforms the capsule → mechanically sensitive ion channels open → receptor potential → an action potential if it reaches threshold
  • Frequency coding: a stronger, longer stimulus → a higher-rate train of action potentials that lasts longer
  • Every receptor responds quickly at onset; they differ in how fast they adapt to continued pressure
  • Labelled line coding: each receptor has its own "private line", so the brain knows which receptor type an axon carries · perception depends on which axon fires, not on how it was stimulated · banging the funny bone fires the ulnar nerve at the elbow and the fingers tingle
3. The two pathways

rows: Large dorsal root axons climb the same side in the dorsal columns → cuneate nucleus (arm) or gracile nucleus (leg) in the medulla
Small dorsal root axons synapse in the spinal grey matter at the level of entry

blocks.html:
• Somatotopy in the dorsal columns: new afferents join laterally as the cord ascends, so at high cervical levels leg fibres are medial, trunk in the middle, arm lateral
  • At the dorsal column nuclei (the first synapse), convergence and centre-surround inhibition reshape the signal: a stimulus in the centre of the field excites the neuron and one in the surround inhibits it through an interneuron, sharpening edges (as in the retina) · many afferents converging on one neuron = a large field and poor acuity (two-point discrimination on the back vs the fingertip)

blocks.alt: dorsal column-medial lemniscus vs spinothalamic pathway - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: Dorsal column-medial lemniscus pathway (crossing in the medulla) beside the spinothalamic tract (crossing in the spinal cord)

blocks.html: 4. Clinical use

• Cord hemisection (Brown-Sequard syndrome): the two pathways climb in different columns and cross at different levels, so a right hemisection cuts
    • fine touch and proprioception from lower segments on the right (same side)
    • pain and temperature from lower segments on the left (opposite side)
  • Dermatome = the skin supplied by one spinal nerve · neighbours overlap, more for touch than for pain and temperature → test pain or temperature to find the level of a segmental nerve injury
5. Primary somatosensory cortex

• S1 = areas 3a, 3b, 1 and 2 on the postcentral gyrus, each with its own distorted body map (the sensory homunculus) · fingers and lips are over-represented, like the fovea in vision · the posterior parietal cortex (areas 5, 7) lies behind it
  • Each area extracts a different feature

rows: Size and shape of objects · preferred-direction cells

blocks.html: • Higher somatosensory areas represent increasingly complex features, as in vision

lectures.name: Neurophysiology of the Cerebellum and Basal Ganglia
lectures.title: Neurophysiology of the cerebellum and basal ganglia
lectures.framing: Two side loops tune movement without commanding it: the cerebellum corrects errors and teaches motor skills, the basal ganglia release the wanted movement and suppress the rest. Damage gives movement disorders with normal power, and the tremor, the tone and the course tell a cerebellar lesion from Parkinson disease.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Cerebellar disease = can start but inaccurate, intention tremor, low tone, same-side signs, stable or improving; Parkinson disease = can't start, rest tremor, rigidity, progressive; and neither is an upper motor neuron disorder. Vestibulocerebellum = balance and nystagmus · spinocerebellum = gait and tone · cerebrocerebellum = dysmetria and intention tremor. Purkinje cells are the only output of the cerebellar cortex, and they inhibit. Climbing fibres teach. Dopamine turns the direct pathway up and the indirect down; Huntington disease loses the indirect pathway; too much L-dopa over-drives the direct pathway; both give chorea.

blocks.html: 1. Side loops in the motor system

• Both take input from wide areas of the cerebral cortex and send output through the thalamus back to the sensorimotor cortex; both also project to the brainstem
  • They do not contribute directly to the descending tracts, so they have no upper motor neurons → not upper motor neuron (UMN) disorders
2. Cerebellum: what it does

• Corrects errors in movement commands and imparts motor skills · in: motor, somatosensory and parietal association cortex, plus sensory input from the brainstem and cord · out: corrections to motor cortex (through the ventral lateral thalamus), brainstem and cord
  • Cortex folded into folia and deep fissures, which hold half of all the neurons in the brain

rows: Vestibular organs → vestibular nuclei → eye, limb, trunk muscles
Wide-based ataxic gait (looks drunk) · Romberg sign: imbalance worse with eyes closed · nystagmus
Vision, hearing, skin and muscle afferents → fastigial (vermis) or interposed (intermediate) nucleus → spinal cord
Ataxic gait (poor leg control) · falls walking heel-to-toe ("drunk-driver test") · hypotonia
Copy of the cortex's motor command → dentate nucleus → motor and premotor cortex
Ataxia in skilled movement · dysmetria (inaccurate) · dyssynergia (segments poorly coordinated) · intention tremor · fails finger-to-nose

blocks.html: • Cerebrocerebellar deficits present on the SAME (ipsilateral) side (often one-sided, depending on the lesion) · intention tremor comes near the end of a movement, from over-responses of the long-loop reflex through the motor cortex

blocks.alt: cerebellum functional zones vermis intermediate lateral - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: Cerebellum from behind: vermis, intermediate and lateral zones; anterior, posterior and flocculonodular lobes

blocks.html: 3. The cerebellar circuit and motor learning
The basic circuit is the same everywhere in the cerebellum, with three parts:

1. Direct path: sensory input → deep cerebellar nuclei (or vestibular nucleus) → motor systems

2. Mossy fibres → granule cells → parallel fibres → Purkinje cells: a weak, widely broadcast signal (~200,000 parallel fibres reach one Purkinje cell)

3. Climbing fibres → Purkinje cells: the error signal ("something needs to change") · one climbing fibre per Purkinje cell, many synapses · it modifies the parallel-fibre connection

• Purkinje cells INHIBIT the deep cerebellar (or vestibular) nuclei, and that is the only output of the cerebellar cortex
  • Climbing fibre = the teacher, parallel fibre = the student: that is motor learning
    • Vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR): turning the head turns the eyes equally the other way (a 3-neuron reflex: semicircular canal → vestibular nucleus → eye muscle). When the image slips on the retina (ageing, new glasses), climbing fibres report it and change the Purkinje output onto the vestibular nucleus, re-tuning the reflex's gain; they stop firing once there is no slip
    • Prism goggles: healthy subjects adapt their dart throws and show an after-effect when the prisms come off · cerebellar patients show no adaptation and no after-effect
  • The "repair shop": it masks motor disorders from lesions elsewhere, so cerebellar lesions themselves cause longer-lasting disorders
4. Basal ganglia: release and suppress

• Release appropriate movements and suppress inappropriate ones from the premotor and motor cortex · damage contributes to Tourette syndrome (inappropriate utterances released)
  • In: frontal, parietal and temporal cortex converge on the striatum (caudate + putamen) · out: the globus pallidus (external and internal segments) → ventral anterior / ventral lateral thalamus → motor cortex
  • Modulators: the subthalamic nucleus (reciprocally connected with the globus pallidus) and substantia nigra pars compacta (dopamine to the striatum) · the substantia nigra pars reticulata projects to the superior colliculus for eye movements
  • Disinhibition is the core idea: at rest the globus pallidus fires steadily and inhibits the thalamus

rows: The same, plus an extra inhibitory synapse in the globus pallidus and a side loop through the subthalamic nucleus
Striatum inhibits the globus pallidus → disinhibits the thalamus → excites UMNs in motor cortex → releases the movement

blocks.html: 5. Basal ganglia disorders

rows: Too much inhibition → too little drive back to premotor and motor cortex
Spontaneous movements (chorea), as in Huntington disease

blocks.html:
• L-dopa = a dopamine precursor that crosses the blood-brain barrier, the treatment for Parkinson disease
  • In Parkinson disease, well-practised or externally cued actions can be spared (a patient who freezes walking can ride a bike), from residual dopamine or circuits less dependent on the basal ganglia
6. Cerebellar disease vs Parkinson disease

rows: Ataxia: movements can start, but are inaccurate (dysmetria) and poorly coordinated (dyssynergia)
Akinesia: often can't start voluntarily, needs an external sensory trigger · what moves is slow (bradykinesia) · freezing, slow shuffling gait
Intention: near the end of a movement or holding a position · none at rest
At rest, usually starts in the hand ("pill-rolling"), lessens with movement
Worsens (ongoing loss of pars compacta dopamine cells)

blocks.title: Schulich Reviews
blocks.html: • A cerebellar lesion can also cause dysarthria (slurred speech); this lecture does not list it among the cerebellar signs.

lectures.name: Neurophysiology of Reflexes
lectures.title: Neurophysiology of reflexes
lectures.framing: Motor control is a hierarchy, from the motor unit up to the prefrontal cortex: how force is graded, how the muscle's own sensors drive the spinal reflexes, how the motor cortex sets those reflexes, and why a lesion of the upper or the lower motor neuron looks so different at the bedside.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ UMN lesion = flaccid at first, then spastic, hypertonic, hyperreflexic with clonus and an upgoing big toe, no fasciculations and no severe atrophy; LMN lesion = flaccid, hypo- or areflexic, fasciculations, fibrillations, severe atrophy. Spindle = in parallel, length, Ia, monosynaptic stretch reflex; Golgi tendon organ = in series, force, Ib, inhibits its own muscle. Small motor neurons are recruited first. Fibrillation = one fibre (EMG only); fasciculation = a whole motor unit (visible); spasm = a whole muscle (descending control). Supplementary motor area lesion → apraxia on both sides.

blocks.html: 1. Lower motor neurons and motor units

• Lower motor neuron (LMN) = innervates muscle fibres directly · cell body in the ventral horn (cervical enlargement C3-T1 for the arm, lumbar L1-S3 for the leg) or the brainstem
    • alpha motor neurons → force · gamma motor neurons → fusimotor drive to the muscle spindle
  • Motor unit = one alpha motor neuron + all the muscle fibres it innervates (the smallest unit of motor control) · motor neuron pool = all the alpha motor neurons to one muscle
  • Innervation ratio (fibres per motor unit): leg muscles > 1000 · eye or finger muscles < 10 · smaller ratios allow finer gradations of force
2. Grading muscle force
Action potentials are all-or-none, so force is graded two ways:

• Fire faster: at higher frequencies one fibre's twitches fuse
  • Recruit more motor units (the size principle): smaller motor neurons have lower thresholds and are recruited first, and their units are fatigue-resistant · larger motor neurons join only for large, brief forces (walk → run → gallop → jump)

blocks.cap: Size principle: slow fatigue-resistant units carry standing and walking; fast fatigable units are added for running and jumping

blocks.html: 3. Neuromuscular junction and spontaneous firing

• Neuromuscular junction: one of the largest synapses in the body · in health one action potential releases enough acetylcholine to contract the motor unit (one-to-one fidelity) · target of poisons (botulinum toxin, curare) and disease (myasthenia gravis)

rows: Changed excitability of the fibre: denervation or motor neuron death
Hypersensitive motor neuron, or injury to the axon before it enters the muscle
The whole muscle or a group of muscles
Many causes, typically pathology in descending motor control

blocks.html: 4. Muscles are sensory organs too

rows: In parallel with the muscle fibres (its length changes with the muscle)
In series with the muscle fibres, in the tendon
Muscle force (contraction stretches the tendon and squeezes it)
Ia (the fastest conducting in the body) · plus gamma motor neurons to set the spindle's length

blocks.html: 5. Spinal reflexes

rows: Ia axon synapses on every alpha motor neuron in that muscle's pool and on synergists · and on an inhibitory interneuron to the antagonist
Agonists contract, antagonists relax, countering the stretch · tested clinically by the tendon tap
Rising force → Golgi tendon organ fires
Ib axon → interneuron that INHIBITS the same muscle's alpha motor neuron
Keeps tension constant (a steady grip on a paper cup)
A more complex circuit across the cord

blocks.html:
• Central pattern generators: walking is hardwired in the spinal cord · people with a severed cord can be trained to step on a moving platform · they simplify the job of descending control
  • The spinal reflexes are governed by descending motor control

blocks.cap: Monosynaptic stretch reflex: a passive stretch excites the spindle, Ia afferents fire the same muscle and inhibit its antagonist

blocks.html: 6. Motor cortex and the lateral corticospinal tract

• Primary motor cortex (M1) = area 4 (precentral gyrus), lowest stimulation thresholds · a motor homunculus, with the face and hand (fine control) over-represented
  • M1 maps movements, not muscles: one M1 neuron drives several muscles · a column drives a synergy (muscles acting together) · the same muscle can be driven by different columns
  • Lateral corticospinal tract: the longest tract in the central nervous system (so vulnerable) and one of the largest (~1 million axons) · not fully developed at birth
    • from ⅓ area 4 (primary motor) · ⅓ area 6 (premotor + supplementary motor) · ⅓ primary somatosensory cortex
    • crosses at the pyramidal decussation (medulla-cord junction) → lateral motor neurons → monosynaptic connections onto motor neurons of distal muscles (fingers) → finely controlled finger movement
  • Anterior (ventral) corticospinal tract: from area 4 + area 6 only (no sensory cortex) · fewer axons · stays uncrossed until the spinal cord, then makes bilateral, polysynaptic connections onto medial motor neurons of proximal and axial muscles → posture
  • Two jobs for M1 corticospinal neurons
    • Starting a movement: planning activity in premotor cortex (area 6) can lead the movement by up to 800 ms, then M1 fires · the command goes to alpha and gamma motor neurons together (alpha-gamma co-activation) · M1 firing rate sets the force
    • Shaping the stretch reflex: stretch also triggers a cortical long-loop response, which is voluntary and context-dependent (catching a ball: resist the stretch or give way)
7. Upper vs lower motor neuron lesions

• Upper motor neuron (UMN) = any neuron with a descending projection that controls lower motor neurons
  • A small M1 lesion may leave only one lasting deficit: loss of independent finger movement on the opposite side
  • A larger lesion of motor cortex or the lateral corticospinal tract evolves: flaccid paralysis first, spasticity later

cols: LMN lesion (or its axon, e.g. a cut nerve)
rows: Spastic: excessive contraction to stretch (alpha motor neurons more sensitive to spinal reflexes and brainstem input) · spasms
Hyperreflexia + clonus (oscillating stretch reflexes in opposing muscles)
Big toe extends up, toes fan (normal in babies, before the tract matures)

blocks.html: • The bedside approach to a weak patient (UMN or LMN, then where) is drawn on the Approach to Weakness chart.
8. The motor hierarchy

• M1 gets input from area 6 (premotor and supplementary motor areas), which get input from the prefrontal and posterior parietal cortex; the higher the area, the more abstract its signal and the more cognitive the deficit when it is damaged
  • Supplementary motor area: active in executed or imagined movement sequences · lesion → apraxia (complex motor acts lost, simple movements intact) · a one-sided lesion gives a two-sided deficit (a planning problem)
  • Prefrontal cortex = the rule or context · lesions fail the Wisconsin card-sorting task (can't link a rule to the right action)
  • Posterior parietal cortex = spatial attention · hemispatial neglect after a parietal stroke, neither purely sensory nor purely motor

lectures.name: Spinal Cord
lectures.title: Spinal cord
lectures.framing: Find the level, then the pattern: upper vs lower motor neuron signs say cord or root, the lowest sensory level approximates the cord level, and which modalities are lost, and on which side, names the cord syndrome, which in turn points to the cause.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Anterior cord loses movement and pain but spares vibration and position; posterior cord loses vibration and position but spares movement; central cord hits the hands hardest; Brown-Séquard loses power and position on the lesion's side and pain and temperature on the other. Complete injury = no rectal tone and no perianal sensation. Cervical cord lesion = UMN signs in arms and legs; cervical root = LMN signs in one arm. Bilateral leg pain, saddle anesthesia and bowel or bladder loss = cauda equina, an emergency. A cervical disc hits the lower root; a lumbar disc catches the traversing root.

blocks.html: 1. Anatomy that decides the pattern

• The cord runs from the foramen magnum to about L1/L2; beyond the conus the nerve roots run on as the cauda equina
  • Three pathways to consider

cols: A one-sided cord lesion loses it on the
rows: Lateral corticospinal (cell bodies in the cortex)
Medullary pyramids; synapses in the ventral horn

blocks.html: • Blood supply: one anterior spinal artery + two posterior spinal arteries · the central area supplied only by the anterior spinal artery is mostly motor
2. Assessing the cord

• Sensory: dorsal columns (proprioception, vibration) · spinothalamic (pain, temperature) · light touch uses both · look for a sensory level
    • dermatome = the skin supplied by a single spinal root
  • Motor: bulk, tone, power, reflexes
    • myotome = the muscles one root supplies · not easy to test on a screen, so test movement at a joint (elbow flexion = C5, C6)
    • key movements on the International Standards (ISNCSCI, ASIA) chart: elbow flexors C5 · wrist extensors C6 · elbow extensors C7 · finger flexors C8 · finger abductors T1 · hip flexors L2 · knee extensors L3 · ankle dorsiflexors L4 · long toe extensors L5 · ankle plantar flexors S1 · plus voluntary anal contraction and deep anal pressure
  • Three possible motor results

rows: Wasting, low tone, decreased strength, diminished or absent reflexes
Subtle loss of bulk, increased tone, decreased strength, hyperreflexia, upgoing toe

blocks.html: • UMN = brain or spinal cord · LMN = spinal nerve roots or peripheral nerve
3. Cord (myelopathy) vs root (radiculopathy), by level

rows: Most likely: both legs ± bowel and bladder
Most likely: one leg · but beware cauda equina syndrome

blocks.html: • Cord dysfunction gives UMN findings and presents as a syndrome; root compromise gives an LMN pattern with more isolated signs
4. Spinal cord injury: complete vs incomplete

• Complete: no sensory or motor function below the clinical level, including loss of rectal tone and perianal sensation
  • Incomplete: the level separates normal function from partial impairment below it · grouped by the part of the cord hit:

rows: anterior spinal artery occlusion: atherosclerosis · aortic aneurysm, thrombosis, dissection, surgery · compression (disc, tumour, posterior osteophyte, kyphoscoliosis) · stab injury
Normal (corticospinal weakness only if posterior compression is severe)
vitamin B12 deficiency · syphilis · posterior extrinsic mass · spinal cord tumour surgery
Hands profoundly affected, strength returns going up the arm
Usually spared (light touch too: dissociated sensory loss)
Commonest pattern in elderly trauma (hyperextension) · syrinx · intrinsic tumour · multiple sclerosis
Rare · trauma or a process inside the cord · usually incomplete

blocks.alt: spinal cord syndromes - anterior posterior central Brown-Sequard.jpg
blocks.cap: The four incomplete cord syndromes: which part of the cord is damaged and where motor and sensory function is lost

blocks.html:
• Anterior cord also brings autonomic dysfunction: orthostatic hypotension, and bladder, bowel and sexual dysfunction depending on the level
  • Cauda equina syndrome (roots, not the cord): bilateral leg pain or paresthesia, LMN paraparesis, saddle anesthesia, impaired bowel or bladder control · an EMERGENCY
5. Causes: not just trauma or tumour
Think through every category:

• Vascular: stroke, arteriovenous malformation, fistula
  • Infectious: epidural abscess, viral, syphilis (tabes dorsalis)
  • Trauma: fracture, stab, disc, radiation
  • Autoimmune: lupus
  • Metabolic: subacute combined degeneration (vitamin B12)
  • Inflammatory: multiple sclerosis
  • Neoplastic: metastatic, extradural, intrinsic
  • Congenital: achondroplasia, "trisomy 23" (as printed in the source; there is no trisomy 23, probably trisomy 21 is meant)
  • Degenerative: disc herniation, arthritis, motor neuron disease (ALS)

Grouped another way: compressive (bone lesion, disc herniation, epidural hemorrhage, abscess, tumours, arteriovenous malformation, syringomyelia) vs non-compressive (transverse myelitis, demyelination such as multiple sclerosis and neuromyelitis optica, spinal artery thrombosis and vasculitis, toxins and radiation, degenerative disease, B12 and vitamin E deficiency, paraneoplastic).
6. Nerve roots (radiculopathy)

• Radicular pain · paresthesia or numbness in a dermatome · LMN weakness in a myotome
  • Which root a disc hits: in the neck, a herniation compresses the lower root (a C5-6 disc → the C6 root, which runs in the C5-6 foramen over that disc) · in the lumbar spine it catches the traversing root (an L5-S1 disc → the S1 root)
  • Worked example, right C6 radiculopathy: neck pain, weak biceps and brachioradialis, mildly weak wrist extension, reduced biceps and brachioradialis reflexes, numb outer arm and radial forearm, thumb feels "wooden" → anterior cervical discectomy and fusion
  • Right S1 radiculopathy: low back pain radiating down the back of the leg into the sole, pins and needles in the sole, weak foot · weak plantar flexion, decreased ankle reflex, downgoing toes, reduced light touch and pinprick on the sole, positive straight leg raise → discectomy

blocks.title: Schulich Reviews
blocks.html:
• Anterior cord syndrome can follow a hyperflexion injury.
  • Central cord syndrome: classically an older patient with existing cervical spine disease who has a hyperextension injury.
  • Brown-Séquard syndrome: penetrating trauma or lateral compression · a Brown-Séquard pattern in the legs only, arms spared = a thoracic hemisection.

lectures.name: Neurophthalmology
lectures.title: Neuro-ophthalmology
lectures.framing: Visual symptoms that do not come from the eyeball itself: double vision, eyes that will not hold still, unequal or sluggish pupils, and a missing part of the visual field. Each one points to a place along the nerves and brain pathways, so the lecture is really about localizing.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Anisocoria worse in the light = the big pupil cannot constrict (parasympathetic); worse in the dark = the small pupil cannot dilate (sympathetic, Horner, rule out carotid dissection). A third nerve palsy with a blown pupil is compressive (aneurysm); pupil-sparing is microvascular. Fourth = head tilt, often congenital; sixth = cannot abduct, think raised intracranial pressure. Gaze-evoked nystagmus beats toward the gaze and comes from the cerebellum, brainstem or a toxin. RAPD = that optic nerve. Bitemporal hemianopia = chiasm; temporal lobe = superior defect, parietal = inferior.

blocks.html: 1. Double vision (diplopia)

• Diplopia arises when the two eyes are not aligned: one eye looks at the target and its image falls on the fovea (the actual image, in the centre) · the other looks elsewhere and its image falls off the fovea (the false image, off-centre)
  • Which nerve moves which muscle: lateral rectus = VI, superior oblique = IV, all the rest = III (medial, superior and inferior rectus, inferior oblique)

rows: It can spare the pupil or involve it: a "blown pupil" (large, not reactive to light) is bad, because it means compression (aneurysm) of the parasympathetic fibres on the nerve's surface · a pupil-sparing palsy is microvascular (the nerve's deep vessels)
Cannot abduct, turned in · head turned toward the weak side
Ask: underlying raised intracranial pressure? (look for papilledema; the nerve runs a long course from the pons)

blocks.html: 2. Nystagmus

• Nystagmus = an eye movement disorder: a slow drift of the eyes away from the target
    • pendular: the eyes drift back, so they seem to wobble
    • jerk: they snap back quickly · most nystagmus is jerk · it "beats" in the direction of the fast (snapping) phase
  • Gaze-evoked nystagmus, the most common form: trouble holding eccentric gaze, so it beats toward the gaze (left-beating on left gaze, right on right, up on upgaze, down on downgaze)
    • Why: the circuit that holds eccentric gaze is in the brainstem and cerebellum; a lesion lets the eyes drift back to the midline (slow phase), then they saccade back to the target (fast phase) · an "ataxia of the eyes"
    • Causes
      • structural lesion in the cerebellum (or brainstem): stroke · bleed · tumour · demyelination · degeneration (e.g. alcohol)
      • inherited: hereditary ataxia syndromes
      • toxins: alcohol · phenytoin (Dilantin) and other antiseizure drugs · lithium
3. The pupil
• Pupil size = parasympathetic tone (constricts) vs sympathetic tone (dilates)

rows: Optic nerve (the afferent) → pretectal nucleus (midbrain) → both Edinger-Westphal nuclei → third nerve → ciliary ganglion → pupil sphincter

1st neuron: hypothalamus → ciliospinal centre (C8-T1) · 2nd: over the lung, past the subclavian artery → superior cervical ganglion · 3rd: along the internal carotid → long ciliary nerves → pupil dilator (and Müller's muscle of the lid)
Each pretectal nucleus feeds both Edinger-Westphal nuclei, so both pupils constrict to light in one eye

blocks.alt: pupillary light reflex pathway - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: Pupillary light reflex: optic nerve to the pretectal area, then both Edinger-Westphal nuclei, cranial nerve III and the ciliary ganglion to each constrictor

blocks.html:
• Anisocoria (unequal pupils): first ask is one pupil big, or the other small? (a parasympathetic paresis on one side, or a sympathetic paresis on the other) → compare them in bright light and in the dark
    • difference worse in bright light → the big pupil cannot constrict → parasympathetic (e.g. a compressive third nerve palsy)
    • difference worse in the dark → the small pupil cannot dilate → sympathetic: Horner syndrome → rule out internal carotid artery dissection
4. Relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD)

• RAPD = a defect of one optic nerve, the afferent arm of the light reflex
  • Found with the swinging flashlight test: light in the good eye → both pupils constrict · swing to the bad eye → both pupils dilate, because less light is "seen" · the efferent (third nerve) side is intact, which is why it is relative
5. Visual field defects

• Fibres from the nasal half of each retina cross at the chiasm; temporal fibres do not, so each side of the brain sees the opposite visual field
  • Pathway: optic nerve → chiasm → optic tract → lateral geniculate nucleus → optic radiations (temporal and parietal lobes) → occipital cortex

rows: Back of the optic nerve (at the chiasm)
That eye blind + a junctional scotoma (upper temporal) in the other eye
Bitemporal hemianopia (e.g. a pituitary macroadenoma pressing from below)

blocks.cap: Visual pathway lesions and the field defect each one causes

blocks.title: Schulich Reviews
blocks.html: • An RAPD is often from optic neuritis, which can be a sign of multiple sclerosis.

lectures.name: Cortical Syndromes
lectures.title: Cortical syndromes
lectures.framing: Some deficits can only come from the cortex, so finding one tells you where the lesion is. Language problems point to the dominant hemisphere; neglect points to the non-dominant one. Knowing them also stops an aphasic patient being written off as "confused" or delirious.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Aphasia = dominant hemisphere; neglect = non-dominant hemisphere. Broca's (inferior frontal) = halting speech, understanding intact; Wernicke's (posterior temporal) = fluent nonsense, understanding lost; global = full MCA territory. Any cortical sign rules out a pure subcortical or brainstem lesion. Cortical sensory signs only count if primary sensation is intact. Test comprehension with motor, not verbal, commands.

blocks.html: 1. Why cortical signs matter

• They help localize the lesion (for example, a stroke), explain the presentation, and show that pathology is present
  • ⚠ They stop a patient with aphasia being mistaken for confused or delirious
  • Where a sign points:

rows: Aphasia · neglect · apraxia · cortical sensory signs · usually homonymous hemianopia (especially if isolated)
Pure motor weakness of one side · pure sensory change of one side (face, arm, leg) · ataxic hemiparesis (mild ataxia + mild weakness)
vertigo plus another symptom · diplopia plus another symptom · crossed sensory symptoms (face one side, body the other)

blocks.html: 2. The dominant hemisphere

• Dominant = the hemisphere where language is located
    • right-handed people: typically the left
    • left-handed people: left in 60% · right in 19% · both (bilateral language) in 20%
  • A dominant-hemisphere middle cerebral artery (MCA) stroke usually disturbs language
3. Aphasia

• Aphasia = impairment of language (communicating and/or understanding it), from the dominant hemisphere
    • not the same as dysarthria, which is impairment of articulation

blocks.cap: Broca's area, Wernicke's area and the arcuate fasciculus joining them

rows: Slow, halting (speaking or writing) · none if severe · paraphasic errors (combined sounds, wrong word)
Fluent but makes no sense · sounds like a foreign language if severe · real words that do not cohere if mild

blocks.html:
• Naming and repetition are reduced in all three; the keeners' three (conduction, transcortical motor, transcortical sensory) are in the chart above
  • How to test language: naming · comprehension · fluency · repetition · reading · writing (start simple, get harder)

rows: Name pictures or items, simple → complex (cup → button → stethoscope)
Cannot name a watch or pen
Names the item, not its parts (face of the watch)
Follow instructions, simple → complex · the command must be motor, not verbal
Open-ended question, or describe a picture · sounds that make no sense still count as fluent
Repeat a phrase ("no ifs, ands or buts")
Repeats simple phrases, not complex sentences

blocks.html: 4. The non-dominant hemisphere: neglect

• Neglect syndromes go with the non-dominant hemisphere
    • visual neglect: does not attend to visual stimuli on one side, but may still blink to a threat there
    • sensory neglect: does not attend to sensory stimulation on one side
    • asomatognosia: does not recognize their own body parts (thinks their arm is the examiner's)
    • anosognosia: does not recognize that they have a neurological deficit
    • difficulty putting clothes on (dressing apraxia)
5. Apraxia

• Apraxia = cannot carry out a motor task despite having the power to do it
  • A cortical syndrome, typically from a parietal or frontal lobe lesion
  • Recognize it from examples: cannot pretend to use a hammer · cannot form a finger or hand posture · cannot get dressed · cannot whistle · cannot draw
    • you need to understand and recognize apraxia, not the names of the subtypes
6. Cortical sensory signs and extinction

• Cortical sensory signs localize to the sensory association cortex, but only if primary sensation is intact
    • Graphesthesia lost: cannot read a number or letter traced on the skin
    • Stereognosis lost: cannot identify an object by touch alone
    • position sensation: cannot tell the direction a stimulus is moving
  • ⚠ A loss of primary sensation (pin, temperature, pressure, vibration, light touch) cannot be pinned to the cortex: the lesion could be anywhere on the sensory pathway
  • Extinction: detects a stimulus on either side alone, but when both sides are stimulated at once, misses the affected side
    • sensory extinction (simultaneous light touch) → parietal lobe · visual extinction (simultaneous visual cues) → occipital lobe

blocks.title: Schulich Reviews
blocks.html: • Face + arm weaker than the leg = middle cerebral artery (MCA); leg weaker than face + arm = anterior cerebral artery (ACA): on the WEAKNESS chart

lectures.name: Approach to Weakness
lectures.title: Approach to weakness
lectures.framing: Weakness can come from anywhere between the cerebrum and the muscle fibre. The key localizing clues are the type of weakness (upper or lower motor neuron), the signs and symptoms that come with it, and where the weakness falls.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ No sensory loss narrows LMN weakness to the anterior horn cell (segmental), neuromuscular junction (fluctuating, eyes first) or muscle (proximal, symmetric). UMN = spastic, hyperreflexic, upgoing toe, pyramidal (arm extensors and leg flexors weak); LMN = atrophy, fasciculations, reflexes normal or reduced, tone normal. A sensory level means spinal cord; crossed face and body means brainstem. Polyneuropathy is distal; myopathy is proximal.

blocks.html: 1. Weakness, and what mimics it

• Weakness = loss of voluntary movement from interruption of the motor pathway at any point from cerebrum to muscle fibre
  • ⚠ Mimics (function lost for another reason): incoordination (cerebellar disease) · apraxia (cerebral cortical lesions) · severe sensory loss (proprioceptive failure)
2. Upper vs lower motor neuron

• Upper motor neuron (UMN) lesion = disruption of the corticospinal pathway (cortex · subcortical white matter · internal capsule · brainstem · spinal cord)
    • corticospinal input normally suppresses spinal reflexes, so losing it → hyperreflexia and spasticity
  • Lower motor neuron (LMN) lesion = interruption from the anterior horn cell out to the muscle (anterior horn cell · root · plexus · nerve · neuromuscular junction · muscle)

rows: Atrophy (the nerve no longer brings neurotrophic factors)
Possible, especially anterior horn cell and nerve (a motor unit firing on its own)
Pyramidal: brain → one side · spinal cord → both sides below the lesion
<mark class="lo">Fits the level</mark>: root → myotomal · anterior horn cell, nerve, neuromuscular junction and muscle each have their own pattern

blocks.html:
• Pyramidal weakness (UMN; the corticospinal tract runs through the medullary pyramids):
    • arms: extensors weaker than flexors (triceps < biceps, wrist extension < flexion)
    • legs: flexors weaker than extensors (knee flexion < extension, dorsiflexion < plantar flexion)
    • suspect mild pyramidal weakness → examine arm extensors and leg flexors, which go first
    • likely evolutionary: upright humans keep strong arm flexors (feeding) and leg extensors (walking)

blocks.alt: distribution of weakness by lesion site - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: Where the weakness falls for a hemispheric, brainstem, spinal cord, root, nerve, polyneuropathy and muscle lesion

blocks.html: 3. Where it localizes

rows: Hemiparesis, pyramidal · face + arm > leg = middle cerebral artery (MCA) · leg > face + arm = anterior cerebral artery (ACA) · face = arm = leg = internal capsule
Cranial nerve symptoms (diplopia, vertigo) · cerebellar findings · crossed (ipsilateral face, contralateral body)
Sensory level · neck or back pain · urinary symptoms
Trauma · disc herniation · tumour · epidural hemorrhage · MS
Polio and polio-like illness · ALS (also has UMN signs, from the cortical motor neurons)
Myotomal · reflex of that root reduced
Neck or back pain radiating into a limb · dermatomal sensory loss
Many muscles over more than one root level, sometimes both sides
Cauda equina compression · infectious polyradiculitis · leptomeningeal carcinomatosis
One limb, more muscles than one nerve or one root
Ulnar, radial, common peroneal, sciatic palsies
Length-dependent: symmetric, distal > proximal, feet first · or mononeuritis multiplex
Fluctuating · descending: eyes first (ptosis, diplopia), then speech and swallowing
Symmetric, proximal (trunk, shoulder and hip girdle)
No sensory involvement · reflexes often normal
Inflammatory myopathies (polymyositis, dermatomyositis) · muscular dystrophies

blocks.html: 4. History and exam

• History: where (one limb, one side, both sides) · how (abrupt, or gradual and progressive) · functional impact (what is hard) · other symptoms (sensory change · speech, language or swallowing · pain · bowel or bladder)
  • Exam confirms the location, extent and character · know what normal is, so you catch mild weakness and side-to-side differences
  • Medical Research Council (MRC) scale: 0 none · 1 flicker · 2 moves with gravity eliminated · 3 full antigravity power · 4 some power against resistance (4-, 4, 4+) · 5 full power
  • The lecture's cases, one line each:
    • 2 weeks of trouble with stairs and dressing · neck flexors and extensors, deltoids, triceps, hip flexors weak · reflexes, tone and sensation normal → muscle
    • 2 months of trouble walking, numb feet · weak ankles · absent ankle reflexes · pinprick lost to the knee → peripheral nerve
    • weak legs · brisk knees and ankles, upgoing toes · pinprick lost up to the inferior scapula → spinal cord

blocks.title: Schulich Reviews
blocks.html: • Acute weakness: an ischemic stroke follows a vascular territory; a hemorrhage may not, and more often brings a headache; migraine weakness "marches" and comes and goes over minutes; Todd's paresis improves over hours; psychogenic weakness is inconsistent and better when distracted

lectures.name: Approach to Localization
lectures.title: Approach to localization
lectures.framing: Use the same approach for every neurological problem: describe it, localize the lesion, then build the differential from the description and the localization. Localizing helps you plan the right investigations; the time course tells you what kind of lesion it is.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Any cortical sign puts the lesion in the cortex; vertigo or diplopia plus something else, or crossed face-body sensory symptoms, puts it in the brainstem; pure motor, pure sensory or ataxic hemiparesis without cortical signs puts it in the subcortex. Hyperacute = stroke or hemorrhage; subacute = inflammation, infection or tumour. MCA = face and arm >> leg. Dysarthria spares language; aphasia does not. Bilateral leg weakness can be cortex (parasagittal) all the way to muscle.

blocks.html: 1. The approach

1. Describe the problem

- onset: acute · subacute · chronic

- course: progressive · intermittent · stable

- deficits: cognitive · motor · sensory · coordination

2. Localize the "lesion" with your neuroanatomy

3. Offer a differential diagnosis, taking the description and the localization into account
• The tempo predicts the type of lesion:
2. Is it the brain, the cord or the periphery?

• Upper motor neuron (UMN) vs lower motor neuron (LMN) signs, and the pattern of weakness, are on the Approach to weakness chart
  • Bilateral leg weakness can come from: a parasagittal cortical lesion (for example a parasagittal meningioma) · the spinal cord · anterior horn cell disease · multilevel lumbosacral radiculopathies (for example spinal stenosis) · polyneuropathies · myopathy
    • UMN signs in the legs (brisk reflexes, upgoing toes) → spinal cord: look for a sensory level, which tells imaging where to look
3. Where in the brain: the localization pearls

rows: Aphasia · neglect syndromes · homonymous hemianopsia
Pure motor hemiparesis or pure sensory hemibody (face, arm, leg) · ataxic hemiparesis (mild ataxia + mild hemiparesis)
vertigo plus another symptom · diplopia plus another symptom · crossed sensory symptoms (face vs body)

blocks.html:
• Middle cerebral artery (MCA) stroke: the MCA supplies the mid and lower homunculus, so face and arm >> leg
    • frontal lobe only → mostly motor · mostly parietal → mostly sensory · internal capsule → motor and sensory
    • dominant-hemisphere MCA stroke usually disturbs language (aphasia types: on the Cortical syndromes chart)
  • Case: sudden right face and arm (> leg) weakness, no verbal output but follows commands, no neglect → expressive aphasia → left frontal lobe, left MCA territory
4. Difficulty speaking: dysarthria or aphasia?

• Two main neurological causes: dysarthria (articulation) and dysphasia / aphasia (language)
  • Slurred speech with normal comprehension, naming, repetition and fluency = dysarthria
  • Any lesion along the speech production pathway can cause dysarthria:
    • central: cortex (mouth area) · subcortex · thalamus · brainstem · cerebellum and its pathways
    • peripheral: nerve (for example the recurrent laryngeal nerve) · neuromuscular junction (for example myasthenia gravis) · muscle (myopathy)
  • Tell the sites apart by what comes with it: findings only a cranial nerve explains · UMN vs LMN findings · weakness · ataxia · sensory symptoms
5. The cerebellar system

• It coordinates all movement: eyes, articulation, swallowing, the arms and gait (think of someone drunk; alcohol is a cerebellar toxin)
    • nystagmus · dysarthria · dysphagia · finger-to-nose ataxia · dysdiadochokinesia (rapid alternating movements) · heel-to-shin ataxia · gait ataxia · impaired tandem walking
  • Case: slurred speech plus slight right finger-to-nose ataxia → the cerebellar system (here a right cerebellar hemorrhage)

blocks.title: Schulich Reviews
blocks.html: • Localization is the most tested skill: work through the lecture's cases

lectures.name: Neuroembryology
lectures.title: Neuroembryology
lectures.framing: The nervous system comes from ectoderm: the neural tube becomes the central nervous system, and every later structure is a dilation or a layer of that tube. Most of the pathology is a step that failed: a neuropore that did not close, or neurons that did not migrate.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Cranial neuropore fails = anencephaly; failure along the spine = spina bifida - and 400 mcg of folic acid helps prevent both. Myelomeningocele has cord outside; meningocele has only meninges; occulta is skin-covered. High AFP suggests spina bifida. Neuronal migration disorders present with drug-resistant epilepsy: smooth brain (lissencephaly), too many small gyri (polymicrogyria), absent corpus callosum. Alar plate = dorsal, sensory; basal plate = ventral, motor. Myelination runs caudal to rostral, mostly after birth.

blocks.html: 1. Gastrulation and neurulation

blocks.lead:
- Gastrulation (from about day 16, started by the primitive streak) = formation of the 3 germ layers · sets up the body plan (bilateral symmetry, 3 axes) and makes the first neuroepithelium

- the notochord (from the notochordal plate, a mesodermal derivative) tells nearby ectoderm to become neural tissue and sets the axes through gradients of sonic hedgehog

- the neural plate forms first at the cranial end

- Neurulation:

1. dorsal ectoderm forms the neural plate (neuroectoderm), which folds into neural folds and a neural groove (day 18)

2. the folds meet in the midline and fuse cranially and caudally, starting from the cervical region

3. cranial (anterior) neuropore closes on day 24-25

4. caudal (posterior) neuropore closes on day 26-28

5. throughout, neural crest cells "pinch off" and start to migrate

- End product: a continuous neural tube (neuroectoderm lining a fluid-filled centre) along the dorsal embryo, with an enlarged cranial end that dilates and flexes into the early brain
rows: Peripheral and enteric (gut) neurons · glia · pigment cells (melanocytes) · cartilage and bone of the face and skull · smooth muscle
Epidermis · hair · nails · sebaceous glands · olfactory and mouth lining · eyes

blocks.html: 2. Brain vesicles

blocks.cap: The three primary vesicles: prosencephalon (forebrain), mesencephalon (midbrain), rhombencephalon (hindbrain)

rows: Thalamus and hypothalamus · eyes (retina, via the optic cups) · part of the pituitary

blocks.html: • Cranial nerve nuclei (by week 4): CN I from the telencephalon · CN II from the diencephalon (it continues the optic cup) · CN III mesencephalon · CN IV-VIII metencephalon · CN IX-XII myelencephalon
3. Timeline of brain development

• The processes run in parallel, not one after another:
    • neurogenesis: neurons multiply from the ventricular lining of the tube, symmetrically at first, then exponentially · first neurons (about week 4) are motor neurons of the cervical ventral horn · 6 cortical layers by about week 18 · gyri visible by about week 24
    • gliogenesis: follows neurogenesis, peaks around birth, continues after · different glia come from different parts of the telencephalon
    • migration: new neurons form transient structures and the CNS expands fast · genetically controlled, so genetic syndromes can disrupt it
    • synaptogenesis: needs astrocytes, region-dependent · in the cortex from about weeks 24-27, continuing into early adulthood
    • myelination: caudal to rostral (spinal cord and brainstem first), largely after birth · myelin inhibits synaptogenesis and plasticity · corticospinal tract done by 2 years, corpus callosum by late adolescence

blocks.cap: Brain development from neural tube to adulthood: neurulation, migration and neurogenesis early; synaptogenesis, gliogenesis and myelination late

blocks.html: 4. Spinal cord development

• The caudal two-thirds of the tube → spinal cord; its cavity → the central canal
  • The wall splits into a mantle layer (deep → grey matter) and a marginal layer (superficial → white matter, white once its fibres myelinate)
    • the mantle layer forms a floor plate, a roof plate and a lateral mass on each side
  • Alar and basal plates: the roof plate induces the alar plate, the floor plate induces the basal plate

rows: Dorsal horn (sensory) · also the sensory nuclei of CN V, VII, VIII, IX and X
Intermediate plate (mid-portion of the lateral mass)

blocks.cap: Developing spinal cord: alar plate becomes the sensory dorsal horn, basal plate the motor ventral horn

blocks.html: • The spine outgrows the cord: early on the cord runs the length of the embryo · the vertebral column and dura grow faster, so the cord's end rises (making the filum terminale and cauda equina) · it ends at L3 at birth and about L2-L3 in adults
5. Neural tube defects

rows: The upper (cranial) part of the neural tube does not close all the way
The neural tube does not close all the way anywhere along the spine, so the backbone over the cord does not form
Born without parts of the brain and skull (the forebrain) · what remains is often not covered by bone or skin · about 1 in 4,500
Damage to the spinal cord and nerves · physical and intellectual disability, mild to severe, by the size and level of the opening and whether cord and nerves are involved
No cure or standard treatment; almost all die shortly after birth

blocks.html:
• Spina bifida types, most to least severe:
    • Myelomeningocele (most severe): meninges and spinal cord protrude · motor and sensory loss below the level · often needs surgery
    • Meningocele (moderate): meninges only protrude, in a fluid-filled sac · the cord is unaffected
    • Spina bifida occulta (least severe): a small gap in the vertebrae, covered by skin · often unnoticed, no external signs (sometimes a sacral dimple or tuft of hair)
  • Prevention: folic acid before and during early pregnancy, 400 micrograms (mcg) a day, for both
  • Causes: mostly unknown · likely a mix of genetic and environmental factors
  • Prenatal screening for spina bifida: alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) (maternal blood; a high AFP may mean spina bifida; also measured with amniocentesis) · ultrasound
6. Neuronal migration disorders

• Neuronal migration disorders: neurons migrate abnormally (normally in the 2nd month): only some reach the cortex, or they overshoot · the cortical layers are disorganized and the gyri form abnormally
    • ⚠ the most common, nearly universal symptom: epilepsy that does not respond to drugs (pharmacologically intractable)

rows: "Smooth brain": no normal convolutions · gene-linked · small head (head size is usually normal at birth; small at birth = microlissencephaly)

Unusual face · trouble swallowing · failure to thrive · spasms, seizures · severe psychomotor delay · many die before age 10 (aspiration, respiratory disease, seizures) · no cure; supportive care, anticonvulsants
Corpus callosum partly or completely absent · alone or with other malformations
Late milestones (walking, talking, reading) · clumsy, poor left-right coordination · social processing problems that grow with age · treat symptoms and seizures
Too many, unusually small folds · cortex simplified from 6 layers to 2-3

lectures.name: Autonomic Nervous System
lectures.title: Autonomic nervous system
lectures.framing: The autonomic nervous system is the visceral motor supply to the viscera, smooth muscle, cardiac muscle and glands, in two divisions that mostly pull in opposite directions. The clinical payoff is recognizing a cut sympathetic supply to one side of the face (Horner syndrome) and telling it from a third nerve palsy.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Horner = small pupil + milder ptosis + flushing + no sweating, same side, eye directed normally; CN III palsy = dilated pupil + paralysed levator + eye down and out + no accommodation. Sympathetic = thoracolumbar, short pre- and long post-synaptic fibres, synapse in the chain; parasympathetic = cranio-sacral, long pre- and short post-synaptic, synapse near the target. Sympathetics to the head synapse in the superior cervical ganglion and ride the carotid arteries. Parasympathetic empties the bladder; sympathetic holds it.

blocks.html: 1. Organization: two divisions

rows: Leaves the central nervous system at
Thoracolumbar cord · cell body in the intermediolateral horn
Cranio-sacral: cranial nerves (III, VII, IX, and the vagus) · sacral cord
Dilates the pupil · ↑ heart rate and force · dilates bronchioles · dilates vessels to skeletal muscle · constricts vessels to the gut · ↓ peristalsis · activates sweating

blocks.alt: parasympathetic vs sympathetic organ effects - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: Parasympathetic (left) and sympathetic (right) effects on each organ, with the cranial-sacral and thoracolumbar outflows

blocks.html: 2. Sympathetic pathways

• To the limbs: the pre-synaptic fibre enters the chain through the white ramus communicans at its own level, runs up or down the chain, and synapses at another level
    • lower limb → L2-S3 ganglia · upper limb → cervical ganglia · head → superior cervical ganglion
    • the post-synaptic fibre leaves through the grey ramus communicans and travels with somatic nerves
  • To the head: pre-synaptic fibres from about T1-T3 climb the chain without synapsing → synapse in the superior cervical ganglion → post-synaptic fibres leave through the grey ramus and ride the carotid arteries and their branches, then hitch a ride on trigeminal nerve branches near their targets
3. Head and neck: the four parasympathetic ganglia

• Pre-synaptic fibres from nuclei of CN III, VII and IX (the vagus is the exception) → synapse in one of four ganglia → post-synaptic fibres travel with branches of the trigeminal nerve (CN V) to smooth muscle and glands
  • Sympathetics to each ganglion's targets all come from the superior cervical ganglion

rows: Edinger-Westphal (accessory oculomotor) → inferior branch of CN III → short ciliary nerves
Internal carotid plexus through the cavernous sinus → dilator pupillae and superior tarsal muscle
Superior salivatory → CN VII → greater petrosal → nerve of the pterygoid canal
Tears (post-synaptic fibres ride V2 to the lacrimal gland) · nasal, palate and pharynx mucosa
Internal carotid plexus → deep petrosal → nerve of the pterygoid canal → ↓ tears · nasal, palate and pharynx vessels and mucosa
Superior salivatory → CN VII → chorda tympani, joining the lingual nerve (V3)
Facial and lingual arteries → vasoconstriction of those glands' vessels
Inferior salivatory → CN IX → tympanic nerve → lesser petrosal → auriculotemporal (V3)
External carotid branches → vasoconstriction of parotid vessels

blocks.html: • Corneal sensation (the afferent side): cornea → short and long ciliary nerves → nasociliary nerve → trigeminal ganglion → trigeminal nuclei
4. Horner syndrome

• Horner syndrome = interruption of the cervical sympathetic supply to one side of the face · signs on the same side: miosis, ptosis, vasodilation, anhidrosis:
    • miosis (small pupil)
    • ptosis, often less severe than a third nerve palsy (the levator, on CN III, still works)
    • vasodilation (flushing)
    • anhidrosis (no sweating)
  • Where the lesion can be: anywhere on the head's sympathetic route - the T1-T3 cord outflow · the cervical sympathetic chain · the superior cervical ganglion · the internal carotid plexus through the cavernous sinus into the orbit

blocks.alt: oculosympathetic pathway three neurons - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: The three-neuron sympathetic path to the eye: hypothalamus to C8-T1, over the lung apex to the superior cervical ganglion, then along the carotid to the pupil dilator and eyelid

cols: CN III palsy (loss of parasympathetics and motor)

blocks.html: 5. The bladder

rows: Motor to the detrusor (empties) · inhibits the internal urethral sphincter
External urethral sphincter · pelvic and perineal muscles
Inferior bladder (below the pelvic pain line) → with the parasympathetics (voiding reflex) · superior bladder (above it) → with the sympathetics

lectures.name: Neuroradiology
lectures.title: Neuroradiology
lectures.framing: Different objects need to be looked at different ways: pick the modality that best resolves the object of interest. Each one trades three kinds of resolution against cost, availability, invasiveness and radiation; on MRI you also pick the sequence.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Fluid is dark on T1, white on T2, and white on FLAIR except for CSF - so FLAIR makes edema stand out. Radiography has the best spatial resolution, fluoroscopy and ultrasound the best temporal, MRI the best contrast. CT: widely available, but radiation; ultrasound: no radiation; MRI: expensive, limited, long. DWI measures restricted water diffusion (cellularity); SWI shows blood products.

blocks.html: 1. Three kinds of resolution

• Spatial: can you resolve more than one nearby object? (the detail)
  • Contrast: can you resolve objects of similar density? (the range of greys)
  • Temporal: can you resolve objects over time? (as in a video)
2. The modalities

rows: Pulsed X-rays (0.5-16 frames a second) · real-time · digital subtraction removes the baseline image so only new things (contrast, air) show
X-ray attenuation, built into slices · contrast improves contrast resolution · multi-phase scanning adds temporal resolution
Grayscale: speed of sound and time to echo in different media · Doppler: frequency shift off a moving reflector
Differential energy states of protons in a changing magnetic and radiofrequency field

blocks.html: 3. MRI sequences

rows: White except CSF (inversion recovery suppresses the CSF signal)
DWI / ADC (diffusion-weighted imaging, apparent diffusion coefficient map)
Restricted diffusion of water · a measure of cellularity
Hemoglobin in its different oxidation states, including hemosiderin · accentuates an artifact first met on gradient echo (GRE)

blocks.html:
• T2 and FLAIR are the "pathologic" sequences: they suppress "noise" and make pathology stand out
  • Advanced imaging: MR angiography · MR perfusion · MR spectroscopy · functional MRI

blocks.alt: MRI sequences T1 T2 FLAIR DWI SWI - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: The same five sequences: T1 (CSF dark), T2 (CSF white), FLAIR (CSF dark, edema bright), DWI and SWI (dark spots of blood)

blocks.html: 4. Putting it to work
• The lecture's case runs the stroke imaging in order: plain CT → CT angiography (CTA) → CT perfusion (CTP) → catheter angiography (fluoroscopy) → clot pulled out by thrombectomy → DWI afterwards

weeks.label: Week 14 - Head Injury, Stroke, Headache, Seizures & Neuroinfections

lectures.name: Approach to Head Injuries
lectures.title: Approach to head injuries
lectures.framing: Every head injury is a trauma patient first: run the primary survey with the cervical spine protected, then grade the brain injury with the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS). A severe injury is a race against rising intracranial pressure and herniation, settled by a STAT CT and often the operating room; a concussion is a clinical diagnosis, managed by removal from play, brief rest and a graded return.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ A lucid interval after a contact injury is an epidural hematoma until the CT says otherwise - and a symptomatic epidural goes to the operating room. Uncal herniation: same-side blown pupil, opposite-side weakness; Cushing's triad (hypertension, bradycardia, apnea) means the medulla is being compressed. Subdural: bridging veins, falls, the elderly; operate within 4 hours. Diffuse axonal injury: unconscious at the scene and stays in a coma, with a CT that can look nearly normal. Severe = GCS 3-8. Concussion is clinical: most never lose consciousness, no impact is needed, and a helmet does not prevent it. Rest 24-48 hours, then return to learn before return to play.

blocks.html: 1. A trauma patient first

• Advanced Trauma Life Support (ATLS): primary survey and initial resuscitation, then secondary survey and definitive treatment
    • A - airway: cervical spine (C-spine) precautions, intubation with manual in-line C-spine traction if needed
    • B - breathing · C - circulation: large-bore IV, bloodwork to look for coagulopathy
    • D - disability: neurological exam and GCS · E - expose: other injuries
  • A falling level of consciousness or a blown pupil: intubate with C-spine precautions · head of the bed up · IV mannitol or 3% saline for osmotic diuresis · STAT CT scan
  • The module adds: hyperventilation (PaCO2 below 34) to reduce brain swelling · no lumbar puncture when a mass lesion is possible · no corticosteroids - they reduce vasogenic edema and have no role in traumatic brain injury
  • Who: 20 per 100,000 a year · peak age 15-24 · young → motor vehicle crashes · older → falls

blocks.title: Schulich Reviews
blocks.html: • Intubate if the GCS is below 8 (the lecture says intubate as needed, with in-line C-spine traction)
2. Grading severity with the Glasgow Coma Scale

• Three parts, maximum 15: eye opening (4 spontaneously · 3 to speech · 2 to pain · 1 none) · verbal response (5 oriented · 4 confused · 3 inappropriate · 2 incomprehensible · 1 none) · motor response (6 obeys commands · 5 localises to pain · 4 withdraws from pain · 3 flexion to pain · 2 extension to pain · 1 none)
  • Easy to determine · objective · reproducible · predicts outcome

• Mortality in severe injury
    • GCS on admission: above 8 → 12% · 5-7 → 27% · below 5 → 78%
    • coma over 1 day → 30-50% · intracranial pressure over 20 (normal under 15) → 50%
    • Epidural 10-25% vs subdural 45-70%
3. Types of head injury

• Skull fractures: linear · depressed · basilar · open or closed
    • Basilar (base of the skull): raccoon eyes · Battle sign · cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) leaking from the ear or nose · blood behind the eardrum (hemotympanum) · may not show on CT · risk of meningitis
  • Focal injuries: contusions (coup, contrecoup) · hematomas (epidural, subdural, intracerebral) · penetrating injury (knife, missile, gunshot)
  • Diffuse injuries: concussion and shock-wave injury (blasts, sports) · diffuse axonal injury · traumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage
4. The hematomas

rows: Between the inner table of the skull and the dura · frontal or temporal
Middle meningeal artery 50% · middle meningeal vein 33% · diploic vein or dural sinus 17% · torn by the fractured bone edges
Contact injury, not head acceleration (head hits cement, or is struck) · skull fracture in 75-90% of adults
Acceleration-deceleration · falls where the head strikes a broad surface · often with diffuse axonal injury
Lucid period, then coma, as blood gradually accumulates · 33% have another brain lesion
10-15% of severe head injuries · presents within 3 days · 30% of fatal injuries
Surgery: any symptomatic one · asymptomatic over 1 cm · children · conservative only if very small
The 4-hour rule: surgery within 4 hours → 30% mortality, after 4 hours → 90%
Mostly from the underlying brain injury · over 65: 82%, 5% recover function · GCS 3 / 4 / 5 → 76% / 62% / 51%

blocks.alt: epidural vs subdural hematoma - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: Epidural vs subdural hematoma: arterial blood under the skull vs venous blood under the dura

blocks.html:
• Contusions: coup beneath the impact (the skull bends in, then springs back and tears pial vessels) · contrecoup remote from the impact (acceleration)
