    • signs depend on size and site · may cause mass effect and ↑ intracranial pressure · the bruised brain becomes necrotic and patchily hemorrhagic
    • CT: mixed high and low density (blood, edema, dead brain), usually several · repeat CT at 24-48 hours: they evolve, and 20% bleed later
    • small or deep → no surgery · large with mass effect → surgery
  • Traumatic intracerebral hemorrhage: 1-3% · deceleration or contact · one confluent bleed, frontal or temporal in 80-90%, found in 25% of closed head injuries · blood dissects the brain beside it, which is otherwise normal
    • CT: well-defined, homogeneous, hyperdense · large with shift, ↓ consciousness and focal deficits → surgery · mortality 25-72%
  • Diffuse axonal injury: an acceleration injury (shaken baby syndrome) · 50% of all severe brain injuries · unconscious at the scene, then persistent coma · co-exists with other injuries · high morbidity and mortality
    • petechial hemorrhages at the grey-white junction · corpus callosum · dorsolateral pons · cervicomedullary junction - difficult to see on CT
  • Traumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage: same acceleration mechanism and same picture (unconscious at the scene, persistent coma) · pial vessels rupture
5. Why a head injury is so bad: raised pressure and herniation
• Edema · vasodilation · vascular congestion · hematoma → ↑ intracranial pressure → brain herniation

rows: Same-side third nerve palsy · same-side dilated pupil · opposite-side weakness

blocks.cap: Herniation: (a) subfalcine, (b) uncal, (c) central, (d) transcalvarial, (e) tonsillar

blocks.html: • Descending herniation: cranial nerve palsies (III, IV, VI) · brainstem compression · arterial compression → posterior or anterior cerebral artery stroke · vessels shear → Duret hemorrhage · Cushing's triad: hypertension, bradycardia, apnea
6. Concussion

• Definition: mild traumatic brain injury: a diffuse injury without focal neurological deficits, from biomechanical forces · not just sports: occupational injuries and accidents too
    • mechanism: rotational acceleration of the brain · direct impact is not required (a blow to the chest whips the head) · helmets do not prevent it · whiplash often co-exists · 81-92% do not lose consciousness
  • Risk factors: young brain (longer recovery) · female · a previous concussion (less force needed, longer recovery) · ? genes
    • sport: poor technique, head-to-head contact · football (tackling) is the biggest offender, then hockey and female soccer
  • Usual symptoms: headache · dizziness · nausea · imbalance · "seeing stars" · full recovery in 1-4 weeks after a first concussion
  • In the field: Concussion Recognition Tool 5 · remove from play if a concussion is suspected
  • Go to the ER if: GCS under 15 · deteriorating mental status · possible spinal injury · progressive, worsening symptoms or new neurological signs
  • Medical assessment: every concussion is seen by a doctor or nurse practitioner · a clinical diagnosis - no focal signs, and no blood test, CSF marker, CT, MRI or EEG
    • Sport Concussion Assessment Tool (SCAT5): 22 possible symptoms, only 1 is needed for the diagnosis · a version for ages 5-12 · watch for patients playing their symptoms down to stay in the game
  • Management (recognise and remove: when in doubt, remove from play, work or school)
    • mental and physical rest for 24-48 hours, but no extended rest: a cellphone but no texting · one visitor at a time · audiobooks, not reading · naps · no schoolwork · no screen time
    • rest until symptom-free → return to learn → if still symptom-free, return to play, with planning and pacing (cognitive fatigue, sleep) and headache and sleep management
    • return to school (4 stages: home activities → schoolwork at home → part-time → full-time): part time, easiest classes first, permission to leave and rest, limited homework, no gym or dance
    • return to sport (6 stages: symptom-limited activity → light aerobic → sport-specific drills → non-contact drills → full contact practice → game play), about a week · full-time school and a medical clearance letter come before full contact
    • new or worse symptoms at any stage → go back a stage
  • Outcome: 85% of first concussions recover fully in 1-4 weeks · 15-30% still have symptoms
  • Consequences
    • second-impact syndrome (post-traumatic cerebral swelling)
    • post-concussion syndrome: symptoms over 2 weeks in adults, over 4 weeks in youth · more common after repeated concussions · permanent removal from play recommended
    • post-traumatic epilepsy · depression, anxiety, behaviour change, suicide
    • chronic traumatic encephalopathy: a neuropathological diagnosis after repeated concussions · chronic headache, irritability, psychiatric symptoms, suicide, dementia · tau-positive neurofibrillary tangles · apolipoprotein E may raise susceptibility
  • Prevention: primary (no checks to the head, no heading in soccer, no head contact before high school, enforce the rules, neck strengthening) · secondary (remove and rest, a doctor sees every concussion, return-to-play protocol to prevent second-impact syndrome) · tertiary (permanent removal after repeated concussions, to prevent chronic traumatic encephalopathy)

lectures.name: Multiple Sclerosis
lectures.title: Multiple sclerosis
lectures.framing: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is diagnosed by dissemination in space and time - lesions in different parts of the central nervous system at different times, on MRI with cerebrospinal fluid support - once a better explanation is ruled out. A relapse is new neurological dysfunction lasting 24 hours or more with no other cause, and treatment is chosen by category of disease-modifying drug, not drug by drug.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ MS needs dissemination in space (2 typical regions) and time (a new or an enhancing-plus-non-enhancing lesion), and oligoclonal bands can stand in for time - but only once a better explanation is ruled out. A relapse is new, lasts 24 hours or more, and has no other cause. Myelitis ~50%, optic neuritis ~25% (pain on moving the eye), brainstem or cerebellar ~15%. Relapsing-remitting is 85% at onset; primary progressive worsens from the start without relapses. EBV is the leading risk factor: 32-fold, likely necessary but not sufficient.

blocks.html: 1. What MS is, and who gets it

• An immune-mediated attack (B and T cells) on oligodendrocytes (myelin) in the central nervous system → axonal damage, and eventually axonal loss · slowed conduction from the brain and cord to the body
  • Where the lesions sit: cortical or juxtacortical · periventricular · brainstem · cerebellum · spinal cord
  • Who: the most common disabling disease of the central nervous system in Canada (of young adults) · prevalence 240 per 100,000 (Ontario 230) · female 3:1 · age 20-40 · most often white or Northern European
  • Why: genes, environment and lifestyle
    • genes: all known genetic variants explain only 20-30% of MS heritability
    • environment: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV): infection raises MS risk 32-fold (2022) - likely necessary but not sufficient · adolescent obesity · smoking · vitamin D deficiency · low sunlight · shift work · infectious mononucleosis · passive smoking · (oral tobacco, coffee and alcohol go the other way)
    • lifestyle: smoking · obesity · diet · shift work
2. Disease courses

rows: 85% of all MS at onset · attacks, then recovery · disability builds in steps
Relapsing-remitting that turns into steady worsening
Gradual worsening from the start, without relapses

blocks.html:
• Each is also labelled active or not active, and with or without progression (Lublin 2014)
  • Prognosis: 50% have minor disability at 6-8 years · 21% need help walking at 15 years · median time to needing help walking 27.9 years (about age 59)
  • Disability is scored on the Expanded Disability Status Scale (EDSS): 1-2 minimal disability → 6 assistance needed to walk → 10 death from MS

blocks.cap: Courses of multiple sclerosis: disability over time

blocks.html: 3. Relapses: how MS presents

• A relapse: an episode of new symptoms of neurological dysfunction · acute or subacute onset · lasting 24 hours or more · not attributable to another cause · not a pseudo-relapse (the lecture names pseudo-relapse without describing it)

rows: <mark class="lo">Sensory changes · weakness · bladder and bowel dysfunction</mark>

blocks.html: • Other features: sensory disturbances · fatigue · Lhermitte's sign (an electric-shock sensation on bending the neck)

blocks.title: Schulich Reviews
blocks.html: • Charcot's triad: dysarthria, nystagmus, intention tremor
4. Diagnosis: the 2017 McDonald criteria

• Diagnosis = evidence of dissemination, with clinical attacks and MRI or cerebrospinal fluid findings combined
    • in space: lesions in 2 or more typical regions - periventricular · cortical or juxtacortical · infratentorial · spinal cord
    • in time: new lesions on a follow-up MRI, or enhancing and non-enhancing lesions at the same time
    • CSF oligoclonal bands can substitute for dissemination in time
  • MRI is central; a lumbar puncture looks for oligoclonal bands
  • Always rule out a better explanation: neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMO) · myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody disease (MOGAD) · vascular · infection · metabolic

blocks.alt: multiple sclerosis lesions on T2 FLAIR and T1 MRI - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: MS lesions: bright periventricular spots on T2/FLAIR (left), dark holes on T1 (right)

blocks.html:
• Differential (VITAMIN)
    • vascular: headaches and migraine · stroke · CADASIL
    • infection: HIV · syphilis · Lyme disease · West Nile virus
    • toxins: cocaine and its additives
    • autoimmune: of the brain (neuromyelitis optica, MOGAD) · systemic (Sjögren syndrome, Behçet disease)
    • metabolic: vitamin B12 · inflammatory: sarcoidosis · neoplastic: lymphoma
    • the mimics seen most often: neuromyelitis optica, MOGAD, sarcoidosis, lymphoma or other tumour, acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (ADEM), rheumatologic disease
5. Treatment
• Disease-modifying therapy (DMT): learn the categories, not every drug (the lecture's summary names three: injectables, orals, infusions)

rows: An oral drug with long-lasting effects (about 4 years)
B-cell therapies are now very widely used

blocks.html: • Symptomatic therapy

• Coming: a vaccine against EBV is in a phase 1 trial (2025)
  • Early diagnosis and treatment can improve long-term outcomes

lectures.name: Approach to Stroke
lectures.title: Approach to stroke
lectures.framing: Time is brain: localize, then a non-contrast CT rules out hemorrhage before clot-busting with tissue plasminogen activator (tPA, up to 4.5 hours) and clot retrieval (thrombectomy) for a proximal large-vessel occlusion. Once the patient is stable, the cause sets secondary prevention: a clot from the heart → anticoagulant; everything else → antiplatelet.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Non-contrast CT comes first, because any hemorrhage is an absolute contraindication to tPA. tPA up to 4.5 hours; thrombectomy for a proximal large vessel occlusion with a perfusion mismatch, even when tPA cannot be given. tPA exclusions: BP over 185/110, INR over 1.4, platelets under 100,000, a factor Xa inhibitor in 24-48 hours. Neglect or aphasia = cortex (MCA), not a lacune. Heart clot → anticoagulate; everything else → antiplatelet. Endarterectomy only for symptomatic stenosis over 70%. TIA: CT, ASA (add clopidogrel for 21 days if already on it), TIA clinic. Hypertensive bleeds are deep; amyloid bleeds are lobar.

blocks.html: 1. Definitions and causes

• Stroke = sudden onset of a neurological deficit caused by a problem with the brain's blood supply
    • Ischemic = a blocked vessel: a large vessel (e.g. the middle cerebral artery (MCA) or a branch) or a small vessel (lacunar)
    • Hemorrhagic = a ruptured vessel bleeding into or around the brain
  • Transient ischemic attack (TIA) = a brief episode of neurological dysfunction from focal brain or retinal ischemia, symptoms usually under an hour, and no acute infarction
  • Infarction = tissue death from lack of oxygen · penumbra = stunned but still viable brain around the infarcted core

blocks.cap: Ischemic core and penumbra on CT

blocks.html: • Ischemic causes: ① artery-to-artery embolus (carotid, intracranial stenosis, aorta) · ② cardioembolic · ③ lacunar (small vessel) · ④ artery dissection (vertebral, carotid) · ⑤ low perfusion → watershed infarcts between territories (can cause laminar necrosis of the cortical ribbon) · ⑥ cryptogenic
2. Is it a stroke? Mimics of acute weakness

• Ischemic stroke: follows a specific vascular territory
  • Intracerebral hemorrhage: may not follow a territory · more often with a headache
  • migraine: weakness "marches", slow onset and offset · may cross territories · minutes, rarely hours · more often young women
  • Todd's paresis: after a (maybe unwitnessed) seizure · improves gradually over hours
  • Psychogenic: inconsistent, especially when distracted · no vascular territory
  • hypoglycemia can cause focal symptoms (especially over old strokes): check the glucose
3. Stroke syndromes

rows: Aphasia + right face and arm > leg weakness
Neglect of the left side · anosognosia + left face and arm > leg weakness
① clumsy hand-dysarthria · ② pure motor (face, arm, leg equally) · ③ pure sensory · ④ ataxic hemiparesis · ⑤ sensorimotor

blocks.html: 4. Hyperacute management

- Paramedics activate the stroke protocol; the stroke team (neurologist, resident, stroke nurse) waits in the resuscitation room

- On arrival: vitals · cardiac monitor · 2 IV lines (one for tPA) · labs (INR, creatinine, CBC) · point-of-care glucose · past history and medications (they bear on the cause and the tPA risk)

- NIH Stroke Scale (NIHSS): level of consciousness · gaze · visual fields · face · arm and leg · limb ataxia · sensation · language · dysarthria · extinction and inattention → is it a stroke, where, and how severe

- Localize before you look at the scan: you know where to look for subtle early ischemic change and which vessels to study - suspected basilar thrombosis → always a CT angiogram (a normal plain CT has missed basilar clots that ended in locked-in syndrome) - and you will not be misled by incidental findings or old infarcts

- Goals: door to imaging under 25 minutes · door to needle under 60 minutes

- Imaging, in order

1. Non-contrast CT head: rule out hemorrhage (an absolute contraindication to tPA) · look for early ischemic change = infarcted, unsalvageable brain · the more early ischemic change, the higher the bleeding rate with tPA

2. CT angiogram (CTA): a large vessel occlusion?

3. CT perfusion (CTP): a perfusion mismatch = the best measure of salvageable brain

blocks.cap: Early ischemic change on CT: an acute infarct beside normal brain

blocks.html: 5. tPA and thrombectomy

• tPA up to 4.5 hours after onset - the earlier the better
    • 0.9 mg/kg: 10% as a bolus over 1 minute, the rest over 1 hour
    • risk of significant hemorrhage: 6% - vessels downstream of the clot were ischemic and leaky, and leak or burst when flow returns
    • more patients have minimal or no disability at 3 months (+13%, number needed to treat 7.7)
  • Exclusion criteria for tPA
    • intracerebral hemorrhage on CT, or ever · significant early ischemic change (may not treat if over 1/3 of the MCA territory)
    • symptoms suggesting subarachnoid hemorrhage, or a seizure at onset
    • BP over 185/110 despite treatment
    • stroke or serious head trauma under 3 months · major surgery under 14 days · gastrointestinal or urinary bleed under 21 days · arterial puncture at a non-compressible site, or a lumbar puncture, under 7 days
    • platelets under 100,000 · INR over 1.4 · PTT over 40 s · a factor Xa inhibitor in the last 24-48 hours
    • glucose under 3 or over 22 · caution in pregnancy, pericarditis, endocarditis
  • Thrombectomy: a proximal large vessel occlusion with a perfusion mismatch → formal angiogram and clot extraction (stent retriever), under sedation or general anesthetic
  • Only 10-20% are tPA candidates (too late, unwitnessed onset, anticoagulated, too mild, hemorrhagic) and under 5% thrombectomy candidates · not a tPA candidate can still be a thrombectomy candidate (on anticoagulants, over 4.5 hours)

blocks.alt: mechanical thrombectomy stent retriever - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: Thrombectomy: a stent retriever pulls the clot out and restores flow

blocks.html: 6. Stroke unit and finding the cause

• Admission orders: careful BP monitoring for 24 hours · imaging 24 hours after tPA · nothing by mouth until a speech-language assessment · bed rest 24 hours · cholesterol and glucose · telemetry · echo · physiotherapy, occupational therapy, social work
  • No hemorrhage at 24 hours → ASA, DVT prophylaxis and a statin from 24 hours · feeding by the swallowing assessment · intensive rehabilitation · rehabilitation hospital once stable (ideally within a week)
    • intensive rehabilitation offers better outcomes than even tPA · most recovery in 3 months, some up to a year
  • Risk factors: modifiable - hypertension, diabetes, cholesterol, smoking, atrial fibrillation, heart disease, inactivity, obesity, cocaine or amphetamines, postpartum, bleeding disorders and anticoagulants · non-modifiable - age, sex, ethnicity, family history
  • Directed investigations: secondary prevention is aimed at the cause
    • large artery: anterior circulation → carotid imaging · posterior circulation → vertebral and basilar imaging (no need to image the carotids) · MRA, CTA or Dopplers
    • cardioembolic: echo (transthoracic, transesophageal, bubble study for an atrial septal defect or patent foramen ovale) · telemetry or Holter for atrial fibrillation
    • atherosclerosis risk: glucose and HbA1c · lipids · BP
7. Secondary prevention

rows: Anticoagulation, usually started about 2 weeks after the stroke
Antiplatelet: ASA 81 mg for most · clopidogrel if ASA fails · both for some high-risk patients
Symptomatic carotid stenosis over 70% (same side, presumed carotid embolus)
Endarterectomy or stenting · under 70%, or asymptomatic stenosis → maximal medical management

blocks.html:
• Plus: BP under 140/90 · glucose · high-dose statin if tolerated · physical activity · nutrition and weight · smoking cessation
  • Primary prevention: reduce every modifiable risk factor · consider low-dose ASA with multiple risk factors · anticoagulate atrial fibrillation with a high CHADS2 score
8. Transient ischemic attack

• Brief, transient symptoms that resolve completely
  • Immediate management: CT head to rule out mimics (a subdural hematoma or tumour can cause transient symptoms) · start an antiplatelet (ASA in most) · already on ASA → add clopidogrel for 21 days · refer to a TIA clinic
  • Crescendo TIAs (several) → neurology for admission: very high stroke risk
  • TIA clinic: echo · Holter · CTA or carotid Dopplers · lipids, glucose, BP · then manage as secondary stroke prevention
  • Listen to the heart (a cardioembolic source) and for carotid bruits (carotid stenosis)
9. Hemorrhagic stroke

• Intracerebral hemorrhage causes (in order of frequency)
    • hypertensive arteriopathy → deep bleeds (pons, basal ganglia, thalamus, cerebellum)
    • congophilic (amyloid) angiopathy → lobar bleeds in the white matter just under the cortex
    • tumour (usually a metastasis) · arteriovenous malformation, cavernoma, aneurysm · coagulopathy
  • Outlook: good if the bleed does not expand, shift or herniate and complications are avoided - function improves as the blood is reabsorbed
  • Treatment: BP under 160/110 (some studies suggest under 140/90) · hold all antiplatelets and anticoagulants · mechanical DVT prophylaxis, then repeat CT at 24 hours - no clot extension → low-molecular-weight heparin prophylaxis · MRI or CTA for the cause · surgery very rarely (only an accessible clot raising intracranial pressure) · rehabilitation
  • Subarachnoid hemorrhage: a sudden, explosive "worst headache of my life", then nausea and vomiting · usually a ruptured aneurysm (or trauma) · admit to neurosurgery · urgent CTA or MRA to find the aneurysm · coiling or clipping by its shape and site · risks: re-bleeding before it is secured, vasospasm → ischemic stroke, medical complications

blocks.title: Schulich Reviews
blocks.html:
• With no tPA or thrombectomy, BP may be allowed up to about 210/120 for 48 hours, and the antiplatelet is started straight away
  • Subarachnoid hemorrhage: CT, then a lumbar puncture for xanthochromia if the CT is negative (the headache lecture teaches this; see 06 - Approach to Headache)

lectures.name: Approach to Sensory Symptoms
lectures.title: Approach to sensory symptoms
lectures.framing: Localize first: is the numbness central or peripheral, and where along the path? A truncal sensory level with brisk reflexes is the spinal cord; a symmetric, distal, burning picture that develops over years is a length-dependent polyneuropathy (diabetes); weakness ascending over days with lost reflexes is Guillain-Barré syndrome.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ A truncal sensory level (with brisk reflexes below it) is the spinal cord, not a neuropathy. Guillain-Barré: weakness ascending over days after an infection, with lost reflexes - watch the breathing; IVIG shortens it. Diabetic neuropathy: distal, symmetric, burning, with autonomic symptoms; shooting pain down one leg is a root. S1 root: little toe and sole numb, ankle reflex gone. Nocturnal hand tingling relieved by shaking is carpal tunnel: splint, don't image. Demyelination recovers in up to 12 weeks; axons regrow 1-2 mm a day.

blocks.html: 1. Localizing sensory symptoms

• Central or peripheral?
    • central: brain cortex · subcortical · brainstem · spinal cord
    • peripheral: dorsal root ganglion · root · one nerve (mononeuropathy) · many nerves (polyneuropathy: length-dependent, or mononeuritis multiplex)
  • A truncal sensory level is what best separates an acute spinal cord lesion from an acute peripheral nerve lesion - bladder urgency, back pain, absent reflexes and symmetric weakness do not
  • A thalamic lesion (e.g. a hemorrhage) → as it recovers, a clumsy hand and burning pain on the opposite side - not neglect (cortex), not muscle atrophy (nerve)
  • A root (e.g. S1 after lifting a heavy patient): back pain radiating down the leg · loss of pinprick and temperature over the little toe and sole · an absent Achilles (ankle) reflex
2. How peripheral nerves are damaged

rows: Channels that keep the resting potential or fire the action potential fail briefly · no gross damage
lidocaine (a sodium channel blocker) · hypothermia · brief compression
The axon breaks down beyond a focal injury in an otherwise healthy nerve
Crush, laceration, injection · severe ischemia (vasculitis) · severe metabolic or toxic insult
Sprouts grow 1-2 mm a day: months to years · depends on the endoneurium, Schwann cells and reaching the right target
The far end of the axon degenerates first, then further back
Metabolic: diabetes, kidney failure · drugs: vincristine, cisplatin, metronidazole · lead, arsenic, mercury, acrylamide · hereditary
Possible if the cause is removed, but slow and often incomplete
Myelin breaks down over one to several internodes → conduction fails
Immune: Guillain-Barré syndrome, chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (CIDP) · diphtheria toxin · hereditary
The cell body dies (anterior horn or dorsal root ganglion)
Motor: amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, polio, West Nile · sensory: paraneoplastic, Sjögren, vitamin B6 toxicity, cisplatin

blocks.html:
• Nerve injury after trauma
    • neurapraxia: functional block and demyelination, axon intact (compression, brief ischemia) → complete recovery in weeks to 3 months
    • axonotmesis: Wallerian degeneration with Schwann cells and endoneurium preserved (many crush injuries) → 3-12 months, may be incomplete over long distances
    • neurotmesis: axon and connective tissue cut, complete loss of function → limited regrowth, surgical repair often needed

blocks.cap: Where neuropathy causes act: systemic causes everywhere, root and plexus causes proximally, compression and trauma distally

blocks.html: 3. Characterizing a peripheral neuropathy

• Which fibres: sensory · motor · autonomic - sensory only, sensorimotor, or sensory and autonomic?
  • Time course: acute (days to 6 weeks) · subacute (6 weeks to 6 months) · chronic (over 6 months)
  • Pattern (once a root or plexus is excluded): length-dependent polyneuropathy · mononeuropathy · mononeuritis multiplex
  • Axonal or demyelinating: best shown on EMG
4. Three patterns to tell apart

rows: Everything below a level on the trunk
Can reach the cranial nerves and breathing muscles → respiratory failure, sometimes intubation
MRI of the brain and spinal cord (suspicious for MS)
Treat the pain: an analgesic or an antidepressant
IVIG shortens the course · slow recovery over weeks to months · best treated by a neurologist

blocks.html:
• Diabetes is the most common cause of peripheral neuropathy in Canada: axonal (large and small fibres) · distal (stocking-glove) · symmetric · sensorimotor · often painful
    • shooting pain down one leg is a root, not the diabetic neuropathy (he also has degenerative disc disease)
    • other causes: infection (HIV, leprosy) · drugs · metabolic (uremia, thyroid) · autoimmune · hereditary · idiopathic
  • Guillain-Barré syndrome = acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (AIDP): autoimmune, antibody-mediated, often after an infection (antigen mimicry)
  • Hands numb at night, relieved by shaking, normal exam → carpal tunnel, not MS: no imaging; nocturnal wrist splints help
  • MS in brief: the most common acquired demyelinating disease of the central nervous system · patchy plaques in the brain and cord · dissemination in time and space · 85% relapsing-remitting (some become secondary progressive), 15% primary progressive (see 02 - Multiple Sclerosis)

blocks.cap: Stocking-and-glove distribution of a length-dependent polyneuropathy

lectures.name: Neuropathic Pain
lectures.title: Neuropathic pain
lectures.framing: Neuropathic pain comes from a damaged or malfunctioning nervous system, not from injured tissue, so it is treated differently from ordinary (nociceptive) pain. Recognize it by its symptoms, find the cause, then choose one agent to fit what else the patient has and titrate it slowly to the maximum dose.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Allodynia = pain from a non-painful touch; hyperpathia = too much pain from a painful one; dysesthesia = uncomfortable sensations such as burning. Neuropathic pain is not treated like nociceptive pain: acetaminophen and NSAIDs are for tissue pain. Poor sleep or cost → amitriptyline; depression → duloxetine; trigeminal neuralgia → carbamazepine; narcotics last. One drug at a time, titrated to the maximum - change it for side effects first, or no effect after a month at the top dose. CRPS: more pain, for longer, than the injury explains, with swelling, temperature, colour and skin changes.

blocks.html: 1. Two kinds of pain

rows: Tissue injury, inflammation, temperature, pressure or stretch
Peripheral or central nervous system injury or dysfunction

blocks.html: 2. Symptoms

• Allodynia = pain from a non-painful touch (sheets brushing across the feet)
  • Hyperpathia = a painful stimulus provokes an exaggerated amount of pain (pinprick testing is extremely painful)
  • Dysesthesia = uncomfortable sensations (burning pain)
  • Descriptors patients use: electrical · shooting · burning, hot or cold · pins and needles
3. Causes

rows: Length-dependent neuropathy: diabetic · small fibre sensory · chemotherapy-induced
Lesions of the thalamus · brainstem · spinal cord
Radiculopathy · postherpetic neuralgia · trigeminal neuralgia · nerve injury
Phantom limb pain likely has a central part

blocks.html:
• Small fibre neuropathy (toes "on fire" at night, a length-dependent small fibre neuropathy): diabetes is the most common cause; without diabetes most are idiopathic, and some are genetic (from the module)
  • If neuropathic pain is present: evaluate the cause and examine - is there an important neurological diagnosis? Some causes are reversible, and classic syndromes respond to specific drugs (trigeminal neuralgia → carbamazepine)
  • Complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS): an uncommon chronic pain syndrome after a focal tissue or nerve injury, with inflammatory and autonomic features · pain greater than the injury explains, lasting longer than healing should take · the limb: severe pain and allodynia, swelling, temperature and colour changes, skin and hair changes · peripheral and central sensitization · treatment is hard and multidisciplinary
  • Background, nice to know: after nerve damage, ↑ sodium and ↓ potassium channels make neurons hyperexcitable, firing on their own (spontaneous, paroxysmal pain) · injury can cause central sensitization in the spinal cord, which early treatment can avoid · norepinephrine and serotonin drive the descending pain-inhibiting pathways, so raising them increases inhibition
4. Treatment

rows: gabapentin · pregabalin · in specific situations a sodium-channel drug, carbamazepine
Narcotics only as a last resort

blocks.html:
• Trial and error: trial one agent and titrate it up slowly to the maximum dose
    • significant side effects before an appropriate effect → change the drug
    • no effect after 1 month at the highest dose → change the drug

lectures.name: Approach to Headache
lectures.title: Approach to headache
lectures.framing: Rule out a secondary headache - rare, but potentially life-threatening - while you decide whether there is a primary headache disorder, which can also badly affect quality of life and may need treatment. The SNOOP4 red flags point to the secondary causes; with none, the features of the attack name the primary headache: migraine, tension-type or cluster.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Screen every headache with SNOOP4 first: a thunderclap headache is a subarachnoid hemorrhage until an urgent CT - and a lumbar puncture for xanthochromia if the CT is negative - says otherwise. Over 50 with scalp tenderness and jaw claudication → ESR, CRP and high-dose steroids today, before the biopsy. Fever and a stiff neck → antibiotics before any scan or lumbar puncture. Obese, worse lying down, pulsatile tinnitus, papilledema → MRI and MR venogram before the lumbar puncture. Tension-type: both sides, pressing, no nausea; migraine: one side, pulsating, worse with activity; cluster: strictly one side at the eye, restless, with same-side autonomic signs. Triptans at onset, never with coronary disease; acute drugs on under 2-3 days a week. First preventive: beta-blocker or amitriptyline; high BMI → topiramate.

blocks.html: 1. History and examination

• History: the pain in detail (NILDOCAAFIAT: Nature (quality) · Intensity (0-10) · Location · Duration · Onset (acute or gradual) · Contributing triggers · Aggravating · Alleviating · Frequency · Impact on function · Attribute (what they think causes it) · Treatment tried) + the features of a secondary headache (SNOOP4, below)
  • Examination, and why
    • vital signs: high BP can itself cause headache · infection changes the vitals · some headache drugs change BP and heart rate
    • fundoscopy: papilledema raises concern for raised intracranial pressure
    • pupils, light responses, eye movements, visual fields · neurological exam: a neuro-ophthalmological or focal deficit suggests a secondary headache
    • body habitus: obesity → idiopathic intracranial hypertension; a large neck and obesity → obstructive sleep apnea
    • neck: marked stiffness → meningeal irritation (meningitis) · neck muscle pain can present as headache
    • scalp: tenderness → giant cell arteritis · temporomandibular joint: its disorders can present as headache
2. Red flags: SNOOP4

rows: Systemic symptoms: fever, chills, weight loss
Worse lying down → mass or raised pressure · worse upright → low pressure (intracranial hypotension)
Progressive, or a substantial change in pattern

blocks.html:
• Secondary causes
    • vascular: ischemic stroke · intracerebral hemorrhage · subarachnoid hemorrhage · cerebral venous thrombosis · posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES) · reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome (RCVS) · cranio-cervical artery dissection · vasculitis
    • idiopathic or inflammatory: giant cell (temporal) arteritis · idiopathic intracranial hypertension
    • trauma: after a dural puncture · concussion · drugs and toxins: medication overuse headache
    • neoplastic: meningioma · vestibular schwannoma · pituitary adenoma (apoplexy) · choriocarcinoma · infectious: meningitis, encephalitis · systemic infection
3. Secondary headaches not to miss

rows: Thunderclap: worst ever, peaks within seconds · nausea, vomiting, photophobia · neck stiffness
Urgent non-contrast CT (sensitivity 98% day 0 · 76% day 2 · 50% at 1 week · 30% at 2 weeks) → negative: lumbar puncture for xanthochromia
Secure the aneurysm (03 - Approach to Stroke) · untreated, re-bleeds 15% in 24 hours, 40% within a month
Fever, headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, altered mental status · Kernig and Brudzinski signs
Blood cultures · lumbar puncture if safe (image first if signs of raised pressure)
IV ceftriaxone + vancomycin at once (± ampicillin if elderly or immunocompromised, ± acyclovir if herpes simplex encephalitis is possible) · never delayed for imaging or lumbar puncture
Giant cell arteritis (the most common vasculitis; over 50)
New headache · scalp tenderness · visual disturbance (amaurosis fugax, blurring, double vision) · jaw claudication · constitutional and polymyalgic symptoms · limb claudication
ESR and CRP · temporal artery biopsy or ultrasound · can be normal: the disease is patchy
High-dose glucocorticoids started at once, without waiting for confirmation, then tapered · untreated → permanent vision loss
Steady, persistent, often worse in the morning · nausea or vomiting · worse with coughing, exercise or position · does not respond to usual remedies · personality change, seizure, focal deficit
Urgent MRI with contrast (CT if no MRI) · papilledema = raised pressure · CT chest, abdomen and pelvis: primary or metastasis?
Worse lying down · pulsatile tinnitus · horizontal double vision (sixth nerve palsy) · transient visual obscurations · visual defects · risk: obesity, steroids, vitamin A, tetracycline
MRI with MR venography before the lumbar puncture (empty sella, flattened posterior globe, venous sinus stenosis) · opening pressure over 250 mm H2O
Weight loss · acetazolamide, topiramate · shunt or optic nerve sheath fenestration · close eye follow-up

blocks.html: 4. Primary headaches: migraine, tension-type, cluster

rows: 3rd most prevalent, 7th most disabling condition worldwide
15-180 minutes, every other day to 8 a day
Strictly one side: around and above the eye, temple
Nausea or vomiting · light AND sound sensitivity
No nausea, at most one of light or sound sensitivity
Same-side red, watering eye · blocked or runny nose · forehead sweating · small pupil, droopy eyelid · lid swelling

blocks.html:
• Migraine phases: prodrome (2-48 hours: yawning, fatigue, mood change, cravings, neck stiffness) → aura in 25-30% (5-60 minutes per symptom: gradually spreading, fully reversible - mostly visual zigzags and scintillating scotoma, or tingling; less often speech, motor, brainstem, retinal) → headache (4-72 hours untreated) → postdrome (24-48 hours, "migraine hangover")
    • abnormal activation of the trigeminovascular system releases neuropeptides, especially calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP)
    • diagnosis without aura: 5-4-3-2-1 - at least 5 attacks · 4-72 hours (4 hours to 3 days) · 2 of 4 (one side, pulsating, moderate-severe, worse with routine activity) · 1 of 2 (nausea or vomiting; light and sound sensitivity)
  • Tension-type diagnosis: at least 10 episodes (or 3 months if chronic) · 30 minutes to 7 days · 2 of 4 (both sides, pressing, mild-moderate, not worse with activity) · no nausea or vomiting and no more than one of light or sound sensitivity
  • Cluster is a trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia, driven by the hypothalamus: hence its circadian and seasonal clustering

blocks.cap: Phases of a migraine attack: triggers, prodrome, aura, headache, postdrome

blocks.html: 5. Managing primary headaches

• Medication overuse headache: headache on 15 or more days a month in someone with a primary headache, from overusing acute drugs for over 3 months - simple analgesics and NSAIDs on 15 or more days a month, triptans on 10 or more · it usually resolves once the overuse stops · frequent acute use → consider prevention
  • Tension-type: acute - over-the-counter acetaminophen, ibuprofen, naproxen · preventive - amitriptyline, mirtazapine, venlafaxine, tizanidine
  • Migraine, acute: treat EARLY in the attack · use on under 2-3 days a week · combine treatments for a better effect
    • NSAIDs: ibuprofen 200-800 mg (max 2,400 a day, rapid) · diclofenac 50 mg (max 150) · naproxen 550 mg (max 1,375, slow) · ketorolac 30-60 mg IM or IV · avoid with a gastrointestinal bleed, bleeding risk, peptic ulcer, kidney impairment, pregnancy
    • Triptans (serotonin 5-HT1B/1D agonists): take at onset, repeat in 2-24 hours if needed · can combine with an NSAID · subcutaneous sumatriptan 6 mg · nasal sumatriptan or zolmitriptan · oral sumatriptan, zolmitriptan, rizatriptan, naratriptan, almotriptan, eletriptan · side effects: nausea, chest and jaw tightness, flushing · not with coronary or cerebrovascular disease, uncontrolled hypertension, Raynaud's or peripheral vascular disease
    • antiemetics: dopamine blockers (metoclopramide 10 mg, prochlorperazine, promethazine) · ondansetron · antihistamines
  • Migraine prevention: when: disabling despite acute treatment · more than 4 attacks a month · acute drugs fail, are contraindicated or cause side effects · risk of medication overuse
    • how: match the drug to the patient's comorbidities, contraindications and side-effect profile (Canadian guidelines, 2012) · the module's example: with asthma, diabetes and obesity, choose topiramate - propranolol is relatively contraindicated by asthma and diabetes, and amitriptyline causes weight gain

rows: Beta-blocker (propranolol, nadolol, metoprolol) or tricyclic (amitriptyline, nortriptyline)
Candesartan · magnesium citrate, riboflavin (vitamin B2), coenzyme Q10
Venlafaxine (tricyclics do not treat mood at migraine doses)
Divalproex, pizotifen, flunarizine (more side effects) · verapamil, gabapentin, lisinopril (weak evidence)

blocks.html:
• strong recommendations: topiramate, propranolol, metoprolol, amitriptyline (high-quality evidence) · nadolol, gabapentin, candesartan, butterbur (moderate) · riboflavin, coenzyme Q10, magnesium (low)
  • OnabotulinumtoxinA: approved for chronic migraine only · every 3 months (12 weeks) · about half respond · well tolerated, effect sustained over years
  • CGRP inhibitors (newer): anti-CGRP monoclonal antibodies (erenumab, fremanezumab, galcanezumab, eptinezumab) - prevention, injection monthly or quarterly, slow onset, injection-site reactions and constipation · gepants (ubrogepant, rimegepant acute; atogepant, rimegepant preventive) - oral, acute ± prevention, rapid, nausea and sleepiness
  • lifestyle, SEEDS: Sleep · Exercise · Eat and drink well · Diary (Canadian Migraine Tracker app) · Stress
  • Cluster: acute - 100% oxygen, 12-15 L/min for 15 minutes by non-rebreather mask · subcutaneous sumatriptan 6 mg (most effective) · nasal sumatriptan or zolmitriptan · preventive - verapamil (most used) · lithium · topiramate · galcanezumab (episodic cluster) · bridge with prednisone or nerve blocks while prevention takes effect

blocks.title: Schulich Reviews
blocks.html:
• More than 4 migraine features → likely migraine
  • Acute migraine drugs by line: 1st ibuprofen 400 mg, ASA 1,000 mg, naproxen 500-550 mg or acetaminophen 1,000 mg · 2nd a triptan (subcutaneous sumatriptan if vomiting early) · 3rd naproxen + a triptan · 4th codeine combinations, not routinely
  • Cervical artery dissection: headache spreading to the neck or face + Horner syndrome · can cause a stroke
  • OnabotulinumtoxinA for chronic migraine is 31 injections

lectures.name: Approach to Altered Level of Consciousness
lectures.title: Approach to altered level of consciousness
lectures.framing: Consciousness has two parts: alertness (being awake: wakefulness, vigilance, responding to stimuli) and awareness (the content: everything the cortex does). First find what is treatable, then let the exam - brainstem reflexes, breathing, the motor response, eye opening, any sign of awareness - place the patient on the spectrum from brain death to minimally conscious.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Vegetative state is awake but not aware; locked-in syndrome is aware but cannot move - only upward gaze and eye opening are left. Look for the treatable causes (glucose, shock, drugs, meningitis, encephalitis, hematoma) before labelling a coma. Coma needs both hemispheres, both thalami, or the brainstem above the mid-pons. Decorticate = arms flex, above the red nucleus; decerebrate = all extend, below it; triple flexion is spinal. Minimally conscious minus vs plus = command following. The FOUR score works in an intubated patient; the GCS verbal score does not. GCS ≤ 8 = severe. Brain death = no brainstem reflexes + no breathing on apnea test + no confounders.

blocks.html: 1. What keeps us conscious

• Alertness (arousal) is the volume; awareness (content) is the tuning: you can be alert without being aware, but not aware without being alert
  • Both are kept up by the ascending reticular activating system: the reticular formation in the upper pons and midbrain projecting widely to the cerebral cortex, through the thalamus (intralaminar nuclei) and through the hypothalamus and basal forebrain

blocks.alt: ascending reticular activating system - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: Ascending reticular activating system: reticular formation in the upper pons and midbrain projecting through both thalami to the cortex

blocks.html: 2. Causes of coma, and what else to consider

• Coma = loss of both alertness and awareness · the system has to fail in one of three places:
    • both hemispheres (global cortical dysfunction): metabolic, toxic, hypoxic-ischemic injury, trauma, large bilateral destructive lesions
    • both thalami or the hypothalamus: stroke ("tip of the basilar" syndrome), destructive lesions (hemorrhage, tumour)
    • the brainstem above the mid-pons: trauma, stroke, herniation (central, uncal, falcine, midline shift) · consciousness falls with the degree and rate of shift, not its direction
  • Treatable causes to find first: shock or low blood pressure · low blood glucose · diabetic ketoacidosis · hypertensive encephalopathy · drug intoxication · bacterial or fungal meningitis · herpes simplex encephalitis · brain abscess · epidural or subdural hematoma
  • Other causes of an altered level of consciousness: syncope · seizure · the post-ictal state · encephalopathy or delirium
  • Coma mimics (aware, but cannot show it): locked-in syndrome · severe neuromuscular disease (Guillain-Barré syndrome, myasthenia gravis) · neuromuscular blockade (iatrogenic) · akinetic mutism · psychogenic unresponsiveness
3. Examining the unconscious patient

• Observe: how much stimulation it takes to get a response · agitation · any communication · breathing pattern and ventilator needs · spontaneous or asymmetric movement · automatisms (yawning, sneezing, coughing, swallowing, hiccoughing) · fundoscopy
  • Cranial nerve reflexes

rows: Size, shape, reactivity · a "blown" (Hutchinson) pupil = uncal herniation · a small pupil with ptosis = sympathetic loss (Horner's syndrome)
Only if there is no cervical spine concern · localizes supranuclear, internuclear, nuclear or nerve lesions
COWS is for awake patients only · in coma, an intact reflex = slow deviation toward the cold ear, no fast phase
Lift both lids, touch each cornea with a cotton wisp (or tissue, eye drops); watch for closure
Gag often absent in the ICU · suction catheter down the breathing tube for a deep cough · cough is often the last reflex lost

blocks.html:
• Motor: tone · spontaneous movement and command following (is it reproducible, not just a reflex?) · pain: central (sternum, trapezius, supraorbital ridge, mandible) or peripheral (nail bed) → grimace, localizing, withdrawal · tendon reflexes and plantar responses
    • Decorticate (flexor): arms flex, legs extend → lesion above the red nucleus (midbrain or above)
    • Decerebrate (extensor): arms and legs extend → lesion below the red nucleus (lower brainstem)
    • Triple flexion (hip, knee, ankle) = a spinal reflex, needs no brainstem
  • Coma scales

rows: Verbal cannot be scored: E2 VT M4 = 6T
Built for head trauma · does not assess the brainstem well

blocks.html: 4. Disorders of consciousness, and brain death

• Five syndromes: coma · vegetative state (unresponsive wakefulness syndrome) · minimally conscious minus · minimally conscious plus · emergence · locked-in syndrome is compared with them but is not a disorder of consciousness
  • Vegetative state: awake (sleep-wake cycles, autonomic function kept) but not aware · reflexive only: grimace, yawn, roving eyes, flexion withdrawal, decorticate posturing, brief unsustained pursuit · no language, no purposeful response, incontinent
  • Minimally conscious: limited but definite awareness · minus = visual pursuit, localizes pain, smiles or cries to stimuli, no commands · plus = follows commands · emerged = functional communication and object use
  • Functional MRI can show awareness the bedside misses (imagining tennis lights the motor areas as in healthy people)
  • Brain death (Canadian criteria), all of: a known cause and no reversible mimic · deep unresponsive coma, no motor response (spinal reflexes allowed) · no brainstem reflexes: gag, cough, and on both sides corneal, pupillary (pupils mid-size or larger), vestibulo-ocular · no breathing effort on the apnea test · no confounders · EEG electrocerebral silence · legally dead

blocks.cap: Disorders of consciousness: coma, unresponsive wakefulness, minimally conscious minus and plus, emergence; locked-in syndrome off to the side

lectures.name: Approach to Seizures
lectures.title: Approach to seizures
lectures.framing: After a first seizure the questions come in order: was it a seizure, was it provoked, and how likely is another? The workup exists to estimate that last number: a recurrence risk of 60% or more is the threshold for treatment, and the lesion on MRI or the discharges on EEG are what push it there.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ A single unprovoked seizure with a normal MRI and EEG → discuss treatment; a structural lesion, epileptiform discharges or a second unprovoked seizure over 24 hours apart makes it epilepsy (recurrence ≥ 60%) → recommend treatment. Provoked seizure (immediate post-traumatic, fever, glucose, sodium, alcohol) → treat the cause, no drug. Remote stroke or old trauma = unprovoked, not provoked. Onset not seen = unknown onset. Every first seizure gets an MRI and an EEG. Drug-resistant = 2 appropriate, tolerated drugs failed → refer to a comprehensive epilepsy centre (a third drug can be tried alongside the referral).

blocks.html: 1. Seizure, and how seizures are classified

• Epileptic seizure = a transient occurrence of signs or symptoms from abnormal excessive or synchronous neuronal activity in the brain
  • Classified by where it starts (International League Against Epilepsy, 2017)

rows: Motor onset (automatisms, clonic, tonic, epileptic spasms)
Non-motor = absence (3-Hz generalized spike-and-wave on EEG)

blocks.html: • A seizure that cannot be placed is unclassified

blocks.alt: focal vs. generalized vs. unkown onset seizures.png
blocks.cap: Focal, generalized and unknown onset seizures, with their secondary classifications

blocks.html: 2. The first seizure: was it one, and was it provoked?

• History is the key: details of the event · speak with witnesses, review ambulance records · anything that needs urgent evaluation (fever, trauma)
  • Seizure risk factors: febrile seizures or childhood epilepsy · significant head trauma · past meningitis or encephalitis · family history of seizures or epilepsy
  • Physical exam is often normal · tongue biting, musculoskeletal injuries · ⚠ enduring confusion, a low level of consciousness or a persistent focal deficit → urgent evaluation

rows: A transient factor acting on an otherwise normal brain temporarily lowers the threshold
No temporary or reversible factor · an enduring epileptogenic abnormality
Genetic conditions · remote structural lesions: brain tumour, old stroke, old brain trauma

blocks.html: 3. Investigations: estimating the risk of another seizure

• Bloodwork as the history needs · electrolytes, including extended electrolytes
  • CT often done acutely in the emergency department · rules out a clear structural cause (hemorrhage, tumour)
  • MRI is required in every first-seizure workup · epilepsy protocol, with a dedicated look at the temporal lobes · a structural abnormality raises the recurrence risk
  • EEG is required · epileptiform activity raises the recurrence risk · childhood absence epilepsy: abrupt 3-Hz generalized spike-and-wave with staring
4. To treat or not to treat

rows: Do not treat - treat the underlying cause

blocks.html:
• Epilepsy (operational definition), any one of:
    • 2 unprovoked (or reflex) seizures more than 24 hours apart
    • 1 unprovoked seizure + a recurrence risk of at least 60% over the next 10 years (as after two seizures: a lesion on MRI, discharges on EEG)
    • an epilepsy syndrome
  • Classifying an epilepsy: seizure type → epilepsy type (focal, generalized, combined generalized and focal, unknown) → epilepsy syndrome · etiology at every level:
    • structural (stroke, trauma, tumour, mesial temporal sclerosis) · genetic (inherited, de novo or mosaic, polygenic) · infectious (viral encephalitis, bacterial meningitis, neurocysticercosis) · metabolic (inborn errors) · immune (autoimmune or paraneoplastic: anti-NMDA receptor, anti-LGI1, anti-Hu, anti-GAD65) · unknown
  • Syndromes (by age): childhood absence epilepsy · juvenile myoclonic epilepsy · benign Rolandic epilepsy · West syndrome · Dravet syndrome · Lennox-Gastaut syndrome
  • Comorbidities: non-epileptic seizures · depression, anxiety, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder · migraine · cognitive impairment · sudden unexpected death in epilepsy (SUDEP)
5. Chronic management of epilepsy

• Choosing a drug: one drug or several · treats a comorbidity too (headache, mood) · side effects · dose range · adherence · blood levels · titration, cross-titration, weaning · drug interactions · cost and coverage · age · pregnancy: teratogenicity

• Drug-resistant epilepsy = 2 tolerated, appropriately chosen and used drugs (alone or combined) have failed to give sustained seizure freedom (3 times the prior gap between seizures, or 1 year, whichever is longer)
    • first drug → second drug (switch or combine) → refer to a comprehensive epilepsy centre, trying a third drug alongside the referral: confirm it is epilepsy · rule out non-epileptic seizures and pseudoresistance (wrong diagnosis, wrong dose, nonadherence) · ketogenic diet, behavioural therapy
    • presurgical evaluation: MRI, PET, ictal SPECT, functional MRI · long-term video-EEG · neuropsychological testing · Wada test → intracranial EEG if needed
    • surgery: resection (temporal-lobe surgery beat medical therapy in a randomized trial) · laser thermal therapy (deep lesion, mesial temporal sclerosis) · responsive neurostimulation (onset in eloquent cortex, or 2 foci) · vagus nerve stimulation (generalized onset, or more than 2 foci)

blocks.title: Schulich Reviews
blocks.html:
• Focal seizures (one hemisphere, usually under 2 minutes): aura or prodrome, automatisms, Jacksonian march, non-motor symptoms; generalized seizures start with loss of consciousness and usually last under 5 minutes
  • Todd's paresis = post-ictal weakness of the involved limb, lasting minutes to 36 hours
  • Triggers to ask about: sleep deprivation, alcohol
  • Creatine kinase peaks about 6 hours after a tonic-clonic seizure
  • Status epilepticus = a continuous seizure over 5 minutes · complications: cerebral edema, hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis, cardiovascular failure
  • Acute treatment: IV lorazepam or diazepam → IV fosphenytoin, valproic acid or levetiracetam
  • Long-term first line: lamotrigine for focal, valproate for generalized, ethosuximide for absence
  • A first focal aware seizure in an older adult: CT head, complete blood count, electrolytes, glucose in the emergency department; EEG and MRI later

lectures.name: Recovery in the Nervous System
lectures.title: Recovery in the nervous system
lectures.framing: A cut axon always loses its far end; whether it grows back depends on where it is. Peripheral axons can regrow along the empty Schwann cell tube when the stumps meet; central axons are held back by their surroundings, not by an inability to grow, and the brain recovers mainly by plasticity.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Central axons regrow inside a peripheral nerve graft (Aguayo) - so it is the central environment, not the neuron, that blocks regeneration. Peripheral regrowth needs stump-to-stump contact and the empty Schwann cell tube, helped by laminin and nerve growth factor. Crush injury → poorer regeneration and traumatic neuroma. Facial nerve regrowth gone wrong → synkinesis, including tears while eating. After axotomy: Wallerian degeneration distally, central chromatolysis in the cell body.

blocks.html: 1. From axotomy to reconnection

• Both stumps swell, the proximal and the distal
  • Beyond the cut (distal): Wallerian degeneration - myelin breaks into myelin ovoids · the segment cut off from the cell body degenerates and is cleared · the muscle it supplied atrophies
  • The cell body: central chromatolysis (the Nissl substance disperses)
  • Across synapses: trans-synaptic degeneration can spread upstream or downstream
  • Regrowth: sprouts with growth cones extend from the proximal stump in search of a target, steered by trophic factors and extracellular matrix molecules - not at random → reconnection with a target
  • Not the same as segmental demyelination (myelin lost, axon intact) or axonal degeneration (the axon dying back from its far end)

blocks.cap: After a cut: Wallerian degeneration of the distal axon, debris cleared, then the axon regrows and is remyelinated

blocks.html: 2. Peripheral vs central regeneration

rows: Sprouts grow from the proximal stump along the empty distal Schwann cell tube
Stump-to-stump contact · laminin, nerve growth factor and other factors
Albert Aguayo: central axons regrew into a peripheral nerve graft → the central environment, not the neuron, blocks it
Plasticity: ongoing remodelling of dendrites and dendritic spines

blocks.html: • Conditions for peripheral regeneration: close stumps · an intact Schwann cell tube to follow · a clean cut rather than a crush or maceration (a crush makes regeneration less likely)
3. When regeneration goes wrong

• Misguided, haphazard sprouting reaches the wrong target
  • Synkinesis: after a facial nerve injury, fibres reinnervate the wrong target · orbicularis oculi instead of orbicularis oris · the lacrimal gland instead of a salivary gland (tears while eating) · it shows that regeneration happened
  • Traumatic neuroma: a tangle of regrowing axons · more likely after a crush or macerating injury than a clean cut · can cause chronic pain

lectures.name: Neurosurgical Emergencies
lectures.title: Neurosurgical emergencies
lectures.framing: Headache, coma, a new neurological deficit or trauma bring a patient to neurosurgery, and the cause is almost always PRESSURE inside a closed skull: hemorrhage, tumour or trauma. The decision is what is taking up the space, because emergency neurosurgery is decompression, and blood, a tumour's edema and trapped cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) are each removed or shrunk a different way. Head injury grading and the herniation types are in 01 - Approach to Head Injuries.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Mannitol shrinks brain that still has an intact blood-brain barrier; dexamethasone shrinks a tumour's vasogenic edema by restoring a broken one. Epidural: lens-shaped, arterial, lucid interval, blown pupil on the same side - early decompression does predictably well. Acute subdural: crescent, bridging veins, outcome unpredictable. Ruptured aneurysm: re-rupture 6% day 1, 20% at 2 weeks, 50% at 6 months - repair early. Hydrocephalus: external ventricular drain now, shunt later; untreated it kills by herniation. Intubate for GCS < 9.

blocks.html: 1. The neurosurgical exam: localize, don't just reassure

• Level of consciousness: Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS): eyes /4, verbal /5, motor /6 · ⚠ intubate for GCS < 9 to protect the airway
  • Cranial nerves: II acuity, fields, fundus · III pupillary response and eye movements · V facial sensation, chewing muscles, corneal reflex · VII facial droop · VIII hearing · IX and X gag · XI shrug · XII tongue
  • Motor: pronator drift · bulk, tone, power, reflexes · hands, arms, legs, feet · compare the sides
  • Sensory: light touch, pinprick, proprioception · find the sensory level on the trunk · cerebellar exam
  • ⚠ "GCS 15, moving x 4" can hide a patient with 1/5 hand intrinsics and 0/5 legs: a T1 spinal cord injury
2. The bleeds: which space, and what to do

rows: Middle meningeal artery, between dura and skull
Bridging veins to the dural sinuses, under the dura
Ruptured aneurysm, in the subarachnoid space
Blow to the side of the head · stunned · lucid interval (played on with a headache) · then cannot be woken
High-energy trauma (rollover, intoxicated, on ASA) · comatose
Explosive headache unlike any other · vomiting · photophobia · stiff neck · retinal hemorrhage · can be GCS 15
Blown pupil on the side of the clot (third nerve) · the opposite side weaker
<mark class="lo">Blood in the subarachnoid space</mark> · lumbar puncture: blood in the CSF
Evacuate · outcome unpredictable, set by the brain injury underneath
Early aneurysm repair · protects against the next bleed only

blocks.html: • Why a ruptured aneurysm is an emergency: a single hemorrhage brings 50% death and 75% disability · re-rupture: 6% on day 1, 20% by 2 weeks, 50% by 6 months · outcome depends on the neurological status at presentation

blocks.alt: epidural vs subdural hematoma CT - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: CT: epidural hematoma is lens-shaped (convex), subdural hematoma is a crescent

blocks.html: 3. Lowering the pressure: medical decompression

rows: Make room for a mass or swollen, damaged brain
Restores the blood-brain barrier in leaky tumour vessels → the edema and the "effective" tumour size shrink
Osmotic shrinkage of brain with an intact blood-brain barrier

blocks.html: • Brain tumour: weeks of progressive deficit (word-finding difficulty, slurred speech, a clumsy hand) then a rapid fall in consciousness → intubate if GCS < 9 → image → dexamethasone + mannitol → resect once stable (72 hours later in the lecture's case)
4. Hydrocephalus

• Hydrocephalus: CSF trapped in the ventricles squeezes the brain from inside · e.g. after bacterial meningitis: a febrile teenager who cannot be roused, dysconjugate gaze, cloudy CSF
  • Untreated hydrocephalus can kill: death and disability come from brain herniation
  • Divert the CSF: short term an external ventricular drain (placed in the emergency department) · long term a ventriculoperitoneal shunt · treat the cause (antibiotics)

blocks.title: Schulich Reviews
blocks.html:
• Epidural hematoma: a contact injury (a fall onto cement), skull fracture in about 80%; torn dural vessels, the middle meningeal artery in about 50%; brief loss of consciousness → lucid interval → coma; operate if symptomatic or an acute clot is 1 cm or more; mortality about 25%
  • Subdural hematoma: acceleration-deceleration (car accident); elderly and people with alcohol use disorder; slow, progressive fall in consciousness; goes with diffuse axonal injury; mortality about 30%, worse with a lower GCS
  • Traumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage: torn pial vessels; blood is patchy or lobar, where an aneurysmal bleed sits near the cisterns and the middle, anterior and posterior cerebral arteries; CT angiography next; complications include intraventricular hemorrhage and hydrocephalus
  • Traumatic intracerebral hemorrhage: a well-defined, homogeneous, hyperdense bleed on non-contrast CT, in the frontal and temporal lobes; control the blood pressure, reverse any coagulopathy; half die within a month
  • Lowering intracranial pressure: head of the bed up 30°, neck midline, collar loosened · intubate, sedate, cool, drain CSF, paralyze, temporary hyperventilation · adequate blood pressure · mannitol or hypertonic saline (23.4% bolus, 3% longer term)
  • Hydrocephalus is common in children; a child weeks after meningitis with headache, an abnormal gait, raised pressure and no fever = hydrocephalus

lectures.name: Neuroinfections
lectures.title: Neuroinfections
lectures.framing: Suspected meningitis is a race: culture the blood, then start empiric treatment at once - never held back for the CT or the lumbar puncture. The CT comes first only with focal signs or a decreased level of consciousness; the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) then tells bacterial from viral, and cortical signs (language trouble, focal seizures) point to herpes simplex encephalitis.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Blood culture, then empiric treatment at once (ceftriaxone + vancomycin + dexamethasone with the first dose, + acyclovir; + ampicillin if over 50 or immunocompromised); CT first only with focal signs or a decreased level of consciousness. Neutrophils + low glucose (ratio < 0.3) + positive Gram stain = bacterial; lymphocytes + normal glucose = viral. Language trouble, focal seizures and no stiff neck → herpes simplex encephalitis: mesial temporal MRI, CSF HSV PCR, IV acyclovir 10 mg/kg q8h. Listeria: over 50 or immunocompromised. Neonates: E. coli and group B strep. Gram-negative diplococci = N. meningitidis.

blocks.html: 1. Infections of the central nervous system

• Four kinds of organism: bacterial (bacterial meningitis, abscess) · viral (viral meningitis, viral encephalitis) · fungal (cryptococcal) · protozoal (neurocysticercosis)
  • Where it sits: meningitis (the meninges) · encephalitis (the brain tissue) · abscess (walled off)

blocks.cap: Meningitis, encephalitis, meningoencephalitis and abscess: where in the brain each infection sits

blocks.html: 2. Meningitis vs encephalitis: how they present

• Classic triad of meningitis: fever · altered mental status · nuchal rigidity
  • Aseptic (viral) meningitis: no organism isolated · headache, fever, mild meningeal signs, photophobia, rash · not very sick
3. The plan for suspected meningitis

• 1. Culture a blood sample → 2. start empiric antibiotics → 3. focal CNS signs or a decreased level of consciousness? absent → lumbar puncture · present → CT/MRI first (a mass lesion → neurosurgery, none → lumbar puncture) → 4. adjust the antibiotics
  • CT before the lumbar puncture (PUNISH): Papilledema (or poorly visualized fundi) · Unconscious or abnormal level of consciousness · Neurologic deficit (focal) · Immunocompromised · Seizure (new, within a week) · History of CNS disease (mass, stroke, focal infection) · also anyone from an area where neurocysticercosis is endemic
4. Reading the CSF

• Glucose ratio (CSF ÷ serum, drawn together): normal > 0.6 · < 0.3 identifies 70% of bacterial meningitis (the summary table uses < 0.4)
  • In the blood: a CRP > 40 and positive blood cultures also point to bacteria
5. Empiric treatment of bacterial meningitis in adults (all IV)

rows: H. influenzae · N. meningitidis · penicillin-susceptible S. pneumoniae · MSSA
In the lecture's empiric order for a healthy adult
10 mg with the first antibiotic dose, then every 6 h for 4 days
↓ illness and death, most for S. pneumoniae

blocks.html:
• Complications: sepsis · hydrocephalus · cranial nerve palsies · vasculitis → stroke · cerebritis · abscess · seizures · coma · death
  • Aseptic meningitis: supportive, rehydration
6. Herpes simplex encephalitis

• The most common and important viral encephalitis · headache, fever, language disturbance, confusion, decreased awareness
  • Confirm the diagnosis: CT/MRI of the mesial temporal lobe · CSF HSV PCR · EEG (temporal spikes) · biopsy
  • Treat: IV acyclovir 10 mg/kg every 8 h, dosed on ideal body weight (700 mg for a 70 kg patient)

blocks.alt: HSV encephalitis temporal lobe MRI - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: MRI in herpes simplex encephalitis: bright signal in the temporal lobes

blocks.title: Schulich Reviews
blocks.html:
• Bacterial meningitis = "sick"; viral meningitis = "lousy" (headache, stiff neck, fever) → an NSAID and reassurance
  • Kernig's sign = knee extension resisted with the hip flexed · Brudzinski's sign = neck flexion makes the hips flex · jolt accentuation of the headache
  • Empiric bacterial meningitis treatment as "CAAV + D": ceftriaxone, acyclovir, ampicillin (elderly or immunocompromised), vancomycin + dexamethasone; give antibiotics and the steroid early (less death and hearing loss); dexamethasone can stop if it is not bacterial
  • S. aureus after head trauma or neurosurgery; neonates (E. coli, group B strep) → ampicillin + gentamicin
  • A brain abscess is an organized infection
