lectures.name: Multidisciplinary Care in ALS
lectures.title: Multidisciplinary care in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
lectures.framing: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) has no cure and only two modestly effective drugs, so the most important treatment is the team. Recognise the mixed upper and lower motor neuron picture, then know who handles what as the weakness spreads.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ ALS = UMN and LMN signs together in two or more regions, with no prominent non-motor involvement. Riluzole (glutamate antagonist) and edaravone (antioxidant) are the only drugs, both modest; BiPAP also extends life. Death is from respiratory muscle failure or aspiration pneumonia, on average 3 years from onset. Swallowing and speech = speech-language pathologist; cough, breathing, ankle-foot orthoses = physiotherapist; hand splints and home changes = occupational therapist; tube-feeding teaching = dietitian; prescribing BiPAP = physician.

blocks.html: 1. What ALS is

• Definition: a neurodegenerative disease causing upper motor neuron (UMN) and lower motor neuron (LMN) weakness
    • motor neurons are lost in the motor cortex and the spinal cord (anterior horn cells)
  • How common: 2-3 per 100,000
  • Cause: 5-10% hereditary (autosomal dominant and autosomal recessive patterns) · the rest sporadic, the cause uncertain: probably genetic predisposition + environmental exposures + chance
  • Presents as: hand weakness · foot drop · slurred speech (dysarthria) · trouble swallowing (dysphagia) · shortness of breath (dyspnea) → progressive weakness that spreads to most of the body
  • Course: average survival 3 years from onset · death usually from respiratory muscle failure or aspiration pneumonia

blocks.alt: ALS symptoms by body region - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: ALS symptoms by region: bulbar (speech, saliva, swallowing), respiratory, upper body (hand weakness, dressing, handwriting) and lower body (tripping, stairs, weak feet)

blocks.html: 2. Diagnosis

• History: progressive, relatively isolated motor symptoms
  • Exam: LMN signs (atrophy, fasciculations) + UMN signs (hyperreflexia, spasticity) in at least two regions, without prominent extra-motor involvement
  • Investigations only to rule out other explanations, as appropriate: nerve conduction studies · cerebrospinal fluid · MRI · metabolic tests
3. Treatment

• No cure
  • Only two approved drugs, both modestly effective:
    • Riluzole: glutamate antagonist, reduces excitotoxicity
    • Edaravone: antioxidant
  • Bilevel positive airway pressure (BiPAP) can extend life once symptoms of breathing insufficiency appear
  • Most important treatment = managing symptoms and function through multidisciplinary care · seen in the clinic every 3-6 months to maximize function and minimize symptoms
4. The multidisciplinary team

rows: Communication: dysarthria (spastic, flaccid or both) → compensatory strategies for patient and family · augmentative and alternative communication devices, high- or low-tech · strategies for language and cognition · Swallowing (food, drink and saliva): bedside clinical assessment, modified barium swallow, fiberoptic endoscopic evaluation of swallowing · texture changes (minced, puree, thickened liquids) · discusses feeding tubes

Breathing: shortness of breath on exertion and orthopnea (balancing activity, raising the head of the bed) · signs and prevention of chest infection · keeping the airways clear · cough and secretion clearance (deep breathing and coughing, manually assisted cough, breath stacking, chest percussion, mainly oral suction at home) · Limbs: range-of-motion exercises (prevent frozen shoulder) · protect the shoulders from strain · stretching for spasticity · gait aids: ankle-foot orthoses for foot drop, canes, walkers

Keeps independence and participation: activities of daily living, environment and accessibility, work and leisure · compensatory techniques, equipment (hand splints), resources, home and vehicle modifications

First visit: psychosocial assessment (family and community supports, work, income and insurance, wills and powers of attorney) · later: care needs, disability financial options, adjustment to disability and mood

Eating routine, swallowing limits, nutritional adequacy, other conditions, drug-supplement interactions, bowels, fluids, skin · weight monitoring · supplements, high-protein high-energy diet, texture changes · enteral (tube) feeding: whether it is needed, supplies, teaching
Explains the team, the contact between visits (troubleshoots with patient and local caregivers) · coordinates team meetings, follow-up and clinical trials · advance care planning

Confirms the diagnosis · drugs for drooling (sialorrhea), spasticity, pain, constipation, depression, pseudobulbar affect · starts and monitors BiPAP with a respirologist · end-of-life discussions · trial recruitment

blocks.title: Schulich Reviews
blocks.html:
• ALS is a diagnosis of exclusion: also rule out Lyme disease and heavy metals
  • Baclofen for spasticity

lectures.name: Brain Tumors
lectures.title: Brain tumours
lectures.framing: A brain tumour shows itself by raised intracranial pressure, a focal deficit, a change in the person or a seizure, and the red flag tying them together is that the symptoms keep progressing. Metastases are more common than primary tumours; among primaries gliomas lead, and contrast enhancement (grade) decides how fast to treat.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Progressive symptoms are the red flag for a brain tumour: weeks to months suggests a highly malignant tumour, months or longer a benign or slow-growing one. Raised-ICP headache is worse lying down, in the morning and with coughing or Valsalva; papilledema comes late. Uncal herniation = same-side third nerve palsy and dilated pupil with opposite-side weakness. Metastases outnumber primaries (lung, breast, melanoma, renal cell); gliomas are the commonest primary. Contrast MRI is the test; enhancement means a high-grade glioma; tissue is still needed. Glioblastoma = maximal safe resection, then radiation with temozolomide; a low-grade glioma with only controlled seizures is watched with serial MRI. Primary CNS lymphoma: B-cell, in the immunosuppressed and HIV.

blocks.html: 1. Intracranial pressure (ICP)

• Normal: adults 5-15 mmHg (7.5-20 cm of water) · young children 3-7 · infants 1.5-6
  • Monro-Kellie hypothesis: the skull is a rigid box of constant volume, so brain + cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) + blood + any mass must share it → the brain compensates by pushing out venous blood and CSF, up to a point · past it, pressure rises
  • Measuring it
    • lumbar puncture, lying on the side with the legs extended · ⚠ caution with a space-occupying lesion (PUNISH)
    • intracranial monitor, with or without a ventricular drain (advantage: it can drain CSF)
  • What raises it (mass effect)
    • focal: tumour · hemorrhage (spontaneous or traumatic) · infection (brain abscess) · brain infarction
    • generalized: hydrocephalus · meningitis or encephalitis · brain edema (trauma, hypoxia, drowning, after CPR)
  • Symptoms of raised ICP (after compensation fails)
    • decreased level of consciousness (reticular activating system)
    • headache, nausea and vomiting · vomiting from irritation of the vomiting centre and chemoreceptor trigger zone in the area postrema of the medulla
    • Cushing response: hypertension with reflex bradycardia
    • papilledema, only LATE
    • herniation: brain shifts from one compartment to another → cranial nerve palsy (third most common, also fourth and sixth) · posterior cerebral artery compression and infarction · decreased consciousness and death
  • Raised-ICP headache, a red flag in any headache history: holocephalic or localized · persistent, progressive, positional (worse lying down) · worse in the morning, wakes the patient · worse with coughing or Valsalva (lying down lowers central venous return; Valsalva raises central venous resistance)

rows: same-side third nerve palsy · same-side dilated pupil · opposite-side weakness

blocks.html: • Descending herniation: cranial nerve palsies (third, fourth, sixth) · brainstem compression · posterior and anterior cerebral artery strokes · vessel shearing (Duret hemorrhage) · Cushing's triad: hypertension, bradycardia, apnea

blocks.cap: Types of brain herniation: subfalcine, uncal, central, transcalvarial and tonsillar

blocks.html: 2. When to suspect a brain tumour

• Headache: persistent · progressive · positional, worse lying down · often worse in the morning · wakes the patient · with nausea and vomiting · worse with coughing and Valsalva
  • Focal symptoms: weakness · sensory loss · trouble speaking (dysphasia) · gait or visual disturbance · begin insidiously and progress
  • Mental status change: apathy, withdrawal · personality change · confusion · altered consciousness · may be mistaken for depression or dementia
  • Seizures, especially focal
  • Key red flag = progressive symptoms · duration helps: weeks to a few months → highly malignant · months or longer → benign or slow-growing
  • Diagnosis: history → exam → confirmatory imaging → tissue from biopsy or resection
  • Imaging (primary and secondary alike): contrast-enhanced MRI with gadolinium = test of choice · contrast-enhanced CT otherwise
3. Primary vs secondary

rows: More common: the most common CNS tumours · 15% of people dying of cancer have them at autopsy · 15-20% of cancers first show up as a brain metastasis
Gliomas most common · meningiomas · CNS lymphoma · nerve sheath tumours (schwannoma, neurofibroma) · sellar tumours (pituitary adenoma, craniopharyngioma) · germ cell tumours
Lung (16%; small cell and adenocarcinoma) · breast · melanoma · renal cell · rarely prostate, gastrointestinal, bladder, gynecologic
Classified by benign vs malignant · cell of origin · grade · molecular markers
Contrast MRI; a CT must have contrast · tissue still required
Resect if accessible and causing symptoms (biopsy only if difficult) → whole-brain radiotherapy or stereotactic radiosurgery · treat the primary · choice depends on clinical status and prognosis
Varies with type and grade: surgery, radiation and chemotherapy all play a role, but cure is rare

blocks.alt: glioma grades on contrast MRI - low grade, anaplastic, glioblastoma - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: Contrast MRI: a low-grade glioma does not enhance, an anaplastic oligodendroglioma enhances, a glioblastoma enhances around a necrotic centre

blocks.html: 4. Gliomas

• Most common primary brain tumours · vary in histology, aggressiveness, response to treatment and prognosis
  • By cell of origin: astrocytoma · oligodendroglioma · ependymoma

• WHO 2016 integrated diagnosis = histology + grade + molecular markers (e.g. "oligodendroglioma, grade 2, IDH-mutated and 1p/19q co-deleted")
    • IDH-mutant, 1p/19q co-deleted → better prognosis · IDH wild-type, 1p/19q intact → worse
    • low grade grows more slowly than high grade, but all except grade 1 are malignant · astrocytoma is more aggressive than oligodendroglioma
5. Treating gliomas

- High grade (3 and 4) → treat immediately · some low-grade tumours need immediate treatment, others can be observed

- Gliomas (except grade 1) are not surgically curable, but removing all visible tumour improves prognosis

- Glioblastoma

1. maximum safe resection; if not safe (deep), stereotactic biopsy for the diagnosis

2. cranial radiation, 15-30 treatments depending on age · early: transient worsening of symptoms, hair loss, dermatitis, otitis externa, fatigue · delayed: neurocognitive impairment, focal brain necrosis, radiation vasculitis (stroke), second cancer

3. temozolomide (oral) during and for 6-12 months after radiation · adds 2-3 months of median survival but triples the 2-year survivors

- median survival: radiation alone 10-12 months · radiation + chemotherapy 14-15 months · surgery + radiation + chemotherapy 18 months (2-year survival 40%) · worse with age and poor performance status

- Low-grade glioma

- no symptoms, or only seizures easily controlled with medication → careful observation with serial MRI · biopsy deferred

- treat when: new or progressive symptoms · clear progression on imaging, especially if it starts to enhance · patient preference · possibly older patients and very large tumours

- then confirm by biopsy (or resection) → post-operative radiation most common · chemotherapy alone for some oligodendrogliomas · observation if fully resected

- median survival 5-15 years, better for oligodendroglioma, especially with 1p/19q deletion
6. Primary CNS lymphoma

• The only brain tumour arising from non-neural tissue · confined to the CNS (not spread from systemic lymphoma)
  • B-cell non-Hodgkin type in 90%
  • Risk: immunosuppression, HIV · also immunocompetent patients · incidence rising
7. Paraneoplastic neurologic syndromes

• Damage remote from the tumour or its metastases · rare (0.01% of cancers) · mostly immune-mediated
  • The cancer is often silent: the neurologic symptoms bring the patient in, weeks to months before the cancer is found

rows: Small cell lung cancer, osteosclerotic myeloma

blocks.title: Schulich Reviews
blocks.html: • In a headache history, smoking → think metastasis · fever and chills → think abscess

lectures.name: Movement Disorders
lectures.title: Movement disorders
lectures.framing: Movement disorders give too much movement (hyperkinetic) or too little (hypokinetic). The clinical work is telling essential tremor from parkinsonism, then Parkinson's disease from the other causes of parkinsonism, and treating Parkinson's disease only once it limits function.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Parkinson's tremor is at rest and asymmetric, with slowness and rigidity and small handwriting; essential tremor comes with posture or action, is symmetric, involves head and voice, gives large handwriting and gets better with alcohol. Parkinsonism is a syndrome: ask about antipsychotics and antiemetics (prochlorperazine, metoclopramide) before calling it Parkinson's disease. Treat only when it limits function; levodopa (with carbidopa) helps bradykinesia and rigidity most and must never be stopped suddenly. Rigidity is velocity independent; spasticity is velocity dependent. Vertical gaze palsy + early falls = PSP; autonomic failure + parkinsonism or cerebellar signs = MSA.

blocks.html: 1. Hyperkinetic vs hypokinetic

rows: Ballismus · chorea · athetosis · tremor · dystonia · tics
Parkinsonism: bradykinesia (slow movement) · akinesia (trouble starting movement)

blocks.html: 2. Parkinson's disease

• What it is: a neurodegenerative disease from degeneration of dopamine-producing neurons in the substantia nigra
  • How common: 1% of people over 60 · average onset age 60 · mostly sporadic, rarely hereditary
  • Features: T.R.A.P.
    • T - tremor: usually asymmetric, often only at rest early · hands or feet · "pill-rolling"
    • R - rigidity: the same at any speed (velocity independent), unlike spasticity, which is velocity dependent · often increases with augmentation (opening and closing the other hand)
    • A - akinesia / bradykinesia: akinesia = trouble starting (getting out of a chair, starting to walk) · bradykinesia = slowness (finger tapping, fist open-close, miming turning a doorknob, foot tapping)
    • P - postural instability: trouble with balance
  • Common findings, top to bottom: less blinking · less facial expression (hypomimia) · soft, mumbling voice · asymmetric features · resting tremor (an action tremor too if severe) · rigid, not spastic tone · bradykinesia of the arms or legs · small handwriting (micrographia) · less arm swing · stooped posture · turning "en bloc" · postural instability
  • Prognosis: slowly worsens · dyskinesias develop (chorea and dystonia) · depression often · dementia · death usually from aspiration pneumonia

blocks.alt: substantia nigra pigment loss in Parkinson disease - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: Midbrain: the normal substantia nigra contains pigmented cells (left); in Parkinson's disease the pigmented cells are lost (right)

blocks.html: 3. Treating Parkinson's disease

• No treatment needed if the symptoms do not limit function · once they do, dopamine replacement
  • Dopamine itself cannot cross the blood-brain barrier

rows: Dopamine precursor that DOES cross the blood-brain barrier · given with a peripheral dopa decarboxylase inhibitor: carbidopa (Sinemet) or benserazide (Prolopa), or it would all become dopamine outside the brain
Most effective · bradykinesia and rigidity benefit most, tremor variably · start low, titrate slowly · ⚠ never stop suddenly: withdrawal suddenly worsens symptoms
Stimulates regions of the basal ganglia

blocks.html:
• Complications of levodopa: motor fluctuations ("on-off", wearing off) · dyskinesias (abnormal involuntary movements: chorea or dystonia) in 50% of those treated 5 years or longer
  • Other symptomatic therapies · no proven neuroprotective drug yet
4. Parkinson's disease vs parkinsonism

• Parkinsonism = a clinical syndrome of tremor, bradykinesia, rigidity and postural instability, in any combination · Parkinson's disease is one specific cause, not the only one
  • Other causes
    • basal ganglia disease: stroke, bleed, tumour, infection
    • drugs: antipsychotics and antiemetics (prochlorperazine, metoclopramide)
    • repeated head trauma
    • other neurodegenerative syndromes: multiple system atrophy, progressive supranuclear palsy, diffuse Lewy body disease
    • toxins: carbon monoxide, cyanide
5. Essential tremor vs Parkinson's tremor

rows: May be hereditary · worsens over time
None if mild · beta-blocker or primidone · other anticonvulsants · deep brain stimulation if refractory

blocks.html: 6. Progressive supranuclear palsy and multiple system atrophy

rows: Vertical supranuclear gaze palsy: impaired vertical eye movements · "supranuclear" = the pursuit and saccade problems can be overcome by vestibular input (vestibulo-ocular reflexes)
Early falls and major balance trouble · axial tone increased more than limb tone · parkinsonism

  • PSP also brings dementia

lectures.name: Non-Mendelian Genetics
lectures.title: Non-Mendelian genetics
lectures.framing: Two ways inheritance breaks Mendel's rules: mitochondrial DNA comes almost only from the mother and is shared out unevenly between cells, and a triple nucleotide repeat grows as it is passed on. That is why mitochondrial disease varies by tissue and worsens with time, and why repeat disorders start earlier and hit harder in each generation (anticipation).
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Mitochondrial DNA comes almost only from the mother, and heteroplasmy (a random mix of normal and mutant copies) with a tissue threshold explains why the same mutation looks different in each tissue and worsens over time. Point mutations are maternal; deletions and duplications are sporadic; nuclear-gene mitochondrial disease is Mendelian. Suspect mitochondrial disease when 2 or more systems are involved; lactate is raised in blood and cerebrospinal fluid. Anticipation = the repeat grows each generation, so onset is earlier and disease worse. Huntington: CAG in HTT, 40 or more repeats = will develop HD, 36-39 = may not; juvenile HD is rigid, not choreic. Myotonic dystrophy: CTG in DMPK, cannot let go of a grip; over 1,000 repeats = congenital. Pre-symptomatic HD testing only after counselling by a geneticist or genetic counsellor.

blocks.html: 1. Mitochondria and their DNA

• Mitochondria = the cell's "power houses": oxidative phosphorylation by the 5 complexes of the respiratory chain makes ATP · they also import proteins from the cytosol and assemble their own
    • 100s to 1000s per cell · four compartments: outer membrane, intermembrane space, inner membrane folded into cristae (holds the respiratory chain), matrix (holds 1-10 identical mitochondrial DNA molecules)
  • Mitochondrial disorders include: pyruvate dehydrogenase complex defects · Krebs cycle defects · respiratory chain defects · disorders of mitochondrial DNA replication, maintenance and repair → ↓ ATP production
  • Dual control by nuclear and mitochondrial genes
    • Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA): circular, 37 genes (13 respiratory chain proteins, 2 rRNAs, 22 tRNAs), 1-10 copies per mitochondrion
    • Nuclear DNA: over 300 genes for respiratory chain proteins, mtDNA replication, expression and repair, antioxidant defence, iron homeostasis, import machinery
2. Mitochondrial DNA disease: heteroplasmy, threshold, maternal inheritance

• Homoplasmy = every copy of mtDNA identical (healthy) · heteroplasmy = a mixture of normal and mutant mtDNA (disease)
  • Point mutations: maternal inheritance · deletions and duplications: sporadic
  • Why it progresses: in dividing cells mitochondria are shared out at random, so cells get different numbers of mutant and healthy ones · in non-dividing cells (neurons, muscle) mitochondria replicate with metabolic demand and exercise → mutant mtDNA accumulates in affected tissues → symptoms worsen over time
  • Threshold effect: a tissue fails only once its non-functioning mitochondria pass a threshold, which differs between tissues · any organ can be affected, but high-energy tissues suffer first: brain, retina, skeletal muscle, heart
  • Maternal inheritance: the egg has many mitochondria, the sperm only a few, so mtDNA passes almost only through the mother
  • Genetic bottleneck: a germ cell carrying mutant mtDNA makes eggs with high, intermediate or low mutant loads → affected, mildly affected or unaffected children

blocks.cap: Replication and random segregation of mutant mtDNA: from homoplasmy through heteroplasmy, with the mutant phenotype appearing once a threshold is crossed

blocks.html: 3. Nuclear-gene mitochondrial disease

• Nuclear DNA mitochondrial diseases follow Mendelian inheritance: autosomal recessive, X-linked, autosomal dominant
  • Mitochondrial depletion syndromes: nuclear gene mutations in mitochondrial nucleotide synthesis or mtDNA replication → too little mtDNA for the key respiratory chain subunits → too little energy
4. When to suspect a mitochondrial disorder
• Consider it when 2 or more suggestive findings are present:

rows: hypotonia · ataxia · intellectual disability · seizures · migraines · dementia · sensorineural hearing loss
retinitis pigmentosa · optic atrophy · nystagmus · ophthalmoplegia (eye muscle paralysis)
diabetes mellitus · diabetes insipidus · exocrine pancreatic dysfunction · short stature
Gut dysfunction, intestinal pseudo-obstruction · liver dysfunction or failure · renal tubular acidosis · Fanconi syndrome

blocks.html: 5. Investigations and treatment

• ↑ lactate in blood and cerebrospinal fluid · MRI or magnetic resonance spectroscopy: lactate peak, basal ganglia changes, leukodystrophy, atrophy
  • Muscle biopsy: immunohistochemistry and respiratory chain enzyme analysis · gene panels: mtDNA and nuclear mitochondrial genes
  • No effective treatment · a "mitochondrial cocktail" of respiratory chain cofactors: riboflavin, coenzyme Q10, thiamine
6. Triple nucleotide repeat disorders and anticipation

• Anticipation: the expanded repeat is unstable and tends to grow as it is passed to each generation, so offspring of an affected person can have earlier and more severe disease · the larger the repeat, the earlier the onset and the worse the disease
  • All are autosomal dominant · treatment is supportive · genetic counselling, family planning, prenatal and preimplantation genetic diagnosis

rows: CAG in the HTT gene → expanded polyglutamine tract in huntingtin → the protein aggregates in neurons → selected neurons degenerate

Mean onset 35-44 years · 2/3 neurologic, 1/3 psychiatric · early: clumsiness, minor involuntary movements, personality change, psychiatric symptoms, may keep working · middle: prominent chorea, dysarthria, dysphagia, weight loss, cognitive decline, cannot work, still independent in basic daily activities · late: completely dependent, mute, incontinent, rigid, slow, cannot walk, choking
Myotonia (sustained contraction): cannot let go of a grip (jars, a key) · weakness, fatigue, poor exercise tolerance · narrow face, ptosis, balding · cataracts · cardiac arrhythmia
MRI: diffuse cortical atrophy with marked atrophy of both caudate nuclei
Median survival 15-18 years after onset · average death at 54-55 years, 15-25 years after onset
Average age of death: mild 60 to normal · classic 48-55 · congenital 45
Juvenile: rare, 60-100 repeats, rigidity, less or no chorea, seizures, cognitive and behavioural problems, rapid progression, poor prognosis

Congenital: all muscles including the face (expressionless, sunken cheeks, bilateral ptosis, cannot lift the corners of the mouth) · respiratory failure, high newborn death rate · hypotonia improves if they survive · cardiac conduction defects · possible cognitive impairment

blocks.html:
• Huntington CAG repeats: 26 or fewer normal · 27-35 premutation (will not develop HD, but a child might) · 36-39 reduced penetrance (may or may not develop symptoms) · 40 or more full penetrance (will develop HD)
  • Myotonic dystrophy CTG repeats: 35-49 premutation (no signs) · 50-150 mild (cataracts, mild myotonia, onset 20-70) · about 100-1,000 classic (weakness, myotonia, cataracts, balding, arrhythmia, onset 10-30) · over 1,000 congenital (onset birth to 10)

blocks.cap: Huntington's CAG repeat length: normal, premutation, reduced penetrance and full penetrance

blocks.html: 7. Testing for Huntington disease

• 70-80% of relatives of someone with HD decide against testing · some are tested and never come back for the result · hasty or insensitive counselling can do more harm than good
  • Pre-symptomatic testing: only with adequate preparation, information and support · pre-test counselling by a geneticist or genetic counsellor
  • Symptomatic testing: any physician can order it, usually a neurologist, at any age
  • Counselling covers: sources of emotional support · how they would cope with an abnormal result · their reasons (resolve uncertainty, remove the risk from children born or planned)

lectures.name: Pediatric Neurology
lectures.title: Pediatric neurology: the floppy infant, the seizing child, the ataxic child
lectures.framing: Three presentations, one habit: an unstable child gets ABCDE (and a glucose) before anything else. Then the exam sorts it: a floppy infant is central (brain) or peripheral (motor neuron, junction, muscle); a febrile seizure is simple or complex, and any seizure past 5 minutes is status epilepticus; an ataxic child has one of three common causes or one of three can't-miss ones.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Floppy + weak + absent reflexes = peripheral (spinal muscular atrophy, junction, muscle: check creatine kinase); floppy + strong + brisk reflexes + global delay = central (infection, hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy, chromosomal, metabolic). Hypotonia right after birth → hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy or chromosomal; after day 1 → metabolic. Simple febrile = generalized, < 15 minutes, once in 24 hours, 6 months-5 years: reassure and discharge; any focal feature, > 15 minutes or a repeat in 24 hours = complex. A seizure past 5 minutes is status: benzodiazepine (2-3 doses), then levetiracetam (phenobarbital under 30 days), then intensive care. Check glucose in every seizing or floppy child. Ataxia: intoxication, postinfectious and tumour are the common three; stroke, meningitis and tumour can't be missed; image for any other neurologic sign, a subacute course or trauma, not for a simple ingestion. Tumour with hydrocephalus → neurosurgery now.

blocks.html: Part 1: the infant with hypotonia
1. What hypotonia is

• Hypotonia = decreased muscle tone: less resistance of the muscles to passive stretch · these infants are called "floppy"
  • Not the same as weakness (decreased power or strength): not every hypotonic infant is weak
2. The unstable infant with acute hypotonia

• Acute causes: infection (sepsis, meningitis) - the most common · central nervous system (stroke, seizure) · endocrine (hypoglycemia, electrolytes, thyroid, congenital adrenal hyperplasia) · surgical (volvulus, necrotizing enterocolitis) · toxin ingestion · metabolic (urea cycle defects) · non-accidental trauma: always on the list when the history does not fit the infant or keeps changing
  • ABCDE first, as for any unstable child
    • Airway: patent?
    • Breathing: rate, oxygen saturation · oxygen, assist breathing if needed
    • Circulation: heart rate, blood pressure, capillary refill, central pulses (femoral is best in infants) · isotonic fluid (normal saline) if circulation is poor · consider inotropes (epinephrine)
    • Disability / Dextrose: check the blood sugar and treat hypoglycemia immediately · level of consciousness
    • Expose: signs of injury or bleeding
  • Stable: history and exam pinpoint the diagnosis in about 50%
3. Central vs peripheral

rows: Any systemic disease affecting the brain · the most common cause in newborns
Infection (sepsis, meningitis, herpes simplex virus, TORCH) · hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy · chromosomal (trisomy 21, Prader-Willi syndrome) · metabolic disorders

Spinal muscular atrophy (motor neuron) · congenital myasthenic syndromes (junction) · infant botulism (Clostridium botulinum) · drug toxicity (aminoglycosides) · congenital muscular dystrophy (muscle)
Normal speech and cognition, delayed gross and fine motor
Weak (cannot lift limbs against gravity) · facial weakness, feeding and breathing difficulty
Normal or exaggerated, primitive reflexes persist, may have clonus

blocks.html: • Timing of onset narrows it: right after birth → central nervous system (hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy, chromosomal) · after the first day of life → metabolic
4. History and exam

• History: onset · how motor development was noticed (missed motor milestones?), better, worse or the same, any lost skills (→ degenerative, e.g. metabolic) · prenatal and perinatal: maternal drugs and infections, pregnancy complications, gestational age, delivery, APGAR scores, NICU stay · overall development (fine motor, gross motor, verbal, social) · family history of hypotonia, delay, metabolic or chromosomal disease · medications, allergies, immunizations
  • General look: normal tone = arms and legs slightly flexed, good head control · hypotonic = limbs hang loosely, poor head control · respiratory distress (indrawing, grunting, tracheal tug) · dysmorphic features · plot weight, length and head circumference
  • Tone manoeuvres
    • Vertical suspension (held under the arms): normal = shoulders press down on your hands · hypotonic = slips through your hands
    • Horizontal suspension: normal = lifts head, keeps trunk extended for a while · hypotonic = flops over your arm in a "U"
    • Pull to sit: normal = flexes neck and helps with the arms (head lag is normal in newborns and gone between 2 and 6 months) · hypotonic = significant head lag, no help from the arms, cannot stabilize the trunk
  • Full exam: heart failure → muscle disease or mitochondrial disorder · enlarged liver and spleen → lysosomal or glycogen storage disorder
5. Investigations and management

• Brain: CT or MRI if a central cause is suspected · blood: electrolytes, extended electrolytes, TSH, ammonia (metabolic screen), specialized metabolic tests, karyotype, genetic tests · creatine kinase: raised in most muscle disorders · electromyography (muscle and motor neuron health) · muscle biopsy
  • Management depends on the cause: early referral to pediatric neurology (and metabolics and genetics) · supportive care: physiotherapy, occupational therapy, nutrition, psychology, speech-language pathology
Part 2: the child with a seizure
6. What a seizure is

• Seizure = abnormal, excessive, synchronous neuronal discharge in the brain
  • Types: focal (one side or one limb) · generalized (whole body) · atonic (loss of tone) · clonic · tonic-clonic
  • Most seizures stop on their own within 5 minutes · convulsive status epilepticus is most common under age 2
  • Convulsive status epilepticus: continuous generalized tonic-clonic seizure > 30 minutes, or 2+ seizures without return to baseline between them · impending status = > 5 minutes without recovery · prolonged seizures raise the brain's oxygen demand and kill cells, so time matters
  • Subtle seizures in newborns, infants and children: lip smacking, sucking, chewing, tongue movements, bicycling or swimming limbs, eye deviation, eye fluttering, blinking, autonomic or vital-sign changes, rhythmic jerking, stiffening, posturing, myoclonic jerks, behaviour change in older children · subclinical seizures show only on EEG
7. Febrile seizures

• Febrile seizure: a seizure with fever, without a central nervous system infection, an acute electrolyte imbalance or a history of afebrile seizures · loss of consciousness, blue face, eyes rolling up, jerking limbs

rows: Generalized · < 15 minutes · once in 24 hours · age 6 months to 5 years · no neurologic or developmental problem
Fever + any one: focal features · > 15 minutes · recurs within 24 hours · focal signs after the seizure · known neurologic condition
Observe or admit, by time to baseline, neurologic signs, family comfort
Discharge once back to baseline · reassure and educate
Consider neurology referral · counsel about recurrence and an epilepsy workup

blocks.html: • When to worry (red flags): not back to baseline · meningeal signs or a toxic look · developmental delay or a neurologic condition
8. Evaluating the child

• History: onset (timing, duration, frequency) · witness description (movements, eyes, focal or generalized) · consciousness during and after, and recovery · preceding features: fever, infection, trauma, head injury, toxins, medication use or withdrawal · prior neurologic history, milestones, family history of epilepsy or genetic disease
  • Exam: ABCs and vital signs first (temperature, heart rate, perfusion, oxygen saturation) · neurologic: level of consciousness, pupils (size, symmetry, reaction), cranial nerves, tone, reflexes, raised intracranial pressure (bulging fontanelle, papilledema), focal deficits · skin: café-au-lait spots → neurofibromatosis
  • Investigations, step by step from the top differentials
    • Every child, at the bedside: glucose + blood gas with electrolytes (hypoglycemia, hyponatremia)
    • bloods: electrolytes, calcium, magnesium, antiseizure drug levels if on one
    • infection: complete blood count, C-reactive protein, blood cultures, cerebrospinal fluid if stable
    • head CT if head injury, focal signs or raised intracranial pressure (pupil changes, hypertension with bradycardia, vomiting, lethargy) → bleeding
    • EEG if unclear, non-convulsive or subtle newborn seizures · MRI when stable, for structure
9. Causes, by age

• Acute symptomatic (common): CNS infection (meningitis, encephalitis) · anoxia · metabolic (low or high glucose, low sodium, low calcium) · trauma · drugs (antiseizure drug non-adherence or withdrawal, overdose) · prolonged febrile seizure
  • Remote / structural: brain malformations · perinatal hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy · neurodegenerative disease · old brain injury (stroke, trauma, meningitis) · idiopathic epilepsy
  • Newborns, in addition: inborn errors of metabolism · genetic epilepsy syndromes · electrolytes (low glucose, calcium, magnesium) · intracranial hemorrhage, stroke · infection from pregnancy or birth · hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy
  • Precipitants: fever, dehydration, missed medication, toxins
10. Management (convulsive status epilepticus)

• ABCDE: airway (bag-mask, laryngeal mask, endotracheal tube if needed) · breathing · circulation (fluid bolus if hypotensive) · disability (pupils: pinpoint or dilated → ingestion; blown or non-reactive → raised pressure, bleeding; glucose) · exposure (safety, skin)
  • Recognize status early: the 5-minute rule · time it, keep the child safe, take the history, bedside glucose and electrolytes
  • > 5 minutes → benzodiazepine: IV lorazepam or midazolam · no IV: sublingual lorazepam or intranasal midazolam · repeat every 3-5 minutes · watch breathing and blood pressure · after 2-3 doses → second line
  • Second line (IV over 20-30 minutes): levetiracetam (most used), phenytoin / fosphenytoin, or phenobarbital (more effective under 30 days old)
  • Refractory → intensive care: benzodiazepine infusion, ketamine, advanced antiseizure therapy
  • Treat the cause
    • hypoglycemia → IV dextrose by the rule of 50 (concentration × mL/kg = 50: D10 at 5 mL/kg most often, D5 at 10 mL/kg) · D25 and D50 never through a peripheral line (thrombosis, phlebitis)
    • hyponatremia → 3% hypertonic saline, 3-5 mL/kg IV
    • meningitis → antibiotics
    • inborn error of metabolism → high dextrose load (D10) for an anabolic state, nothing by mouth until tested
    • bleeding → neurosurgery emergently
  • Seizure first aid: stay, keep safe, time it · if unconscious turn on the side, something soft under the head, loosen the collar · never restrain, nothing in the mouth · call 911 if > 5 minutes or repeating, pregnant or injured, first seizure, in water, or not back to normal
Part 3: the child with ataxia
11. What ataxia is and where it comes from

• Ataxia = inability to make accurate, smooth, coordinated movements · a clinical sign, not a diagnosis
  • Causes of the incoordination: cerebellum (trouble walking or sitting, falling to one side, slurred speech, low tone, intention tremor) · vestibular (severe vertigo, nausea and vomiting, positional vertigo, severe unsteadiness) · weakness, or loss of sensation and proprioception
  • Cerebellar hemisphere → appendicular (limb) ataxia: over- or underreaching, "clumsy" · vermis (midline) → truncal ataxia: cannot sit upright, wide-based unstable gait
12. Presentation and exam

• Depends on the skills the child has: not yet walking → cannot sit without support, over- or undershoots when reaching · walking → wide-based unsteady gait, clumsy, dysmetria, intention tremor · a new walker is unsteady anyway
  • Over 5: the full adult neurologic exam
  • Under 5, tricks: dysmetria (reach for a toy or food with each hand) · nystagmus (follow a toy) · sensation (poke the foot while distracted; looking at it = intact) · gait (walk to the caregiver; is it different from baseline?) · speech (slurred?)
13. Causes

rows: 3 most common AND can't miss
Medulloblastoma, cerebellar astrocytoma · invades the cerebellum or blocks CSF → hydrocephalus
Occlusion or bleeding in the cerebellum's vessels
Viral or bacterial infection of the central nervous system
Known or witnessed ingestion, substances at home, unsupervised time, abuse red flags (unexplained bruises, changing story) · improves with supportive care
Abrupt onset · loss of consciousness or seizure · trigger (chiropractic adjustment → artery dissection, car crash) · clotting disorder
Fever, meningismus, headache, vomiting, altered consciousness, seizures

blocks.html: • Hereditary: remember Friedreich ataxia: autosomal recessive, slowly progressive ataxia, slurred speech, absent deep tendon reflexes, nystagmus
14. Who needs head imaging

• MRI preferred; CT is more accessible and rules out the life-threatening causes
  • No imaging: a toxic ingestion, not significantly altered, watchable in the emergency department
  • Low threshold: suspected postinfectious ataxia (young children get frequent viruses, so a recent one does not confirm it)
  • Imaging required: ataxia + any other neurologic finding · subacute (slowly over weeks to months) · trauma
15. Management

• Depends on the cause; discuss with pediatrics
  • Intoxication compromising the ABCs → resuscitate · concern for intoxication → call Poison Control · brain tumour → neurosurgery and oncology · hydrocephalus → neurosurgery (emergently) · hemorrhage or infarction → pediatric neurology and intensive care, Code Stroke if applicable
  • Supportive: vomiting → IV fluids and anti-emetics · ongoing unsteadiness → supervise whenever walking, no stairs

lectures.name: Monocular Vision Impairment
lectures.title: Monocular vision impairment
lectures.framing: Vision loss in one eye puts the problem in front of the optic chiasm; loss in both eyes puts it behind. Then sort by pain and tempo: sudden painless loss is sorted by the pupil and the fundus, and three of the five causes need emergency measures and ophthalmology now. Gradual loss is sorted by which part of vision goes: the periphery (glaucoma), everything hazy (cataract) or the centre (macular degeneration).
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ A white retina with a cherry-red spot and an RAPD is a central retinal artery occlusion: massage the eye now, refer emergently, then find the embolus's source. Swollen disc with an RAPD: older with headache, jaw claudication and scalp tenderness is giant cell arteritis (ESR, CRP, steroids, biopsy); a healthy young woman is optic neuritis (look for multiple sclerosis). Flashes, floaters and a curtain = retinal detachment. Glaucoma is silent and takes the periphery first; only lowering the pressure treats it. Cataract = leading reversible cause of blindness; macular degeneration = leading irreversible cause over 50.

blocks.html: 1. History and exam

• History: pain? · transient, persistent or progressive? · one eye or both? · all or part of the field? · timeline (abrupt, hours, days, weeks) · baseline acuity
    • past medical history: diabetes, cardiovascular disease, autoimmune disease, hypertension
    • past eye history: diabetic retinopathy, glaucoma, eye surgery, contact lenses
  • Exam
    • visual acuity · confrontation visual fields
    • swinging flashlight test: a relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) (Marcus Gunn pupil) - moving the light from the normal eye to the abnormal one, the pupil dilates instead of constricting = a significant lesion of the retina or optic nerve of that eye · the key sign in monocular loss
    • red reflex: dull = a media opacity (cloudy cornea, lens or vitreous) · ophthalmoscopy
    • pressure (tonometry)
2. Sudden painless vision loss

rows: Older · inflammation of large and medium vessels (cranial arteries, proximal aorta)
New headache, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, tender thick temporal artery, weight loss, fever, malaise · polymyalgia rheumatica
Flashes, new floaters, a "curtain", peripheral field loss · acuity may be normal
Dark mobile spots in the red reflex · usually not seen with a direct ophthalmoscope
Proliferative retinopathy: fragile new vessels bleed
Ocular massage (heel of the hand, 10 s press, 10 s release, for 5 min) · emergent referral · find the source (carotid atheroma, heart valves)
ESR + CRP now (ESR usually > 60) · visual symptoms → IV methylprednisolone 1 g × 3 days; none → prednisone 40-60 mg daily · emergent referral for temporal artery biopsy
Neuro-ophthalmology · MRI, possible IV corticosteroids · neurology to rule out multiple sclerosis
Pan-retinal laser photocoagulation by a retina specialist

blocks.cap: Central retinal artery occlusion beside a normal fundus: pale retina with a cherry-red macula

blocks.html:
• Emergency measures and referral: CRAO · ischemic optic neuropathy · giant cell arteritis
  • High-dose steroids in GCA protect the other eye and prevent occlusions elsewhere (stroke, aortic arch syndrome)
3. Glaucoma (primary open-angle)

• Progressive, irreversible optic neuropathy with typical disc and field changes · 3.5% of the world · raised eye pressure is the main risk factor, not the definition (normal tension glaucoma)
  • Presents as: nothing at first · peripheral vision goes first · acuity falls very late
  • Risk factors: open angle = family history, older age, Black, raised pressure, myopia, past eye trauma, steroids, vasospasm (Raynaud's, migraine) · angle closure = family history, older age, Asian, female, hyperopia
  • The angle = where the cornea and iris meet, the eye's drainage system
  • Pressure: normal 10-21 mmHg · Goldmann applanation, Tono-Pen, air puff
  • Disc: normal cup-to-disc ratio < 0.5, usually symmetric (a difference > 0.2 is suspicious) · Field: arcuate defect, nasal step
  • Refer: pressure > 21 or a suspicious disc · timely, not same-day unless the pressure has spiked > 30
  • Treatment: lowering the pressure is the only treatment: drops, laser, surgery

blocks.cap: Optic disc in glaucoma: the cup enlarges as the nerve is lost

blocks.html: 4. Cataract

• Opacity or discolouration of the lens · leading cause of reversible blindness
  • Risk factors: age, genetics, trauma, steroids, eye inflammation, metabolic disease (diabetes), radiation, prior eye surgery, UV exposure
  • Presents as: reduced acuity · glare, starbursts or halos · trouble driving at night · "second sight" (lens myopia improves near vision) · varies with where the opacity sits
  • Exam: acuity down · hazy view on ophthalmoscopy · a dense cataract dulls the red reflex or whitens the pupil · pressure normal · types: nuclear sclerosis, posterior subcapsular, cortical
  • Treatment: non-urgent referral · visually significant or hiding the retina → extraction with an intraocular lens
5. Age-related macular degeneration

• Leading cause of irreversible blindness over 50 (North America) · central acuity ↓ + distortion (metamorphopsia) · Amsler grid
  • Refer if any: central acuity ↓ · new distortion · drusen or blood at the macula

rows: Choroidal neovascular membrane: leaky vessels break through to the retina, bleed, leave exudates
Anti-VEGF (vascular endothelial growth factor) injections into the eye (bevacizumab, ranibizumab, aflibercept)
Slow it: AREDS2 formula vitamins (C, E, lutein, zeaxanthin, zinc, copper), nutrition, stop smoking

lectures.name: Red Eye and Ocular Trauma
lectures.title: Red eye and ocular trauma
lectures.framing: Most red eyes are harmless; the job is to catch the few that threaten sight. The red flags do it: severe pain, photophobia, haloes or reduced vision, and on exam a ciliary flush, a cloudy cornea, an abnormal pupil, a shallow chamber or a high pressure. With none, it is the lids, the conjunctiva, a burst vessel or a scratch. With any, it is keratitis, iritis or angle closure, and urgent referral to ophthalmology. In trauma, look for an open globe first.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Pain, photophobia, haloes or reduced vision turn a red eye into keratitis, uveitis or acute angle closure glaucoma, and an urgent referral. Conjunctivitis by discharge: watery after a cold = viral (no antibiotics); lids glued with yellow-white pus = bacterial (fluoroquinolone); pus within 12-24 hours = gonococcal (ceftriaxone + azithromycin, refer); itch = allergic. An abrasion stains but the cornea stays clear; keratitis is a white infiltrate in a hazy cornea. Uveitis has a low or normal pressure; angle closure is rock hard with a shallow chamber. Never prescribe anesthetic drops, and leave steroid drops to the ophthalmologist. Trauma: a peaked pupil or positive Seidel means an open globe - shield and refer.

blocks.html: 1. History and exam of a red eye

• History: onset (sudden or progressive) and timeline · one eye, both, or a sector · pain or photosensitivity · discharge (serous or mucopurulent, how much) · itch · vision change · recent cold · family members with a red eye · contact lenses: the 3 S's (swim, sleep, shower in them?) · recent trauma or eye surgery
    • past eye history · autoimmune disease · eye drops (over the counter or prescribed) · other medications · family eye history · occupation, recreational drugs
  • Exam
    • visual acuity with glasses, one eye at a time - reduced vision is a red flag
    • pupils: shape, size, light reaction (direct, consensual, swinging flashlight, accommodation) · eye movements in all directions
    • head and neck: lymph node in front of the ear, a dermatomal rash (herpes zoster ophthalmicus) · proptosis, bruising, bony step-off
    • lids: edema, lesions (stye, chalazion), scaling at the lash base (blepharitis) · evert the lid for a foreign body · discharge amount and character
    • conjunctiva: hemorrhage · diffuse conjunctival hyperemia vs ciliary flush · chemosis (edema)
    • cornea: haze, edema, opacities · fluorescein with cobalt blue light shows a broken epithelium · foreign body (slit lamp, or penlight and magnifier)
    • anterior chamber: blood (hyphema) or pus (hypopyon) · shallow chamber → think acute angle closure glaucoma
  • Red flags: blurred vision (if it clears with blinking it is discharge) · severe pain (keratitis, ulcer, iritis, scleritis, acute glaucoma) · photophobia (iritis) · coloured halos (corneal edema, often from high pressure) · ↓ acuity · ciliary flush · corneal opacity · pupil abnormality · shallow chamber · raised pressure · proptosis
  • Not vision threatening: blepharitis · stye or chalazion · conjunctivitis · dry eye · corneal abrasion · subconjunctival hemorrhage · Vision threatening: scleritis · corneal ulcer or keratitis · uveitis · acute angle closure glaucoma · trauma · orbital cellulitis
2. Red eye causes compared

blocks.html: 3. Ocular trauma

• Anatomy: orbital bones, nerves, arteries and muscles (detail in 10 - Orbital Anatomy)
  • Exam signs of a serious injury: 360° subconjunctival hemorrhage · dark tissue at the limbus (extruded uvea) · depth of the wound · shallow chamber · peaked pupil · Seidel sign (fluorescein washed out by leaking aqueous = full-thickness wound)
  • Also examine: orbital rim pain or displacement · air under the skin · lacerations (lid? full thickness? tear duct?) · forehead and cheek sensation (V1, V2) · eye movements · proptosis or sunken eye

rows: Metal on metal · foreign-body feeling, tearing · body on the cornea ± rust ring · epithelial defect · check iris and lens, Seidel · evert the lid

High speed → x-ray or CT for an intraocular foreign body · remove with a tuberculin syringe, burr the cornea · antibiotic drops × 7 days · refer if an intraocular body is possible, removal is hard, or it is in the visual axis
Blunt trauma to the globe · pain, photophobia, ↓ acuity · blood in the anterior chamber (full = black "8-ball") · pressure normal or high
Shield, refer ASAP · restrict activity · avoid blood thinners · steroid and pressure drops - topical steroids only from an ophthalmologist
After blunt trauma · red, photophobic, ↓ acuity · cells in the chamber, ciliary flush, sluggish or irregular pupil
Refer · steroid drops ± pressure drops · cycloplegic if very photophobic
Dog bites, punches · tearing · vision may be normal · medial lower lid → canaliculus
Lid margin or canaliculus involved → refer to oculoplastics · poor repair → lid notch, chronic tearing
Corneal laceration with iris prolapse (open globe injury) 🚨

lectures.name: Pediatric Ophthalmology
lectures.title: Pediatric ophthalmology
lectures.framing: Anything that blurs, blocks or misaligns one eye while a child's vision is developing can leave that eye permanently weak (amblyopia), so the lecture is about catching it early. Three checks do it: acuity in each eye, alignment, and the red reflex - and a white reflex is retinoblastoma until proven otherwise.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ A white pupillary reflex (leukocoria) is retinoblastoma until proven otherwise - refer immediately. Amblyopia = reduced acuity with no eye disease; refer immediately and patch the good eye, the earlier the better. In the Brückner test the brighter reflex is the turned eye; a dimmer one means refractive error or an opacity. Concomitant squint keeps the same angle in every gaze (childhood); an angle that changes with gaze means a nerve palsy, blowout fracture or thyroid eye disease. Refer a constant turn at any age, an occasional one beyond 3-4 months, and any nystagmus.

blocks.html: 1. Amblyopia
• Amblyopia: reduced visual acuity with no detectable organic disease, from a disruption of normal visual development · usually one eye, can be both

rows: The turned eye is ignored (suppressed) by the brain, so its visual cortex does not develop · in adults a squint causes double vision instead
A difference in refractive error between the eyes: the eye with the smaller error gives the clearer image, and the other becomes amblyopic
Something clouds the view (cataract, corneal scar) or blocks it (ptosis)

blocks.html:
• Testing: acuity in each eye separately
    • newborns: acuity is hard to measure → light reflexes, pupils, fundus
    • infants to age 2: cover each eye in turn - the child objects when the good eye is covered
    • ages 2-5: eye charts (HOTV, tumbling E, picture cards after age 2)
  • Management: immediate referral to a pediatric ophthalmologist for any suspected amblyopia · early treatment · patch the good eye · plus treat the cause: glasses for unequal refraction, surgery for cataract or strabismus

blocks.cap: Amblyopia: one eye sends a clear image and the other a blurred one, so the brain comes to favour the clear eye

blocks.html: 2. Strabismus
• Strabismus = misalignment of the two eyes · esotropia (in) · exotropia (out) · hypertropia (up) · hypotropia (down)

rows: About the same in every direction of gaze
Changes with the direction of gaze
Work normally, the eyes are just not aimed at the same thing
One or more muscles or nerves not working, or mechanically restricted
3rd, 4th or 6th nerve palsy · orbital blowout fracture · restrictive thyroid eye disease (Graves orbitopathy)

blocks.html:
• Testing: acuity · obvious deviation? · nystagmus · the cardinal positions of gaze · corneal light reflexes · cover test (no equipment, from 6-7 months) · red reflex
    • prominent epicanthal folds give pseudostrabismus
  • Treatment: patching, glasses, both, or surgery · no role for vision training or exercises
  • Refer: occasional deviation beyond 3-4 months · constant deviation at any age · any child with nystagmus · abnormal red reflex, especially a white one (immediate)
3. The red reflex

• Red light reflex: light reflected back from the retina, a reddish-orange glow that varies with fundus pigment (the red eye of night-time flash photos) · the most important test in pediatric ophthalmology: contactless, no dilating drops, a few seconds, and it finds several problems at once
  • Brückner test: both eyes at once, from 1/3 m or more, in dim light (big pupils), child looking into the distance · compare brightness, colour, alignment, symmetry · direct ophthalmoscope, retinoscope, or a flash photo; parents may notice the asymmetry
  • ⚠ Disease in both eyes is easy to miss if the two reflexes match

rows: Dimmer or different in one eye, or a visible opacity
Refractive error or something along the visual axis

Myopia, hyperopia, astigmatism (the eye with the larger error is dimmer) · keratoconus ("oil droplet") · cataract (not always white) · corneal abrasion · hyphema · vitreous hemorrhage · retinal pigment changes
Strabismus: the brighter eye is the turned eye
Its pupil looks slightly larger · detects turns as small as 3 prism dioptres · check the corneal light reflexes too
Something destroys, detaches or discolours the retina in line with the pupil, or a dense opacity in front of it

Retinoblastoma first · retinopathy of prematurity · congenital cataract (dense or white) · Coats' disease · persistent hyperplastic primary vitreous · inflammation (toxocariasis, congenital CMV) · coloboma · familial exudative vitreoretinopathy · retinal detachment

blocks.html:
• Physiologic white reflex: light ~15° off axis catches the optic nerve head · common, but not dismissed without referral and a full eye exam
  • Retinoblastoma: the most important and dangerous cause, rule it out first · uncommon, about 1 in 180,000 births · from embryonic retinal cells, so mostly under age 4 · late diagnosis → up to 70% die; optimal therapy → over 95% cured (3-year survival ~96%) · 90% have no family history and are one-sided (15% of one-sided still carry a germline RB1 mutation) · both eyes → ~100% positive family history · treated by enucleation, chemotherapy, radiotherapy, laser ± cryotherapy · germline carriers die more often of a second cancer than of the retinoblastoma
  • Your role with an abnormal reflex: timely referral (amblyopia, life-threatening causes) · stress attending without needless worry · take a family history of eye disease · ask the family to bring old photographs

lectures.name: Hearing Loss
lectures.title: Hearing loss
lectures.framing: Every hearing-loss question turns on one split: is sound failing to reach the inner ear (conductive), or is the inner ear or its nerve failing (sensorineural)? The tuning forks make that split at the bedside, and a sudden sensorineural loss is an emergency where a sudden conductive one is not.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Weber goes to the bad ear in a conductive loss and to the good ear in a sensorineural loss; the Rinne (bone louder than air) confirms the conductive side, so always do both. Sudden sensorineural loss is an emergency: ENT, audiogram, MRI, and steroids within 10 days. Conductive loss leaves an air-bone gap; sensorineural does not. Presbycusis takes the high pitches symmetrically; noise makes a 4,000 Hz notch. One-sided sensorineural loss with tinnitus and imbalance: acoustic neuroma until the MRI says otherwise. With a perforated drum use only non-ototoxic drops (ciprofloxacin + dexamethasone).

blocks.html: 1. Sound and the ear

• Sound = variations in air pressure · frequency (pitch) in hertz (Hz), heard from 20 to 20,000 Hz · intensity (loudness) in decibels (dB), a log scale: every 10 dB is 10 times the intensity, and is heard as about twice as loud
    • 0 dB = the softest sound a normal ear hears · conversation 60 dB · lawnmower 90 · rock concert 120 · gunshot 140 · jet takeoff 150
    • we hear best at 2,000-4,000 Hz, the range of speech
  • Outer ear: auricle (pinna) + a 3 cm canal that protects the drum and resonates at 2,000-4,000 Hz
  • Middle ear: air-filled · tympanic membrane · ossicles (malleus, incus, stapes): sound in air cannot move fluid, so the ossicles turn air pressure changes into mechanical force on the oval window · Eustachian tube to the pharynx equalizes pressure
  • Inner ear: the cochlea (2¾ turns, 3.5 cm unrolled), three fluid chambers: scala vestibuli and tympani (perilymph) · scala media (endolymph)
    • organ of Corti on the basilar membrane: moving the membrane shears the hair cells against the tectorial membrane · inner hair cells transduce, outer hair cells amplify
    • oval window pushed by the stapes · the wave runs scala vestibuli → helicotrema → scala tympani → round window, which bulges out
    • tonotopic: base stiff → high pitch · apex floppy → low pitch · hair cells → spiral ganglion → the cochlear part of cranial nerve VIII
    • pathway: brainstem → medial geniculate nucleus of the thalamus → primary auditory cortex in the superior temporal gyrus, tonotopic all the way
2. History and examination

• History: character (loudness or clarity) · duration · onset (sudden or insidious) · rate of progression · one or both ears · ear pain · discharge · pressure or fullness · tinnitus · vertigo · facial and trigeminal symptoms · symptoms specific to the differential
  • Exam: otoscopy · pneumatic otoscopy shows whether the drum moves (fluid behind it does not)
  • Tuning forks (512 Hz): the office or emergency tool that separates a sudden conductive loss (infection, effusion) from a sudden sensorineural loss (an emergency); always do both
    • Weber: fork pressed hard on the midline (forehead, nasal bone, front tooth) · where is it loudest? (detects a 5 dB difference) · loudest in the affected ear = conductive · loudest in the normal ear = sensorineural
    • Rinne: fork on the mastoid (bone conduction, straight to the inner ear), then beside the ear (air conduction, through drum and ossicles) · normal: air > bone · conductive: bone > air · sensorineural: air > bone
    • worked example: Weber goes to the RIGHT = right conductive OR left sensorineural → Rinne on the right: air > bone = left sensorineural; bone > air = right conductive

blocks.cap: Weber test
Rinne test

blocks.html: 3. Investigations

• Audiogram: hearing level (dB of hearing loss) against frequency
    • air conduction (drum and ossicles): O right, X left · bone conduction (straight to the inner ear): < right, > left · calibrated to be equal, so bone is always the same or better
    • conductive: bone normal, air low (an air-bone gap) · sensorineural: bone abnormal, air the same as bone · mixed: both
  • Auditory brainstem response: screens newborns, who cannot do an audiogram (waves through the auditory nerve and brainstem)
  • CT: bony anatomy and ossicles · MRI ± gadolinium: soft tissue and cerebellopontine angle tumours (acoustic neuroma, meningioma)

blocks.cap: Audiogram

blocks.html: 4. Conductive hearing loss

• Often correctable medically or surgically, but rule out serious pathology
  • Ear canal
    • Impacted wax · foreign body · exostoses (bony growths)
    • Bacterial otitis externa (swimmer's ear): itchy, painful, swollen, sore on pulling the pinna, reduced hearing, maybe watery discharge · Pseudomonas aeruginosa (most common), then Staph aureus, E. coli · microdebride, acidify, stop Q-tips, antibiotics
      • topical antibiotic + steroid: ciprofloxacin + dexamethasone is non-ototoxic (safe with a perforation) · Garasone, Sofracort and Cortisporin are ototoxic: only if the drum is intact
    • Fungal otitis externa: after many antibiotics · severe itch, less pain · recurrent → think diabetes · Aspergillus (black spores) or Candida (white) · clean thoroughly (alcohol, vinegar), antifungal drops (Locacorten-Vioform if the drum is intact; fluconazole or clotrimazole if perforated)
    • chronic otitis externa: a chronic dermatitis, often from Q-tips · subdermal fibrosis traps wax and invites infection · local steroids, or excision and skin grafting
  • Middle ear: otitis media (the most common cause) · perforation · ossicular fixation (otosclerosis) · ossicular disarticulation · cholesteatoma
    • Acute otitis media: sudden middle ear inflammation with pain, fever or irritability, after a cold · bulging drum · overdiagnosed
      • most common at 6-11 months; two-thirds have had it by age 1
      • Streptococcus pneumoniae 30-40% · Haemophilus influenzae 20-30% · Moraxella catarrhalis 10-15% · group A strep 2-4%
      • treatment: if antibiotics are used, high-dose amoxicillin (80-90 mg/kg/day in two doses) is first line · consider observation for 48-72 hours in lower-risk children · treat pain
      • complications in the temporal bone (hearing loss, perforation, effusion, cholesteatoma, mastoiditis, labyrinthitis, facial paralysis) and inside the skull (meningitis, abscesses, lateral sinus thrombosis)
    • Otitis media with effusion: fluid without signs of infection · may be asymptomatic: hearing loss, speech delay · underdiagnosed · fluid in both ears for 3 months → hearing evaluation
    • Tympanostomy tubes: suppurative complications · symptoms despite antibiotics > 6 weeks · effusion in both ears > 3 months with > 20 dB loss in the better ear · persistent fluid with speech delay · intermittent fluid in a hearing-aid user · chronic drum atrophy
    • adhesive otitis media: a collapsed drum with ossicular erosion
    • Perforation: infection or tubes, trauma (compression, barotrauma, penetrating, thermal) · keep dry; 80% heal on their own · tympanoplasty if not
    • Otosclerosis: a disorder of the bony labyrinth (excess vessels and bone) that most often invades the stapes footplate → stapes fixation · conductive loss with a normal drum and no trauma or infection · audiogram: conductive or mixed, rising, Carhart's notch · stapedectomy
    • Longitudinal temporal bone fracture (80%, from the side): canal laceration, ossicular disruption · triad: loss of consciousness, bleeding from or behind the drum, hearing loss
  • Treatment: surgery (tympanoplasty, ossiculoplasty, stapedectomy) · air-conduction hearing aids (behind the ear, in the ear, in the canal, completely in the canal) · bone-conduction aids when air aids cannot work: bone-anchored (BAHA) or the Bonebridge implant
5. Sensorineural hearing loss

• Differential: presbycusis · congenital · sudden (idiopathic) · trauma (temporal bone fracture, noise, barotrauma) · ototoxic · neoplastic (acoustic neuroma, meningioma) · infectious (labyrinthitis, otitis media) · neurologic or vascular (migraine, multiple sclerosis, cryoglobulinemia, sickle cell) · immune (HIV, polyarteritis nodosa) · bone (Paget, otosclerosis)
  • Presbycusis: the most common · 30% over 65, 50% over 75 · slow, symmetric, high-frequency loss of hair cells at the base of the cochlea, then the nerve · more in men · irreversible
  • Noise-induced: over 85 dB (no more than 85 dB for an 8-hour shift at work) · recreational (temporary threshold shift) · 4,000 Hz notch on the audiogram · asymmetric with guns · hearing protection
  • Ototoxins: aminoglycosides (gentamicin is also used as therapy) · cisplatin, carboplatin, vincristine · loop diuretics · ASA and quinine (reversible) · macrolides (temporary)
  • Sudden sensorineural loss: an OTOLOGIC EMERGENCY · onset < 3 days · hearing loss, tinnitus, fullness ± vertigo · workup: tuning forks, ENT referral, audiogram, MRI (2% are an acoustic neuroma) · idiopathic (viral, vascular, membrane rupture) · oral or intratympanic steroids, started within 10 days · 60-80% recover
  • Transverse temporal bone fracture (20%, front-to-back force): violates the otic capsule → sensorineural loss, less likely to recover · facial nerve (VII) involved in 50%
  • Acoustic neuroma (vestibular schwannoma): the most common cerebellopontine angle lesion · unilateral sensorineural loss, tinnitus, imbalance, trigeminal and facial nerve symptoms · slow, benign · observation, stereotactic radiation or microsurgery · bilateral → neurofibromatosis type II
  • Congenital
    • non-syndromic (two-thirds): 70-80% autosomal recessive · most often GJB2 (connexin 26), 20% of all childhood deafness
    • syndromic (one-third): Usher (retinitis pigmentosa) · Waardenburg (pigment changes) · Pendred (thyroid) · Alport (kidney) · Jervell and Lange-Nielsen (long QT)
  • Treatment: damage to the cochlea or nerve VIII cannot be repaired; devices work around it
    • hearing aids raise volume, not clarity
    • Cochlear implant: for severe-profound deafness not helped by aids · an electrode in the cochlea bypasses the hair cells and stimulates nerve VIII directly, using the cochlea's tonotopic map (needs a healthy nerve)

lectures.name: Vertigo
lectures.title: Vertigo
lectures.framing: "Dizzy" can mean anything, so the history does the work (80% of it): first, is it true vertigo (an illusion of rotary movement)? Then how long does each attack last, and is hearing affected? That pair names the peripheral causes.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Attack length and hearing name the cause: seconds = BPPV, 24 minutes to 24 hours with fluctuating low-frequency loss, tinnitus and fullness = Ménière's, days without hearing loss = vestibular neuronitis, with hearing loss = labyrinthitis. BPPV: Dix-Hallpike (latency, torsional, fatiguing nystagmus) to diagnose, particle repositioning to cure (80% after one). COWS: cold opposite, warm same (fast phase). Sound- or pressure-induced vertigo with autophony = superior canal dehiscence. Vestibular neuronitis: oral steroids within 72 hours, no antivirals. Aminoglycoside toxicity: stop the drug; the loss is usually permanent.

blocks.html: 1. Vestibular physiology

• The vestibular apparatus sits in the inner ear beside the cochlea, shares the vestibulocochlear nerve (cranial nerve VIII), and uses the same hair cells (mechanoreceptors): bending toward the tallest hair (the kinocilium) opens potassium channels and depolarizes the cell
  • Two kinds of sensor

rows: Linear movement and head position relative to gravity
Endolymph lags behind (inertia) and bends the cupula
Ear stones (otoconia) weigh down a gel membrane over the macula; tilt or straight-line movement slides it and bends the hairs
Three canals at right angles in each ear: one horizontal, two vertical-oblique · each paired with one on the other side
The two organs lie perpendicular to each other

blocks.html:
• Baseline firing (~100 action potentials a second) lets a hair cell signal both ways: bending toward it → more firing, away → less
  • Canals work in pairs (push-pull): turning right raises the right horizontal canal's firing and lowers the left · the brain reads the difference
  • So a problem in one ear reads as head rotation even when the head is still → vertigo, nystagmus, ataxia, nausea and vomiting
2. Nystagmus and the vestibular reflexes

• Vestibulo-ocular reflex: keeps the image still on the retina as the head moves · as few as 3 neurons, compensating within 10-15 ms, far faster than vision could
  • Nystagmus: rhythmic to-and-fro eye movement with a slow phase (the vestibular drift) and a quick phase (a reset saccade) · named by the fast phase

rows: Spontaneous vestibular: direction fixed, mostly horizontal, suppressed by visual fixation · positional · gaze-paretic · rebound · congenital · dissociated

blocks.html:
• Caloric test (lying down, so the horizontal canal is nearly vertical): water in the ear canal makes the endolymph flow
    • cold lowers firing, as if the head turned away → fast phase to the opposite side · warm raises it → fast phase to the same side: COWS = Cold Opposite, Warm Same
    • in an unconscious patient it tests the brainstem: the eyes should move together · only one eye moves = medial longitudinal fasciculus lesion (conjugate gaze lost) · no movement = low brainstem lesion

blocks.cap: Caloric test

blocks.html: 3. The dizzy patient

• Balance = inputs (vestibular · vision · proprioception; 2 of 3 are usually enough) → processing (central, cerebellum) → outputs (eye muscles, flexors and extensors)
  • History is the most important 80% of the workup · anxiety is often the cause or the effect · then exam, and imaging (CT, MRI)

rows: Hearing (cochlear) symptoms · vagal symptoms (nausea, vomiting, sweating, moving the bowels) · worse with head movement
Cardiac or neurological symptoms · loss of consciousness

Organic: presyncope and vasodepressor syncope, arrhythmia, orthostatic hypotension, hyperventilation, anemia, peripheral neuropathy, poor vision, musculoskeletal, drugs · psychiatric: depression, anxiety, panic disorder, phobic dizziness, somatization

blocks.html: 4. Timing × hearing: naming the cause
5. The peripheral vertigo syndromes

• BPPV (benign paroxysmal positional vertigo): the most common vestibular end-organ disorder
    • brief vertigo (10-30 s) set off by specific head movements (looking up, rolling over in bed) · motion sensitivity when severe · hearing normal
    • cause: idiopathic (degenerative) · head trauma (also iatrogenic; the commonest cause of bilateral BPPV) · mechanism: free-floating particles (otoconia from the utricle) in the posterior canal (canalithiasis); lateral canal variants, superior canal very rare
    • Dix-Hallpike: latency, then direction-specific torsional nystagmus (left ear clockwise, right counterclockwise), limited duration, reverses on sitting up, fatigues with repeats
    • particle repositioning (Epley or Semont): 80% cured after one session, 95% after three · persistent or atypical cases are rare · intractable → posterior canal occlusion
  • Ménière's disease: episodic vertigo, 24 min to 24 h · fluctuating, low-frequency sensorineural hearing loss · tinnitus · aural fullness
    • 2nd most common vestibular disorder (10% of dizzy-clinic visits) · 50-100 per 100,000 · both ears in 25-30%, usually within 5 years · familial < 10% · onset in the 5th, 6th or 4th decade
    • endolymphatic hydrops (less endolymph resorbed, more made) is its histological correlate, though not every hydropic ear has Ménière's · Ménière's syndrome = a secondary cause: syphilis, trauma, labyrinthitis
    • treatment ladder: ① everyone, for 3-6 months: low salt, no caffeine, chocolate, alcohol or tobacco · ② attacks: vestibular suppressant, diuretic, betahistine (Serc) · ③ failing: intratympanic steroids → pressure pulse therapy → intratympanic gentamicin · ④ last: vestibular neurectomy → labyrinthectomy
    • conservative management controls vertigo in 80% · intratympanic treatment has largely replaced surgery · ablative treatment does not "cure" the disease
  • Vestibular neuronitis / viral labyrinthitis: often after a cold · vertigo lasting days · nystagmus beating away from the affected ear · nausea and vomiting · labyrinthitis adds hearing loss and tinnitus
    • treatment: short-term antiemetics and vestibular sedatives · oral steroids if within 72 hours · no evidence for antivirals
  • Aminoglycoside toxicity: usually diagnosed "after the fact"
    • one ear (drops, injections): vertigo and nystagmus beating away from it · systemic: severe disequilibrium, motion sensitivity, oscillopsia
    • stop the aminoglycoside · usually permanent, with some partial recovery
  • Superior canal dehiscence: a third mobile window into the inner ear
    • vertigo and oscillopsia with loud sounds or changes in middle ear or intracranial pressure · hears bone-conducted sounds too loudly: own voice (autophony), footsteps, eye movements · conductive hearing loss with preserved acoustic reflexes
    • sound or pressure evokes vertical-torsional eye movements in the plane of the superior canal
    • audiometry + temporal bone CT · avoid triggers, or surgery
  • Vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma): a benign, slow nerve-sheath tumour of nerve VIII that does not typically cause vertigo: it presents with progressive one-sided sensorineural loss and tinnitus (see Hearing Loss)
