lectures.name: Integration of Medicine and Neurology
lectures.title: Integration of medicine and neurology
lectures.framing: The nervous system is often where a disease of another system shows itself. The lecture works four cases (cancer, breathlessness, nutrition, the heart), and each one asks the same two things: where is the lesion, and how did the illness get there?
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Acute, stepwise deficits in several territories = cardioembolic strokes until proven otherwise; look for endocarditis, take two sets of blood cultures and give no tPA. Wernicke triad: ataxia, ophthalmoplegia, confusion; refeeding without thiamine triggers it, so give thiamine before glucose. Dyspnea worse lying down with a normal heart and chest = bilateral phrenic nerve palsies. Checkpoint inhibitors cause myasthenia gravis and myositis: stop the drug and/or give steroids, with oncology. B6 harms by excess; copper deficiency after bariatric surgery mimics B12's cord damage.

blocks.html: 1. Cancer: how it reaches the nervous system

rows: Primary tumour or metastasis presses on a structure
Spinal cord → myelopathy · nerve root → radiculopathy · peripheral nerve → mononeuropathy
Tumour grows into the nerve, plexus, brain or spinal cord
Metastases to the central nervous system (commonly breast and lung)
The tumour induces an antibody-mediated effect on a non-tumour organ
Limbic encephalitis · dermatomyositis · myasthenia gravis · cerebellitis
Chemotherapy · radiation (immediate or delayed) · resective surgery
Chemotherapy neuropathy · radiation encephalopathy · post-mastectomy pain syndrome
The drug blocks PD-L1 (a brake tumours carry in large amounts), freeing T cells against the tumour and against self

blocks.html:
• Case 1: a man on ipilimumab and nivolumab for metastatic melanoma has 3 weeks of progressive ptosis, neck flexion and proximal weakness, a head drop and a Trendelenburg gait, with normal reflexes and sensation → lower motor neuron, junction or muscle
    • investigations (module): CK (muscle) · acetylcholine receptor antibody (junction) · EMG / nerve conduction studies to tell them apart
  • Management of checkpoint inhibitor autoimmunity: discuss with oncology stopping the inhibitor and/or starting steroids · steroids may reduce how well the tumour treatment works
2. Breathlessness: the neurological causes

• Causes of dyspnea: cardiac (heart failure, ischemia, outflow restriction) · pulmonary (obstructive, restrictive, infiltrative, shunting) · hematologic (anemia) · neurological
  • Neurological dyspnea = respiratory muscle weakness, approached like any other weakness, level by level

rows: Multilevel cervical radiculopathy (C3, 4, 5 keep the diaphragm alive)

blocks.html:
• Case 2: bilateral phrenic nerve palsies - dyspnea worse lying down (she sleeps in a recliner), with a normal heart, chest and neurological exam
    • lying down, the diaphragm does most of the work (it pushes the abdomen down) · upright, the intercostals do
    • investigations: chest X-ray · diaphragm fluoroscopy during inspiration and expiration · lung function seated vs supine · phrenic nerve conduction studies · imaging of the neck and mediastinum
3. Nutrition: deficiencies and excesses

rows: Wernicke's encephalopathy: classic triad of ataxia + ophthalmoplegia + encephalopathy (confusion) · beriberi = sensorimotor peripheral neuropathy · wet beriberi adds a cardiomyopathy
Refeeding without thiamine can trigger it · treatable with thiamine · preventable: give thiamine BEFORE glucose whenever nutrition is in doubt
Subacute combined degeneration: dorsal column dysfunction, peripheral neuropathy, encephalopathy
The deficiency classically tied to neurological symptoms
Impaired gastric absorption, e.g. after bariatric surgery
Electrolytes shift into cells: ↓ sodium, potassium, calcium, magnesium, phosphate → first encephalopathy (confusion, unsteadiness) → then muscle weakness → if severe seizures · arrhythmias
After prolonged starvation (e.g. anorexia), refeed very slowly and check electrolytes often

blocks.html: • Case 3: a 9-year-old eating almost nothing for weeks gets a nasogastric tube; within a day she has diplopia (both 6th nerves), confusion and severe ataxia → cannot be localized to one place: generalized dysfunction with strong pons involvement → Wernicke encephalopathy, triggered by refeeding
4. The heart: strokes in more than one territory

• Multifocal deficits: the time course decides
    • subacute and slowly progressive → multiple metastases or abscesses
    • acute and stepwise → multiple infarcts, and the causes are "cardioembolic stroke, cardioembolic stroke, cardioembolic stroke" · then cerebral vasculitis · multifocal tumours (metastases, lymphoma) · multiple abscesses · demyelination (multiple sclerosis, ADEM)
  • Causes of cardioembolic strokes: atrial fibrillation · infectious endocarditis · non-bacterial endocarditis (cancer-associated, Libman-Sacks) · cardiac tumours
  • Case 4: a 68-year-old with left arm numbness, then word-finding trouble two days later, a temperature of 37.9 and a heart rate of 108 → deficits in several territories (left frontal language, right occipital field, right hemisphere sensorimotor), arriving stepwise → cardioembolic strokes from endocarditis
    • look for endocarditis: murmur · splinter hemorrhages · Janeway lesions · Osler nodes · Roth spots
  • Stroke with suspected endocarditis
    • blood cultures × 2, and ask the lab to keep them for possible HACEK organisms (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella)
    • transthoracic ± transesophageal echo · look for the source of the bacteria (particularly dental)
    • cultures negative → strongly consider non-bacterial endocarditis from a malignancy
    • no clot-busting drug (tissue plasminogen activator, tPA): the lecture asks "would you give him tPA?" and manages him with cultures and echo instead

lectures.name: In-Class - Approach to Seizures
lectures.title: In-class: approach to seizures
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Seizure over syncope: unconscious for more than a minute, eyes turned to one side, side-of-tongue biting, and confusion lasting minutes to hours; a faint lasts under a minute with only brief confusion. Focal slowing or spikes on EEG mean MRI. Valproate is the worst teratogen; levetiracetam and lamotrigine are the safer choices, with folic acid. Never stop antiseizure drugs because of pregnancy. A posterior shoulder dislocation should make you think of a seizure.

blocks.html: A case session built on the first-seizure approach (see the Week 14 approach to seizures chart for the workup and when to treat). What it adds: telling a seizure from a faint, reading the EEG report, and choosing a drug for a young woman.
1. Seizure or syncope?

• Differential of a brief loss of consciousness: syncope (low brain perfusion, cardiac or blood pressure) · seizure · psychogenic · sudden raised intracranial pressure (acute hydrocephalus) · brainstem transient ischemic attack (rare)

rows: None, tonic or clonic · may be asymmetric
Confusion for minutes to hours · possible Todd's paresis

blocks.html: • Movements: clonic = shaking · tonic = stiff · myoclonic = jerks
2. History clues

• Earlier seizures → more likely a seizure
  • Aura · asymmetric onset · deficit afterwards → focal seizure
  • Triggers (sleep loss, drugs or medications, head injury, illness, fever) → provoked vs unprovoked
  • Adults rarely present with a first generalized seizure - they present with focal ones · first generalized seizures are common in children
  • Adult first seizure: electrolytes and CT head now, EEG and MRI as an outpatient (full workup in the Week 14 chart)
3. EEG and juvenile myoclonic epilepsy

• Focal slowing or focal spikes on the electroencephalogram (EEG) = a focal lesion → MRI is required to look for cortical dysplasia, mesial temporal sclerosis, tumour or old infarct
  • Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy: easily controlled - lifestyle (sleep, food, fluids) and low-dose drugs · a sleep-deprived EEG brings out the abnormality
4. Antiseizure drugs in young women

• Older antiseizure drugs weaken oral contraceptives → check interactions
  • Teratogens: always add folic acid · avoid the worst drugs in anyone who could become pregnant

rows: Valproate (highest malformation risk) · phenytoin · several drugs together

blocks.html: • ⚠ Do not stop antiseizure drugs for pregnancy: seizures risk fetal hypoxic injury, maternal status epilepticus and sudden unexpected death in epilepsy (SUDEP)
5. Complications of a seizure
• Posterior shoulder dislocation · injuries from falls · aspiration · status epilepticus (permanent brain injury) · SUDEP

weeks.label: Week 16 - The Dying Patient & the Autopsy

lectures.name: The Dying Patient and MAiD
lectures.title: The dying patient and medical assistance in dying (MAiD)
lectures.framing: Two questions run through the lecture: who decides when the patient cannot (capacity → substitute decision maker), and, when the patient can and asks to die, are they eligible for MAiD, and which stream's safeguards apply? Around both sits palliative care: comfort for the patient and support for the family.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Stream 2 (natural death not reasonably foreseeable) adds an expert assessor, a 90-day wait, and forbids the waiver of final consent. Capacity = understand + appreciate; it is decision-specific and can fluctuate, and the clinician offering the treatment assesses it. Advance care planning wishes are not consent; code status is not goals of care. The SDM order starts with a court guardian and a Power of Attorney for Personal Care, then spouse, child, parent, sibling. Turning the patient and symptom medications do not hasten death. A conscientious objector must still make an effective referral.

blocks.html: 1. Capacity and the substitute decision maker

• Capacity (Health Care Consent Act) has two parts
    • ① the ability to understand the information relevant to the decision
    • ② the ability to appreciate the reasonably foreseeable consequences of deciding (or not deciding)
    • not global: specific to the decision (may be capable about meals but not about treatment) · can fluctuate over time
  • Who assesses it: the health practitioner offering the treatment must determine capacity before treating (this can be delegated)
  • Substitute decision maker (SDM): gives or refuses consent for an incapable patient, taken in this order
    • ① court-ordered guardian of the person · ② attorney under a Power of Attorney for Personal Care (not the one for property) · ③ representative appointed by the Consent and Capacity Board
    • ④ spouse or partner · ⑤ child (16 or older) or parent with right of custody (or the Children's Aid Society) · ⑥ parent with right of access · ⑦ siblings · ⑧ any other relative · ⑨ the Public Guardian and Trustee
2. Code status, goals of care, advance care planning

rows: Which resuscitation (if any) to give if the heart stops or breathing stops
Needs informed consent from the patient or the SDM
Discussions that prepare for consent: who the patient is, how their values shape their goals, and how those fit the clinical picture and the treatments on offer
Code status is not the same as goals of care
Wishes voiced ahead of time to guide a future SDM
Wishes, not decisions: not "advance consent" (the future is speculation) · still prepares the person and the SDM

blocks.html: 3. Palliative care

• Definition (World Health Organization): an approach that improves quality of life for patients and families facing life-threatening illness, preventing and relieving suffering by early identification, assessment and treatment of pain and other problems, physical, psychosocial or spiritual
    • a team approach: practical needs · bereavement counselling · a support system so patients live as actively as possible until death
    • most people would prefer to die at home, so it must be available in the community
  • Symptom management: drug and non-drug measures for pain, respiratory distress, delirium, agitation, knowing their indications, adverse effects and complications
  • Tools
    • Palliative Performance Scale (version 2): disease burden and progress toward the end of life (the most used)
    • Edmonton Symptom Assessment System: screens for symptoms palliative care can manage
  • Routes in: the patient declines or stops treatment · the physician judges treatment futile or likely to cause suffering and suggests it · alongside active treatment for hard-to-control symptoms · after a severe irreversible disability
    • the classic exam example: a severe stroke whose best outcome is full dependence in a nursing home; if that is unacceptable to the patient, focus on comfort and start no tube feeding or intravenous fluids
4. Supporting the patient and family through dying

• Patient- and family-centred: dignity and respect for the patient, family and significant others · speak to the patient even if comatose · look after the family's needs (rest, self-care) · answer questions honestly
  • Uncertainty: outcomes fall on a spectrum; a family told to expect the worst may be angry when the patient does better ("you broke my heart for no reason")
  • Temporary improvement for hours to days after stopping feeds, medications or fluids is common: reassure, use the time together, re-evaluate only if it lasts many days
  • Moral distress when a family's choice clashes with your values: "it's not my journey" · trust the SDM or attorney to choose as the patient would · choose your own SDM and tell them what you would NOT want
  • Myths to answer
    • not starving to death: the organs shut down together, with no hunger or thirst · offer sips and tastes; the patient is in control
    • turning does not hasten death: it relieves pressure and gives staff a brief exam every 4 hours (mottling of the extremities → call the family) · symptom medications do not hasten death either
    • patients often die as they lived (alone, or once the family has gathered) · give the family permission to step away from the bedside
5. Medical assistance in dying (MAiD)

• Legal in Canada since June 2016 · revised in March 2021 into two streams: ① natural death reasonably foreseeable · ② natural death not reasonably foreseeable
  • Eligibility (all of)
    • eligible for publicly funded health services
    • 18 or older and mentally competent
    • a grievous and irremediable medical condition: a serious illness, disease or disability · an advanced state of decline that cannot be reversed · unbearable physical or mental suffering that cannot be relieved under conditions the patient considers acceptable
    • a voluntary request, not the result of outside pressure or influence
    • informed consent: diagnosis, available treatments and the options to relieve suffering, including palliative care
  • Safeguards (both streams): a written request witnessed by an independent witness (a second independent person may sign for a patient who cannot) · 2 independent physicians or nurse practitioners certify eligibility · consent again at the time of MAiD, unless a waiver of final consent was signed
    • the waiver is for a patient whose death is foreseeable and who is at risk of losing capacity
  • Stream 2 adds: one of the two assessors has expertise in the condition and has discussed all treatment options · a 90-day waiting period · no waiver of final consent
  • Practical points
    • most regions have a MAiD coordination service
    • where: home, long-term care bed or hospital · organ donation is still possible (then usually in hospital)
    • method: mostly intravenous, in series: a benzodiazepine → high-dose propofol → a neuromuscular blocker, infused over 10 min, death within 10 more · an oral lethal prescription is possible but rarely used
    • reporting: in Ontario, to the coroner's office
6. Conscientious objection

• A physician need not provide MAiD (College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario), but the patient keeps the right to access care, so an objecting physician must:
    • act in a way that respects dignity and does not impede access
    • tell the patient directly and sensitively that the reason is personal, not clinical
    • not abandon the patient: make a timely effective referral, so delay does not harm them

lectures.name: Autopsy Review
lectures.title: Autopsy review
lectures.framing: Two questions decide everything after a death: who has the authority (the coroner under the Coroner's Act, or the family through informed authorization), and what actually caused it, written as a chain of diseases, not as the way the body stopped.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ A medicolegal autopsy falls under the Coroner's Act, so the family cannot refuse it; a hospital autopsy needs informed authorization (estate trustee first, then spouse and adult children, parents, siblings), and the family may restrict it. Part I runs backwards: each line is caused by the one below it; Part II holds contributors outside the chain. Never write a mechanism ("cardiac arrest", "multisystem organ failure", "sepsis") as the cause. Sudden and unexpected deaths are signed by the coroner, expected natural ones by the doctor. A suspected genetic disease found at autopsy matters to living relatives.

blocks.alt: autopsy and cause of death overview.svg

blocks.html: 1. Two kinds of autopsy
• An autopsy (also necropsy, post-mortem examination) is done by a pathologist · the two kinds are not procedurally different; their focus and emphasis are

rows: May come from hospital (the majority do not)
Natural (family requests, genetics, education, research, quality assurance)
Falls under the jurisdiction of the Coroner's Act
Informed authorization from the estate trustee or next of kin
The Coroner's Act: the family does not authorize it

blocks.html: • When to contact the coroner (any one): family concerns about care · sudden, unexpected death (no clinical history of a potentially fatal illness) · any "unnatural" death (accident, suicide, homicide) · death on a psychiatry ward · maternal death · seizure disorder · Children's Aid Society involvement in a child's death
2. The hospital autopsy

• Informed authorization: has the appropriate person authorized it? In descending order
    • ① the deceased's estate trustee (no will, or not known: whoever is applying to the court to become trustee, if the family agrees; if they dispute it, go down this list)
    • ② spouse (married, or living together in a conjugal relationship for at least a year or as parents of a child) and adult children · ③ parents · ④ siblings · ⑤ any other next of kin who is mentally capable for the decision
  • The approach mirrors the physician-patient interaction: the same duties of consent, professionalism and confidentiality (the CanMEDS roles)
  • Organ retention and restrictions: some organs need further examination (most often the brain and heart) · the family may restrict the autopsy, typically to a limited internal exam or no organ retention
  • What it is for (its value)
    • diagnose disease · the accuracy of the clinical diagnosis, tests and imaging · unresolved clinical issues · the effects of treatment · the extent of disease
    • suspected genetic disease: findings that protect the health of living relatives
    • assuage grief · research · teaching · it informs the death certificate
  • Steps
    • ① clinical history: medical records, ambulance call report, verbal report from the clinician, pathology consultation form
    • ② external exam: nutrition and development, hair, tattoos, scars, all body surfaces, disease, congenital anomalies, injuries, resuscitation
    • ③ internal exam: Y-shaped incision, organs removed as a block, weighed and examined · scalp retracted, calvarium sawn, brain removed · special dissections → a provisional anatomical diagnosis (gross findings ± pending tests)
      • not routinely examined unless indicated: eyes · bowel lumen · limb bones · joints · tendons · back of the neck · back and limb muscles · spinal cord · pelvic and shoulder girdles · parathyroids · middle and inner ear
    • ④ additional tests and consultations (histology, genetics, blood)
    • ⑤ opinion: an integration of everything, read in the context of the case · findings rarely stand alone (the misconception: "all is revealed when one opens the body")
3. The death certificate

• A permanent record of what natural disease, injury, event or combination led to the death · used for statistics (International Classification of Diseases coding uses the underlying cause), surveillance, public health and research funding, and as a legal document (proof of death, family, insurance)
  • Certifies identification · cause of death · manner of death · asks about an autopsy · not used for stillbirths
  • Who signs: sudden and unexpected → coroner or medical examiner · expected natural → doctor or certain nurses
4. Cause of death: the WHO format

• Cause of death = the disease and/or injury that ends life · stated by the WHO method, the common-sense causal chain
  • Part I: the sequence of events, working backwards from the final condition - each condition causes the one above it: (a) immediate ← (b) intermediate ← (c) underlying
  • Part II: other significant conditions that contributed but are not in the chain (often risk factors)
  • Causal chain = cause of death statement · initiating event = manner of death

• Be specific
    • infection: the disease and/or organism, and the site (COVID-19 pneumonia · Haemophilus influenzae meningoencephalitis)
    • cancer: site of origin, metastatic site and type (pulmonary metastasis of colonic adenocarcinoma)
  • Leave out the mechanism of death (the physiological or biochemical process by which death came about): it only attests to the fact of death and adds nothing about the cause - cardiac arrest · arrhythmia · exsanguination · respiratory arrest · multisystem organ failure · sepsis
